會試錄序

仰惟皇上籲俊尊帝，以閎嘉靖無疆之鴻庥，盖七舉會試于兹矣。惟兹甲辰春，復當試期，士之就試于禮部者凡四千有竒。尚書臣璧、侍郎臣承恩、臣成名以考試官請，上命臣汝璧主試事。而同考則修撰臣瓚、臣坤，編修臣山、臣喚、臣鳳、臣煒、臣一鳳、臣份，檢討臣庭機、臣維楨、臣緒，都給事中臣勲、臣寀，給事中臣棐，署
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Metropolitan Examination

We reverently reflect that His Majesty summons men of outstanding talent and honors the Supreme Deity, thereby extending the boundless blessings of the Jiajing reign. By now, the Metropolitan Examination has been held seven times. In the spring of this jiachen year [1544], the examination season came round again, and more than four thousand scholars presented themselves for examination at the Ministry of Rites. The Minister, your servant Bi, and the Vice Ministers, your servants Cheng’en and Chengming, requested the appointment of Examiners. His Majesty commanded me, your servant Rubi, to preside over the examination.

The Associate Examiners were the Senior Compilers, your servants Zan and Kun; the Junior Compilers, your servants Shan, Huan, Feng, Wei, Yifeng, and Fen; the Examining Editors, your servants Tingji, Weizhen, and Xu; the Chief Supervising Secretaries, your servants Xun and Cai; the Supervising Secretary, your servant Fei; and the acting …

臣惟承乏，仰廑簡命，蓋有餘榮矣。顧茲重典，臣以綿力眇焉而勝之，又不能以無懼。夫懼則思奮，榮則思報，二者交激於其中，則臣之所以競職者，固宜百倍於恒矣。臣於是齋瀹洗心，矢公矢慎，率同事者執競以共事。事竣，得儁者三百二十人，遵制裁也。故事有錄，錄中式者氏名及文之優者，以
translation_en:
…acting Bureau Directors, your servants Wenhua and Gu, and acting Vice Director, your servant Jie. Supervising the examination were the Investigating Censors, your servants Heng and Yue. Together with the various personnel serving within and outside the examination compound, all were selected and assembled.
I, your servant, reflect that, merely filling a vacancy for want of someone better, I have received Your Majesty’s gracious attention in being selected and appointed—an honor beyond my deserts. Yet, considering this weighty undertaking, I could not but feel apprehension at bearing its responsibilities with my meager abilities. Apprehension prompts me to exert myself; honor prompts me to repay your favor. With these two impulses stirring one another within me, my diligence in fulfilling my duties should surely be a hundredfold greater than usual. I therefore purified myself and cleansed my heart, vowing impartiality and care, and led my colleagues in striving diligently to perform our shared task. When the work was completed, 320 outstanding candidates had been selected, in accordance with the quota fixed by imperial decree. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
獻以傳之天下臣謹拜手稽首
序諸首簡臣聞取士之法莫
備於周而我
明之監古定制也亦惟周是取
若今會試則周司馬辨論官
材之法也或謂古之辨材以
德行道藝而今也徒以文疑
未足以得材臣則曰文也者
材之華也德行道藝也者材
之本也未有本殖而華弗盛
者其本既撥固未見其能華
也矧茲俊材其生也天之所
篤培也其出也人之所利見
也於是乎秉吾公致吾慎操

translation_en: …to present to the throne and circulate throughout the realm. Your servant reverently bows with clasped hands and touches his forehead to the ground, placing this preface at the beginning of the record. Your servant has heard that no system for selecting scholars was more comprehensive than that of the Zhou. Our Ming dynasty, in consulting antiquity to establish its institutions, likewise took the Zhou as its model. The present Metropolitan Examination corresponds to the Zhou Minister of War’s method of distinguishing and assessing men’s fitness for office. Some say that in antiquity talent was assessed through moral character, conduct, learning in the Way, and cultivated skills, whereas today assessment rests solely on writing; they doubt whether this suffices to obtain talented men. Your servant, however, says: writing is the blossom of talent; moral character, conduct, learning in the Way, and cultivated skills are its root. Never have well-established roots failed to produce flourishing blossoms; once the roots have been uprooted, surely no one has seen them capable of flowering. Moreover, these outstanding talents are nurtured generously by Heaven from birth, and their emergence benefits those who behold them. Thus, maintaining my impartiality, exercising my utmost care, and taking hold of…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
吾繩尺以掄之則誠動神應
將弗得真材以副
上之求邪是故今日之役臣惟即
諸士所試之文而究觀乎其
材則見其魁竒而瓌特者可
以觀志也其敦龐而博大者
可以觀器也其精明而瑩澈
===

確者可以觀節也蓋其需世
利用之具莫不粲然畢陳而
惟臣之所錄其諸弗材與雖

曰是亦可藉手以獻于

punctuated: 吾繩尺以掄之，則誠動神應，將弗得真材以副上之求邪？是故今日之役，臣惟即諸士所試之文而究觀乎其材，則見其魁竒而瓌特者，可以觀志也；其敦龐而博大者，可以觀器也；其精明而瑩澈者，可以觀識也；其剛毅而果確者，可以觀節也。蓋其需世利用之具，莫不粲然畢陳，而惟臣之所錄。其諸弗材與雖材而弗中繩尺者，則既弗錄矣。臣之懼於是乎少釋，且幸曰：「是亦可藉手以獻于
translation_en: …my measuring standards to select them, then sincerity will stir a divine response: could we fail to obtain true talent to meet His Majesty’s wishes? Thus, in undertaking today’s duty, your servant has closely examined the candidates’ abilities through the essays they wrote in the examination. In those whose writing is outstanding and exceptional, one can discern their aspirations; in those whose writing is substantial and expansive, their capacity; in those whose writing is lucid and clear, their discernment; and in those whose writing is firm and resolute, their integrity. Indeed, the qualities that equip them to meet the world’s needs and serve practical ends are all brilliantly displayed, awaiting only your servant’s selection. Those who lack talent, and those who possess talent but fail to meet the standards, have already been excluded. Your servant’s apprehension is thereby somewhat relieved, and he rejoices, saying: “With these, I too have something to present to…”

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
上矣於戲材之盛也如此果何繇
而致哉誠以人材之於氣運
每相須而成是故唐虞之帝
也則有若禹稷皐陶爲帝佐
材殷周之王也則有若伊傅
周召爲王佐材盖天地之元
精聖神之功化以萃則翕以
渙則孚其幾有固然者自漢
以還則寢以微矣惟我
皇上神聖天縱應運而興
明倫盡制以立人極盖已上遡
古帝王之道而統承之矣間
復
敷之箴訓以廸文教則又舉

punctuated: 上矣。於戲！材之盛也如此，果何繇而致哉？誠以人材之於氣運，每相須而成。是故唐虞之帝也，則有若禹、稷、皐陶爲帝佐材；殷周之王也，則有若伊、傅、周、召爲王佐材。盖天地之元精、聖神之功化，以萃則翕，以渙則孚，其幾有固然者。自漢以還，則寢以微矣。惟我皇上，神聖天縱，應運而興，明倫盡制，以立人極，盖已上遡古帝王之道而統承之矣。間復敷之箴訓，以廸文教，則又舉
translation_en:
…to His Majesty. Ah! How has such an abundance of talent indeed been brought about? Truly, human talent and the movement of cosmic forces always depend upon one another for their fulfillment. Thus, the emperors of Tang and Yu had men such as Yu, Ji, and Gao Yao, talented enough to assist emperors; the kings of Yin and Zhou had men such as Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao, talented enough to assist kings. The primal essence of Heaven and Earth and the transforming achievements of sages and divine rulers bring harmony when gathered together and inspire trust when spread abroad. Their workings possess an inherent regularity. From the Han onward, however, these gradually declined.

Our Emperor alone, endowed by Heaven with divine sagacity, arose in response to the movement of cosmic forces. By clarifying human relationships and fully establishing institutions, he set the ultimate standard for humanity. He has indeed traced the Way of the ancient emperors and kings back to its source and inherited its succession. From time to time he has also promulgated admonitions and instructions to advance literary and moral education, and has further taken up…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
祖宗
列聖豐芑之仁益篤而厚之易稱
久而化成茲惟時哉是以元
精之翕萃
神化之渙孚見於邃古者復再
見於
今日而發之乎人材若是其盛
===
也固宜雖然材之盛也以文
見而其所以盛之者匪徒文
也誠也誠則德行道藝之謂
也誠與材合斯可語真材是
故高明博厚本於純一參賛
位育存於中和此立誠之訓
也而古帝王之佐之材寔以

punctuated: 祖宗列聖豐芑之仁，益篤而厚之。《易》稱「久而化成」，茲惟時哉！是以元精之翕萃、神化之渙孚，見於邃古者，復再見於今日，而發之乎人材，若是其盛也，固宜。雖然，材之盛也，以文見，而其所以盛之者，匪徒文也，誠也。誠則德行道藝之謂也。誠與材合，斯可語真材。是故高明博厚，本於純一；參賛位育，存於中和。此立誠之訓也，而古帝王之佐之材，寔以
translation_en:
…the benevolence of the founding ancestors and successive sage emperors in nurturing future generations, strengthening and deepening it still further. The Book of Changes says, “Through endurance, transformation is accomplished.” Surely this is that very moment! Thus the gathering of primordial essence and the far-reaching influence of spirit-like transformation, witnessed in remote antiquity, are once again manifest today. That these should find expression in such an abundance of talented men is only fitting.

Yet although this abundance of talent is revealed through literary composition, what makes it abundant is not merely literary accomplishment: it is sincerity. Sincerity here means virtuous conduct, mastery of the Way, and cultivated skills. Only when sincerity and ability unite can we speak of true talent. Thus loftiness and brilliance, breadth and depth, are rooted in purity and singleness of purpose; assisting Heaven and Earth in establishing their proper places and nurturing all things depends upon equilibrium and harmony. This is the teaching of establishing sincerity, and the talents of those who assisted the ancient sage kings and emperors were indeed grounded in…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
之今臣等之掄材也亦姑即
其文叩其所謂志節器識之
可進於是者而取之而其竟
進與否則有用材者操其繩
尺以擬諸其後也然則諸士
之與茲選也可榮也不亦可
懼乎哉諸士而善用其懼則
===
將進而追古名佐致吾
皇於二帝三王之上而臣益有餘
榮否則即材也猶夫選也而
臣之為懼焉者亦終能釋乎
哉爰是忠告為諸士勸惟諸
士其懋諸
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼

可進於是者而取之而其竟

將進而追古名佐致吾
皇於二帝三王之上而〔臣〕益有餘
榮否則即材也猶夫選也而
〔臣〕之爲懼焉者亦終能釋乎
哉爰是忠告爲諸士勸惟諸
士其懋諸
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼
punctuated:
之。今臣等之掄材也，亦姑即其文，叩其所謂志節器識之可進於是者而取之。而其竟進與否，則有用材者操其繩尺，以擬諸其後也。然則諸士之與茲選也，可榮也，不亦可懼乎哉？諸士而善用其懼，則將進而追古名佐，致吾皇於二帝三王之上，而臣益有餘榮。否則，即材也，猶夫選也，而臣之為懼焉者，亦終能釋乎哉？爰是忠告，為諸士勸。惟諸士其懋諸！
奉議大夫、左春坊左庶子兼
translation_en:
…this. Now, in selecting talent, we your servants provisionally examine the candidates’ writings, probing what they reveal of resolve, integrity, capacity, and discernment that might advance toward this ideal, and select them accordingly. Whether they ultimately make such progress rests with those who employ talent, who will apply their standards to assess them hereafter. Thus, for these gentlemen to be included in this selection is an honor—but is it not also cause for apprehension? If they make good use of that apprehension, they will advance to emulate the renowned ministers of antiquity and raise our Emperor above the Two Emperors and Three Kings; then I, your servant, shall enjoy still greater honor. Otherwise, even if they possess talent and remain among those selected, can the apprehension I feel for them ever finally be dispelled? I therefore offer this loyal counsel to encourage these gentlemen. May they exert themselves!
Grand Master for Court Discussion, Left Vice Supervisor of Instruction in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently serving as…

translation_en:
Metropolitan Examination of the Twenty-third Year of Jiajing (1544).

Officials in Charge of the Examination:
Zhang Bi, Grand Master for Assisting in Governance, Minister of Rites, and concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Chongxiang; he was from Shishou County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).
Sun Cheng’en, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel, Right Vice Minister of Rites, concurrently Household Administrator of the Heir Apparent, and Academician Reader-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhenfu; he was from Huating County in the directly administered metropolitan region and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Examiner:
Jiang Rubi, Grand Master for Court Discussion, Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Maogu; he was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

Associate Examiners:
Mao Zan, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Scholarly Excellence. His courtesy name was Bangxian; he was from Qiantang County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuxu year (1538).
Shen Kun, Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Undertaking Service. His courtesy name was Bozai; he was from Dahe Guard in the directly administered metropolitan region and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).
Wu Shan, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Literary Excellence. His courtesy name was Yuejing; he was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).
Ouyang Huan, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Literary Excellence. His courtesy name was Xuezhang; he was from Wuqiang County in the directly administered metropolitan region and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).
Peng Feng, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Literary Excellence. His courtesy name was Qizhi; he was from Fenyi County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).
Yuan Wei, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Rendering Service. His courtesy name was Maozhong; he was from Cixi County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the wuxu year (1538).
Xing Yifeng, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Rendering Service. His courtesy name was Boyu; he was registered with Longjiang Left Guard in Nanjing, was a native of Xiangfu County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).
Dong Fen, Junior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Yongjun; he was from Wucheng County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinchou year (1541).
Lin Tingji, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service. His courtesy name was Liren; he was from Min County, Fujian, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).
Wang Weizhen, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service. His courtesy name was Yunning; he was from Huazhou, Shaanxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).
Zhang Xu, Examining Editor of the Hanlin Academy, with the rank of Gentleman for Attendant Service. His courtesy name was Qingli; he was from Xiajiang County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the yiwei year (1535).

translation_en:
Lu Xun, courtesy name Ruli, was Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Personnel, with the prestige title Gentleman for Serving. He was from Jinyun County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in 1532.

Zhou Cai, courtesy name Ziliang, was Chief Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Rites, with the prestige title Gentleman for Rendering Service. He was from Ningxiang County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1532.

Chen Fei, courtesy name Ruzhong, was Supervising Secretary of the Office of Scrutiny for Rites, with the prestige title Gentleman for Service. He was from Yanling County, Henan, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1535.

Zhao Wenhua, courtesy name Yuanshi, was Vice Director acting as Director of the Jiangxi Bureau of the Ministry of Justice. He was from Cixi County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1529.

Xu Gu, courtesy name Zhongyi, was Secretary acting as Director of the Bureau of Personnel Appointments in the Ministry of Personnel. He was registered in Wan County, Yingtian Prefecture [?], and was a native of Houguan County, Fujian. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1535.

Gao Jie, courtesy name Gongcheng, was Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Shaanxi Bureau of the Ministry of Justice. He was from Mianzhou, Sichuan, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1532.

Examination Monitoring Officials:

Wang Heng, courtesy name Jiefu, was Investigating Censor for the Henan Circuit, with the prestige title Gentleman for Serving. He was from Jiaohe County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1532.

Shen Yue, courtesy name Zhongfu, was Investigating Censor for the Shandong Circuit, with the prestige title Gentleman for Serving. He was registered with the Nanjing Embroidered-uniform Guard and was a native of Jiangning County, Yingtian Prefecture. He became a metropolitan graduate in 1532.

Proctors:

Wan Shihe, courtesy name Sijie, was Secretary in the Bureau of Ceremonies of the Ministry of Rites. He was from Yixing County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1541.

Qian Xuan, courtesy name Maoxiao, was Secretary in the Bureau of Sacrifices of the Ministry of Rites. He was from Haiyan County, Zhejiang, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1535.

Officials Responsible for Printing Examination Papers:

Wang Ji, courtesy name Weiyi, was Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies of the Ministry of Rites, with the prestige title Grand Master for Counsel. He was from Jinxian County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1535.

Zhang Fu, courtesy name Yuanci, was Secretary acting as Vice Director of the Bureau of Ceremonies of the Ministry of Rites, with the prestige title Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. He was from Guan County, Shandong, and became a metropolitan graduate in 1529.

Officials Responsible for Collecting and Safekeeping Examination Scripts:

Xie Dou, courtesy name Wenzhong, was a Secretariat Drafter, with the prestige title Gentleman for Service. He was from Yuyao County, Zhejiang, and was a student admitted by virtue of an official's status.

Jiang Mingfeng, courtesy name Yingshao, was Judicial Supervisor in the Left Section of the Court of Judicial Review [the transcription repeats “Left Section” [?]], with the prestige title Gentleman for Receiving Virtue. He was from Rui'an County, Zhejiang, and was a “cultivated talent” (xiucai) of the Hanlin Academy [?].

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰事君敬其事而後其食
詩曰不顯惟德百辟其刑之是故君子篤
恭而天下平詩云予懷明德不大聲以
色子曰聲色之於以化民末也詩曰德
輶如毛毛猶有倫上天之載無聲無臭
至矣
使禹治之禹掘地而注之海驅蛇龍而放
===
之葅水由地中行江淮河漢是也險阻
既遠鳥獸之害人者消然後人得平土
而居之
易
同人柔得位得中而應乎乾曰同人
澤上有水節君子以制數度議德行
子曰書不盡言言不盡意然則聖人之意
其不可見乎子曰聖人立象以盡意設
卦以盡情偽繫辭焉以盡其言

第壹場

四書

子曰：「事君，敬其事而後其食。」

詩曰：「不顯惟德，百辟其刑之。」是故君子篤恭而天下平。詩云：「予懷明德，不大聲以色。」子曰：「聲色之於以化民，末也。」詩曰：「德輶如毛。」毛猶有倫。「上天之載，無聲無臭。」至矣！

使禹治之。禹掘地而注之海，驅蛇龍而放之葅，水由地中行，江淮河漢是也。險阻既遠，鳥獸之害人者消，然後人得平土而居之。

易

同人，柔得位得中，而應乎乾，曰同人。

澤上有水，節。君子以制數度，議德行。

子曰：「書不盡言，言不盡意。」然則聖人之意，其不可見乎？子曰：「聖人立象以盡意，設卦以盡情偽，繫辭焉以盡其言。
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said: “In serving a ruler, attend reverently to your duties and put your remuneration afterward.”

The Book of Poetry says: “How illustrious is virtue! The many lords take it as their model.” Thus the gentleman, through wholehearted reverence, brings peace to all under Heaven. The Book of Poetry says: “I cherish luminous virtue, without loud voice or imposing countenance.” The Master said: “Voice and countenance are the least of the means for transforming the people.” The Book of Poetry says: “Virtue is light as a hair.” Yet a hair still has something with which it can be compared. “The workings of Heaven above have neither sound nor smell.” This is the utmost!

He charged Yu with bringing it under control. Yu dug channels through the earth and directed the waters into the sea; he drove away snakes and dragons, banishing them to the marshes [?]. The waters flowed through channels in the land: these were the Yangzi, Huai, Yellow, and Han rivers. Once dangers and obstructions had been removed and the birds and beasts that harmed people had disappeared, people could inhabit the level ground.

Book of Changes

Fellowship with Others: the yielding line obtains its proper position and the central place, and responds to Qian; hence the name Fellowship with Others.

Above the lake there is water: Limitation. The gentleman accordingly establishes numerical limits and measures, and deliberates upon virtue and conduct.

The Master said: “Writing does not fully convey speech; speech does not fully convey meaning.” Does this mean, then, that the sages’ meaning cannot be perceived? The Master said: “The sages established images to convey their meaning fully, set out the hexagrams to represent fully what is genuine and what is false, and appended statements to convey their words fully…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
乾以君之坤以藏之
書
帝曰臣作朕股肱耳目予欲左右有民汝
翼予欲宣力四方汝為予欲觀古人之
象日月星辰山龍華蟲作會宗彝藻火
粉米黼黻絺繡以五采彰施于五色作
服汝明予欲聞六律五聲八音在治忽
以出納五言汝聽
終始惟一時乃日新
===
會其有極歸其有極曰皇極之敷言是彛
是訓于帝其訓凡厥庶民極之敷言是
訓是行以近天子之光曰天子作民父
母以為天下王
公其以予萬億年敬天之休拜手稽首誨
言
詩
如金如錫如圭如璧
彼有不獲穉此有不斂穧彼有遺秉此有

書
帝曰：「臣作朕股肱耳目。予欲左右有民，汝翼；予欲宣力四方，汝為；予欲觀古人之象，日月星辰、山龍華蟲作會，宗彝藻火、粉米黼黻絺繡，以五采彰施于五色作服，汝明；予欲聞六律五聲八音，在治忽，以出納五言，汝聽。」
終始惟一，時乃日新。
會其有極，歸其有極。曰：「皇極之敷言，是彛是訓，于帝其訓。」凡厥庶民，極之敷言，是訓是行，以近天子之光。曰：「天子作民父母，以為天下王。」
公其以予萬億年敬天之休！拜手稽首，誨言。

詩
如金如錫，如圭如璧。
彼有不獲穉，此有不斂穧；彼有遺秉，此有
translation_en:
… Qian presides over them, and Kun stores them.

Book of Documents
The Emperor said: “My ministers serve as my limbs, ears, and eyes. When I wish to assist the people, you must support me; when I wish to extend my efforts throughout the four quarters, you must act. I wish to see the emblematic figures of the ancients: the sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, and pheasants depicted in painting; and ancestral sacrificial vessels, waterweed, fire, grains of rice, axe patterns, and paired bow-shaped patterns worked in fine embroidery. Apply the five colors distinctly to make ceremonial robes: you must see to this clearly. I wish to hear the six pitch standards, the five notes, and the eight kinds of instrumental sound, to discern whether government is orderly or negligent, and thereby to receive and promulgate words set to the five notes: you must listen.”
Remain constant from beginning to end; thus you will renew yourself daily.
Gather toward the supreme standard; return to the supreme standard. It is said: “The promulgated words of the august standard are enduring norms and instructions; they are instructions from the Supreme Lord.” Let all the common people take the promulgated words of the standard as their instruction and put them into practice, thereby drawing near to the radiance of the Son of Heaven. They will say: “The Son of Heaven acts as father and mother to the people, and thus becomes king of all under Heaven.”
May you, Duke, help me reverently receive Heaven’s favor for countless years! With clasped hands I bow and touch my forehead to the ground in acknowledgment of your admonitory words.

Book of Odes
Like gold, like tin; like a jade tablet, like a jade disk.
There is late-ripening grain left unharvested there; here is cut grain left ungathered. There are sheaves left behind there; here there are …

自彼成康，奄有四方，斤斤其明。
春秋
九月丁卯，子同生。桓公六年。吳子使札来聘。襄公二十有九年。
秋，公會衛侯于桃丘，弗遇。冬，十有二月丙午，齊侯、衛侯、鄭伯来戰于郎。桓公十年。春，正月，齊人、衛人、鄭人盟于惡曹。桓公十有一年。
冬，楚人伐黃。僖公十有一年。
宋公伐邾。昭公十有九年。楚子、陳侯、隨侯、許男圍蔡。哀公元年。
禮記
是故聖人南面而立，而天下大治。
夫歌者，直己而陳德也。動己而天地應焉，四時和焉，星辰理焉，萬物育焉。
translation_en:
…ears of grain left ungathered.

Admirable is the noble lord; illustrious is his fine virtue. He treats the common people and the officials fittingly and receives blessings from Heaven. Heaven protects and assists him, grants him its mandate, and renews it.

From the time of those kings Cheng and Kang, they possessed all the four quarters; keen was their discernment.

Spring and Autumn Annals

In the ninth month, on the dingmao day, the son Tong was born. Sixth year of Duke Huan.
The Viscount of Wu sent Zha on a diplomatic visit. Twenty-ninth year of Duke Xiang.

In autumn, the duke went to meet the Marquis of Wei at Taoqiu, but did not meet him. In winter, in the twelfth month, on the bingwu day, the Marquis of Qi, the Marquis of Wei, and the Earl of Zheng came to fight at Lang. Tenth year of Duke Huan.
In spring, in the first month, men of Qi, Wei, and Zheng made a covenant at Ecao. Eleventh year of Duke Huan.

In winter, men of Chu attacked Huang. Eleventh year of Duke Xi.

The Duke of Song attacked Zhu. Nineteenth year of Duke Zhao.
The Viscount of Chu, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Sui, and the Baron of Xu besieged Cai. First year of Duke Ai.

Book of Rites

Thus the sage stands facing south, and all under Heaven is brought into excellent order.

Singing is a means of setting oneself upright and expressing virtue. When one stirs oneself, Heaven and Earth respond; the four seasons are harmonious, the stars follow their proper courses, and the myriad things are nourished.

第五道
問：自唐虞授受，開萬世心學之原，爰及三代，典則詒謀，相守一道。至秦漢以降，則代有不同，其于古心學亦皆有得否邪？我成祖文皇帝編輯《聖學心法》一書，又親為之序，乃有取於唐之《帝範》，何歟？且人倫有五，但言君臣父子而不及其餘，有專言者，有統言者，其說可得聞乎？抑不知于我太祖高皇帝所著《祖訓》《精誠錄》及今上皇帝御製《敬一箴》，同乎否邪？皇太子正位東宮有年矣，他日岐嶷大成，出閤講學，其亦可以此書進讀，用少裨作聖之功乎？願敬陳之，將以轉聞於上。
問：內修外攘，帝王經綸之大業也。稽古者
translation_en:
Fifth Question
Question: The transmission of rulership from Yao to Shun opened the source of the learning of the mind for all ages. Through the Three Dynasties, their enduring standards and plans bequeathed to posterity upheld a single Way. From the Qin and Han onward, however, each dynasty differed. Did they all nevertheless attain some understanding of the ancient learning of the mind?
Our Emperor Wen, Chengzu, compiled the book Essential Methods of the Learning of the Sages (Shengxue xinfa) and personally wrote its preface. Why did he draw upon the Tang work Models for Emperors (Difan)? Furthermore, there are five human relationships, yet the book discusses only ruler and minister, father and son, without treating the others. Some statements address particular matters, while others speak comprehensively: may we hear an explanation of this? We would also ask whether it accords with the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun) and Record of Utmost Sincerity (Jingcheng lu), written by our Emperor Gao, Taizu, and the Admonition on Reverent Unity (Jingyi zhen), composed by His Majesty the reigning emperor.
The Imperial Heir Apparent has occupied his proper position in the Eastern Palace for some years. When, in days to come, his precocious intelligence reaches full maturity and he leaves the inner palace to receive instruction, might this book also be presented for his study, contributing in some small measure to his attainment of sagehood? We ask that you respectfully set forth your views, which will be conveyed to His Majesty.

translation_en:
… invariably praise the fully established Zhou dynasty. The workings of its government—such matters as enfeoffment, the well-field system, schools, and military forces—are recorded in considerable detail in the Rites of Zhou. Yet earlier Confucian scholars repeatedly praised it chiefly through the poems up to and including “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao), concerning governance within, and those from “Gathering Bracken” (Caiwei) onward, concerning governance without. Why is this? Some say that these undertakings were rooted in sincerity of intention; others say that they began in anxious concern and diligent effort. Were these truly two distinct ways? Or did what they called ritual alone lack these qualities? From the Han onward, the reasons can be discussed; concerning the Song, earlier Confucian scholars frequently left judgments. Did they truly understand what they were discussing?

Our sagely founder inaugurated the dynasty, and Chengzu succeeded to the imperial throne. Their brilliant glory and great achievements assuredly bequeathed peace for ten thousand generations. Successive sage emperors continued this excellence, sustaining its flourishing greatness without decline. Now our reigning Emperor, through his divine achievements and sagely virtue, has further exalted and magnified this inheritance, already surpassing the Zhou and rising to the flourishing heights of Tang and Yu, the ages of Yao and Shun. We wonder whether you gentlemen, in your sincerity in offering humble gifts of celery and sunlight, have even one suggestion in ten thousand to present. Please discuss this fully; those charged with conducting this examination wish to hear it.

The distinction between gentlemen and petty men is as clear as that between fragrant and foul-smelling plants; it requires no explanation. Yet gentlemen, too, differ among themselves. text:

士大夫其握沐吐哺之義否邪薦士公
也或多所汲引其子不用或我薦彼攻
益見忠直其舉親舉讎之義否邪察吏
治者或曰昆虫草木皆欲得所柰何錮

不同此其言孰當集衆思者或榜客位

punctuated:
賢，禮也。或不求識面臺官，或請還第見士大夫，其握沐吐哺之義否邪？薦士，公也。或多所汲引，其子不用；或我薦彼攻，益見忠直，其舉親舉讎之義否邪？察吏治者，或曰：「昆虫草木皆欲得所，柰何錮人于聖世？」或者不然，謂一家一路所繫不同，此其言孰當？集衆思者，或榜客位，以奏牘聞朝廷，書狀規過失；或者不然，謂無補於國，惟所陳利害，一切報罷，此其事孰優？任官一也，何却例簿與上百官圖之殊見？事君一也，何起布衣侍講甚莊與耆舊侍對甚恭之異禮？夫尚友論世，天下士也，即當其任，其曷依歸焉？
問：六籍之闕也久矣，而禮為甚。禮有三：《周禮》，其綱也；《儀禮》，其經也；《禮記》，其傳也。粵自漢興，訪求遺書，《周禮》五官出，而冬官逸；《儀禮》十七篇出，而朝覲、會同、郊饗等禮逸；《禮記》雜出於漢儒，而或為八十五
translation_en:
…receiving worthy men accords with ritual propriety. Yet one man did not seek even to make the acquaintance of officials of the Censorate, while another requested permission to return to his residence to receive scholar-officials. Do these actions accord with the principle exemplified by grasping one’s wet hair and spitting out one’s food to receive visitors? Recommending men for office calls for impartiality. One man advanced many others, yet his own son was not employed; another recommended a man who then attacked him, thereby displaying still greater loyalty and uprightness. Do these actions accord with the principle of recommending both relatives and enemies? Among those assessing local administration, one said: “Even insects, plants, and trees should all find their proper place. How can we bar a man from office in this sage age?” Another disagreed, saying that the interests of a single household and those of an entire circuit were different. Whose words were more fitting? Among those who sought to gather the thoughts of many, one posted a notice in the visitors’ quarters inviting written submissions to inform the court and point out faults; another disagreed, saying that this brought no benefit to the state, and rejected all the submissions concerning advantages and disadvantages. Whose conduct was superior? Appointment to office was their common concern: why, then, did one reject the register of precedents while another submit a chart of the officials? Serving the ruler was likewise their common concern: why, then, the difference in ceremonial demeanor between one who rose from commoner status and was very dignified when lecturing in attendance, and another who, as a venerable elder, was very deferential when answering in attendance? You gentlemen of the realm seek friendship with the worthy of antiquity and judge them in the context of their times. If you yourselves were entrusted with these responsibilities, what would you take as your guide?
Question: The Six Classics have long been incomplete, and the ritual texts especially so. There are three ritual works: the Rites of Zhou (Zhou li) provides the framework; the Ceremonies and Rites (Yi li), the canonical prescriptions; and the Record of Rites (Li ji), the commentary. From the rise of the Han, searches were made for surviving books. Five offices of the Rites of Zhou were recovered, but the Winter Office was lost. Seventeen chapters of the Ceremonies and Rites were recovered, but the rites for court audiences, assemblies and meetings, suburban sacrifices, sacrificial feasts, and the like were lost. The Record of Rites emerged piecemeal from the Han Confucian scholars, and in one version comprised eighty-five…

數而言歟迨至胡元為患極矣我

篇，或為四十九篇，其離合異同之故，可考而知歟？抑不知出於何代，獻於何人，而其人之傳之也何自？豈秦燼頗未之及歟？昔之讀《周禮》者，往往疑信相半；《儀禮》則昔賢亦苦其難讀，謂於今誠無所用。此其人之意見，何不同如是歟？然而《復古》《補遺》《考註》等編，則又思以羽翼《周禮》者。至於《儀禮》，有宋大儒嘗修後王朝、邦國、家、鄉、學禮，而以二禮屬之門人矣。又有因其成法而為《經禮補逸》者。要之，皆有裨於禮學也。子諸士亦嘗肄之而能言其意歟？願詳以告，以觀經世之學。
問：夷狄之患，自古有之，雖殷周之盛，所未免也。顧其自治及所以禦之者何如耳。自漢以下，叛服不常，或於治朝則見侵侮，於季世則自臣服，此其故何也？可歷數而言歟？迨至胡元，為患極矣。我太祖高皇帝及
translation_en:
…chapters, or forty-nine chapters: can the reasons for their division and combination, their differences and similarities, be established through investigation? Or is it unknown in what age they emerged, to whom they were presented, and from what source their transmitters obtained them? Could some of them have escaped the conflagration under the Qin? In the past, readers of the Rites of Zhou often entertained doubt and belief in equal measure. As for the Ceremonies and Rites, earlier worthies likewise found it difficult to read and said that it truly had no application in their own day. Why did their opinions differ so greatly? Yet compilations such as Restoration of Antiquity, Supplementing Omissions, and Examination and Annotation sought to support and elucidate the Rites of Zhou. As for the Ceremonies and Rites, a great Confucian scholar of the Song once compiled rites for the royal court, the states, the family, the community, and schools [?], entrusting two of these categories of rites to his disciples. There was also someone who followed this established method to produce Supplementing the Lost Portions of the Canonical Rites. In sum, all these works contribute to the study of ritual. Have you gentlemen studied them, and can you explain their purport? Please set it out in detail, so that we may assess your learning in ordering the world.
Question: The threat posed by the Yi and Di has existed since antiquity; even the Yin and Zhou at their height could not escape it. The issue lies simply in how one governs one's own realm and how one defends against them. From the Han onward, their rebellion and submission have been inconstant. Sometimes they invaded and inflicted humiliation during well-governed reigns, yet voluntarily submitted as subjects during a dynasty's declining years. Why was this? Can you enumerate the instances and explain them? By the time of the non-Chinese Yuan dynasty, the calamity had reached its extreme. Our Emperor Taizu Gao and…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
成祖文皇帝驅逐掃蕩遠遁沙漠頼
皇仁天覆未滅其種百數十年生息滋蔓屢擾
邊陲
皇上赫然震怒命将出師畏威悔禍一歳無警
茲欲撤備恐獸心叵測去而復来備之
則勞師費財亦足慮也宜何如而可

邊陲

punctuated: 成祖文皇帝驅逐掃蕩，遠遁沙漠。頼皇仁天覆，未滅其種，百數十年生息滋蔓，屢擾邊陲。皇上赫然震怒，命将出師，畏威悔禍，一歳無警。茲欲撤備，恐獸心叵測，去而復来；備之，則勞師費財，亦足慮也。宜何如而可？
translation_en: …and Chengzu, the Wen Emperor, drove them out and swept them away, so that they fled far into the desert. Thanks to imperial benevolence, sheltering all like Heaven, their people were not exterminated. Over more than a hundred years, they have multiplied and spread, repeatedly harassing the frontier. His Majesty, in great wrath, ordered generals to lead an expedition. Awed by his might and regretting the trouble they had brought upon themselves, they have caused no alarm for a year. Now, if we wish to withdraw our defenses, we fear that their bestial hearts are unfathomable and that, having departed, they may return. Yet maintaining defenses against them exhausts the troops and drains the treasury—also grounds for concern. What would be the proper course?

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
子曰事君敬其事而後其食
皇甫溍
同考試官都給事中盧批發揮敬事後食之義詞
意真切允宜首録
同考試官編修董批辨義利之分明白痛切
宜録之以示人臣之法
同考試官編修吳批典雅醇正可録
===
同考試官修撰茅批人臣事君之義此作得
之而詞復典雅可取
考試官左庶子江批語意雅健
聖人舉人臣事君之義而祿非所計焉蓋君子
之仕也行其義也而豈以干祿哉聖人以此立
訓所以警為人臣者至矣其意蓋謂義利之幾
甚微而公私之判遂遠一於義則利非所先一
於利則義在所後矣是故人臣之事君也以敬
事為義而不可先以求祿為心夙夜在公皇皇

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

子曰：「事君，敬其事而後其食。」

皇甫溍

同考試官都給事中盧批：發揮敬事後食之義，詞意真切，允宜首録。

同考試官編修董批：辨義利之分，明白痛切，宜録之以示人臣之法。

同考試官編修吳批：典雅醇正，可録。

同考試官修撰茅批：人臣事君之義，此作得之，而詞復典雅，可取。

考試官左庶子江批：語意雅健。

聖人舉人臣事君之義，而祿非所計焉。蓋君子之仕也，行其義也，而豈以干祿哉？聖人以此立訓，所以警為人臣者至矣。其意蓋謂義利之幾甚微，而公私之判遂遠。一於義，則利非所先；一於利，則義在所後矣。是故人臣之事君也，以敬事為義，而不可先以求祿為心。夙夜在公，皇皇
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

The Master said: “In serving a ruler, attend reverently to your duties and put your emoluments afterward.”

Huangfu Jin 皇甫溍

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Chief Supervising Secretary: This develops the meaning of attending reverently to one’s duties and putting emoluments afterward. Its language and ideas are sincere and apt. It certainly deserves to be selected for inclusion first.

Comment by Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler: It distinguishes righteousness from personal gain clearly and forcefully. It should be included to show ministers a model for their conduct.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Compiler: Classical and elegant, sound and orthodox; worthy of inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, Senior Compiler: This composition grasps the proper principles by which a minister serves his ruler. Its language, moreover, is classical and elegant. It merits selection.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Deputy Supervisor of Instruction: Its language and ideas are refined and vigorous.

The Sage sets forth the proper principles by which a minister serves his ruler, leaving salary out of account. For when a gentleman enters office, he does so to put righteousness into practice. How could it be to seek a salary? In establishing this teaching, the Sage gave the fullest possible admonition to those who serve as ministers. His meaning is, it would seem, that the incipient distinction between righteousness and personal gain is exceedingly subtle, yet the resulting division between public duty and private interest becomes vast. If one is wholly devoted to righteousness, gain does not come first; if one is wholly devoted to gain, righteousness is put afterward. Thus, in serving his ruler, a minister takes reverent attention to his duties as his obligation and must not make seeking a salary his foremost concern. Early and late he attends to public duties, anxiously intent…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
如有弗及敬吾官守求以盡其職焉耳矣食固
非所計也朝夕惟寅惓惓如有弗釋敬吾言責

如有弗及，敬吾官守，求以盡其職焉耳矣，食固非所計也。朝夕惟寅，惓惓如有弗釋，敬吾言責，求以盡其忠焉耳矣，食固在所緩也。雖祿以勸賢也，然待勸而行，所行必不力。君臣之倫，固所得於性分，而尚有所待邪？雖祿以報功也，然望報而事，所事必不忠。君臣之義，無所逃于天地，而尚何所望邪？吾知小賢受小祿，大賢受大祿，以分則然也。顧其機在上而不在下，君子則不以不家食為幸，而方以體國為憂矣。小言有小利，大言有大利，以効則然也。顧所利在人而不在己，君子則不以有祿食為榮，而且以素餐為愧矣。吁！一義利之間，公私判焉；一先後之間，得失係焉，可不慎哉？是故聖人之言學也曰「後獲」，而其言仕也曰「後食」，凡以自盡其心也。彼所謂公養之仕者，蓋有不得已焉爾，非事君之常道也，是固不可不辨。

translation_en:
…as though unable to keep pace, reverently attending to the duties of my office and seeking only to fulfill its responsibilities: emoluments are certainly no part of my calculations. Reverent morning and evening, earnestly concerned as though unable to set the matter aside, I respectfully discharge my responsibility to speak out, seeking only to fulfill my loyalty: emoluments certainly come afterward. Although stipends serve to encourage the worthy, those who act only when encouraged will necessarily lack vigor in their actions. The relationship between ruler and minister is inherent in one’s nature and allotted duties; what further inducement should one await? Although stipends serve to reward achievement, those who serve in expectation of reward will necessarily lack loyalty in their service. The obligations between ruler and minister cannot be escaped anywhere between Heaven and Earth; what further reward should one expect?

I know that those of lesser worth receive smaller stipends, and those of greater worth receive larger stipends: this accords with their respective stations. Yet the power to determine this lies with those above, not those below. The gentleman therefore does not count himself fortunate to be supported outside his own household; rather, he concerns himself with serving the state’s interests as his own. Lesser counsel brings lesser benefit, and greater counsel brings greater benefit: this is so in terms of results. Yet the benefit accrues to others, not to oneself. The gentleman therefore does not regard receiving a stipend as an honor; instead, he feels shame at eating without rendering service.

Alas! In the distinction between righteousness and profit, public and private interests part ways; on the distinction between what comes first and what comes afterward, success and failure depend. Can one fail to be cautious? Thus, when the Sage speaks of learning, he says, “Put the rewards afterward”; when he speaks of taking office, he says, “Put emoluments afterward.” Both mean fully exerting one’s heart. As for what is called taking office for public support, this arises only from unavoidable necessity; it is not the regular way of serving one’s ruler. This distinction must indeed be made.

The Book of Odes says: “How manifest is his virtue! The hundred lords take it as their model.” Thus the gentleman is profoundly reverent, and all under Heaven is at peace. The Book of Odes says: “I cherish luminous virtue, without loud voice or imposing countenance.” …

translation_en:
…the underlying character of his stillness and emptiness in repose, and uprightness in action, solemnly sets all transformations in motion without visible form—who could see it? People recognize his dignified solemnity as he presides over them; yet the subtle working by which he embodies trustworthiness and brings harmonious compliance to fruition truly responds to the myriad incipient affairs without leaving a trace—who could know it? He certainly does not display his reverence. Nevertheless, the impulse that inspires trust resides in the ruler above and becomes a model for those below. Those who apprehend it through observing him naturally follow the Lord on High’s standards without knowing it. The influence of utmost responsiveness proceeds from his person and extends to the people: all over whom he presides dwell within the power of the Lord on High, without claiming it as their own. How wondrous is the efficacy of his response! What words could fittingly describe such a thing?

I have considered the ode “August Is the Lord on High” (Huang yi), which says: “I cherish luminous virtue, without loud voice or imposing countenance.” This might seem sufficient to express its subtlety, yet Confucius says: “These are the last things in transforming the people.” Moreover, to say “without loud” still leaves voice and countenance present; this is certainly inadequate. I have also considered the ode “The Multitudes of the People” (Zheng min), which says: “Virtue is light as a feather.” This might perhaps express its subtlety. Yet, in my judgment, these are not the words of one who understands virtue. To call it a feather still leaves something to which it can be compared; this too is inadequate. Only the ode “King Wen” (Wen wang) says: “The workings of Heaven above have neither sound nor smell.” Here form and material force alike vanish from perceptibility, while spiritual transformation operates unfathomably. To express its subtlety in these terms is indeed to reach the utmost!

I know that, in Heaven, the four seasons proceed and the hundred kinds of things are born; its great virtue brings profound transformation, yet cannot be seen. In the sage, Heaven and Earth take their proper places and the myriad things flourish; his undisplayed, profound reverence likewise cannot be seen. Thus, to know Heaven is to know the sage. 考試官左庶子江批敘事中自有議論
觀聖君命臣治水而績用成見世治之一驗也
夫世之治雖由于氣化而亦人事有以成之也
觀諸聖人之治水可見矣此孟子因門人好辨
之疑而歷敘生民之故以曉之也意謂當帝堯
在位之時有洚水儆予之患時則鯀罔績矣乃
舉舜而敷治舜納麓矣復命禹以嗣興以上則
君憂臣勞而弗恤以下則父舍子用而不疑凡
以為天下而已由是禹也掘壅塞而注之海蓋
海為百川之匯也驅蛇龍而放之菑蓋菑乃水
草之鍾也疏道之功既奏地中之水自行南條
如江漢既順其性而于海乎朝宗北條如河淮
亦循其道而于海乎會同昔多險阻今則壅塞
去而滔天者平矣昔多鳥獸今則蛇龍遠而害
人者消矣夫然後降丘宅土而人無巢窟之虞
猶已溺之者固由已而拯也地平天成而人有
粒食之利猶已飢之者亦由已而食也向非堯

…serve as a model for the many scholars.
Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction, comments: Within the narration itself there is argument.
By observing how a sage ruler commanded his ministers to control the waters and how their labors achieved success, we see one demonstration of order in the world. For although order in the world arises from the transformations of vital force, human endeavors also contribute to its accomplishment. This can be seen in the sages’ control of the waters. Here Mencius, responding to his disciple’s doubts about his fondness for disputation, recounts the circumstances of human life through successive ages to enlighten him. His meaning is this: when Emperor Yao occupied the throne, he faced the calamity expressed in the words, “The great flood warns me.” At that time Gun had achieved nothing. Yao therefore raised Shun to office to extend good governance. Shun had been sent into the great forest; Yu was then commanded to carry on the undertaking. Above, the ruler was anxious and his minister labored without concern for himself; below, the father was dismissed and the son employed without misgivings. All this was done solely for the sake of the world.
Thus Yu dug through obstructions and channeled the waters into the sea, for the sea is where the hundred rivers converge. He drove away snakes and dragons and banished them to the marshes [?], for marshes are where water and aquatic plants collect. Once the work of dredging and channeling had succeeded, the waters flowed freely through the land. The southern waterways, such as the Jiang and Han, followed their natural tendencies and paid court to the sea; the northern waterways, such as the He and Huai, likewise followed their courses and assembled at the sea. Formerly there had been many dangerous obstructions; now these were removed, and the waters that had risen to heaven were pacified. Formerly there had been many birds and beasts; now snakes and dragons were far away, and threats to human life had disappeared.
Only then could people descend from the hills and settle on the plains, free from the anxieties of dwelling in nests and caves. Those whose drowning Yu regarded as though he himself had caused it were indeed rescued through his own efforts. The earth was brought to order and Heaven’s work completed, and people enjoyed the benefit of grain to eat. Those whose hunger he regarded as though he himself had caused it were likewise fed through his own efforts. Had it not been for Yao…

translation_en:
…and Shun been vigilant and apprehensive above, and the Great Yu labored diligently below, how could disorder have been transformed into good government? Generally speaking, Heaven brings the cycles of change, while human beings order and encompass them. Heaven gives birth to sages for the sake of the people. Today everyone calls the age of Tang and Yu an age of consummate government, yet they do not recognize Emperor Yao as a ruler skilled in mastering disorder. There are indeed those whom the onward movement of cosmic forces and destiny cannot confine. As for the harm that Yang Zhu and Mo Di did to people’s hearts, it was worse than the calamity of the flood. How, then, could Mengzi have avoided his fondness for disputation? He, too, sought only to save the world. Earlier Confucian scholars said that his achievement was no less than Yu’s. How true!

彖傳本卦體釋同人之義，而著其有同道之益焉。甚矣，中正貫天下之道也！二五中正為應，斯固同道以相益者矣，謂之同人也宜哉！彖傳之意，盖謂天下理一而分殊，君子貴同而賤獨。同之於人，盖必有道矣。而卦之名為同人者，豈無所取乎？試以二五言之。夫二，柔也；二當位且中，是柔之得其中正者也。柔得中正，則是和順以為德者，本之秉彝之懿；而沉潜以為善者，約於義理之衷。其在二也，虛心以受益，夫固有取善之資矣。由是而應乎乾焉，和順者麗於陽明，而相須之勢甚殷；沉潜者濟以剛克，而相與之情益篤。其與五也，比類以成行，夫固有交修之益矣。夫二五中正之應如此，而何以言同人也？盖君子之同也，不求同于人，而求同于理。曰中正而應，則其理同矣；其理同，則無所往而不同也。同之為道也，不于其迹，而于其心。曰中正而應，則其心同矣；其心同，則亦無所往而不同也。此

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Secretariat Supervisor: “The diction and tenor are refined and correct; it merits inclusion.”

The Commentary on the Judgments explains the meaning of Fellowship with Others (Tongren) on the basis of the hexagram’s structure, making manifest the benefit of sharing the same Way. How profoundly centrality and correctness pervade the Way of all under Heaven! The second and fifth lines, central and correct, stand in correspondence: they indeed share the same Way and benefit one another. How fitting that this should be called Fellowship with Others! The Commentary’s meaning is, surely, that principle throughout the world is one, while its particular manifestations differ; the gentleman values fellowship and deprecates isolation. Fellowship with others must therefore follow a Way. Can the hexagram’s name, Fellowship with Others, have been chosen without a basis? Let us explain this through the second and fifth lines.

The second line is yielding. It occupies its proper position and is also central: thus its yielding character attains centrality and correctness. When yielding attains centrality and correctness, the virtue of harmony and compliance is rooted in the excellence of one’s constant, inborn nature; goodness cultivated through quiet immersion is governed by the proper mean of moral principle. In the second line, an open mind receives benefit: it certainly possesses the capacity to draw goodness from others. Hence it corresponds with Qian, the Creative. Harmony and compliance attach themselves to yang brightness, and their mutual dependence is most pressing; quiet immersion is aided by firm self-mastery, and their mutual attachment grows still deeper. In its relationship with the fifth line, association with its kind brings conduct to completion: there is certainly the benefit of mutual moral cultivation.

Such is the central and correct correspondence between the second and fifth lines. Why, then, speak of Fellowship with Others? The gentleman’s fellowship seeks agreement not with other people but with principle. To say that the lines are central and correct and stand in correspondence means that their principle is the same. If their principle is the same, wherever they go they will be in accord. The Way of fellowship resides not in outward traces but in the heart. To say that the lines are central and correct and stand in correspondence means that their hearts are the same. If their hearts are the same, then likewise, wherever they go they will be in accord. 子曰：「書不盡言，言不盡意。」然則聖人之意，其不可見乎？子曰：「聖人立象以盡意，設卦以盡情偽，繫辭焉以盡其言。」

translation_en:
…for they are united through the impartiality of the great Way, beyond what outward forms and conduct can represent; they are brought into accord through the goodness of attaining unity, beyond the constraints of power and station. At court, this is what is meant by ruler and ministers uniting at court and all possessing a single virtue. Throughout the realm, this is what is meant by the myriad people uniting in the countryside and universally practicing your virtue. Is not the meaning of Fellowship with Others (Tongren) thus abundantly clear? Yet to speak of unity is to speak of being without differences. To differ where one could be without differences incurs the harm of estrangement; to unite where one need not unite falls into factionalism. In essence, without difference there can be no unity, and between unity and difference there is a place for discretionary judgment. When the ancients adapted to changing times in order to follow the Way, was it not because they examined differences to achieve unity and possessed a distinctive insight into its depths? Thus it is said: “The way of the noble man is sometimes to enter public service and sometimes to remain in retirement, sometimes to be silent and sometimes to speak.” Alas! Who but one who understands the Way could bring these into accord and unite them?
The Master said: “Writing does not fully convey speech; speech does not fully convey meaning.” If so, can the sages’ meaning never be apprehended? The Master said: “The sages established images to convey their meaning fully, set out the hexagrams to reveal fully what is genuine and what is false, and appended statements to convey their words fully.”
Tang Yu 唐禹
Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Establishing images, setting out hexagrams, and appending statements are precisely the means of revealing their subtle profundities in writing: this was the sages’ original intention in composing the Book of Changes. This essay draws them out [?]; its author has evidently devoted thought to the Book of Changes.”

Associate Examiner Dong, a Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: 〔The essay follows the topic to form a complete composition; its language and meaning are classically elegant.〕
Associate Examiner Wu, a Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: 〔The language is concise yet fully conveys the meaning. The conclusion is especially evocative.〕
Associate Examiner Mao, a Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler, comments: 〔Both expression and reasoning are fully realized. This is a writer skilled at bringing out the sages’ profound insights.〕
Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Supervisor of the Heir Apparent, comments: 〔Its purity and clarity are particularly well suited to the meaning of the Changes.〕
The Great Commentary frames its discussion to probe the sages’ profound insights: these must be discerned in their creation of the Changes. The Changes is the means by which the sages reveal their most subtle teachings. Once the Changes had been created, could any of their profound insights remain unseen? It is fitting that the Great Commentary should frame its discussion to reveal them. It is as though it says: To understand why the sages created the Changes, one must consider the difficulty they faced in fully expressing their meaning. Now, in the sages’ teaching of the world, writings are the means of recording words. Yet there may be something uniquely apprehended in words that writings cannot record. Writings are thus inherently insufficient to convey words fully. As for the means of expressing meaning, these are words. Yet there may likewise be something uniquely apprehended in thought that words cannot express. Words, too, are insufficient to convey meaning fully. If this is so, one certainly cannot seek it in writings, nor can one seek it in words. Must the sages’ meaning, then, remain forever unseen? The sages knew that their words were difficult to transmit, and were still more concerned that their meaning might not be fully expressed. Thus, when the Changes was being created, odd and even lines were drawn and the two images set forth. Yin and yang thereby acquired form, and transformation …

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
化無方含動於寂極天下之至精也寓微於著
極天下之至深也聖人之心其難於形容者固
皆示之於象矣非所以盡意乎然未已也由象
而後有卦則三才既備而六位時成時有消長
所以明淑慝之機也位有當否所以別悔吝之
介也事物之理其相為貞勝者固皆不外於卦
矣非所以盡情偽乎然又未已也由象卦而後
有辭則彖言全體而爻言一節微顯闡幽可以
盡未發之理也廣大悉備可以周無窮之用也
===
聖人之教其示人無隱者又皆得之於辭矣非
所以盡言乎是則立象則意盡於象矣設卦則
意盡於情偽矣繫辭則意盡於言矣至是而書
不能盡者盡之言不能盡者盡之而孰謂聖人
之意終不可見也哉抑言一也而於聖人之意
有盡有不盡者何哉曰聖人之言語上語下其
致不同也而易則性命之書徹上下者也性命
不易言而易之陰陽具有性命之理故不得而
隱也雖然性命之理聖人亦言其所可言者耳

而後有卦則三才既備而六位時成時有消長

之意終不可見也哉抑言一也而於聖人之意

致不同也而易則性命之書徹上下者也性命
不易言而易之陰陽具有性命之理故不得而
隱也雖然性命之理聖人亦言其所可言者耳
punctuated: 化無方，含動於寂，極天下之至精也；寓微於著，極天下之至深也。聖人之心，其難於形容者，固皆示之於象矣，非所以盡意乎？然未已也。由象而後有卦，則三才既備，而六位時成。時有消長，所以明淑慝之機也；位有當否，所以別悔吝之介也。事物之理，其相為貞勝者，固皆不外於卦矣，非所以盡情偽乎？然又未已也。由象卦而後有辭，則彖言全體，而爻言一節。微顯闡幽，可以盡未發之理也；廣大悉備，可以周無窮之用也。聖人之教，其示人無隱者，又皆得之於辭矣，非所以盡言乎？是則立象，則意盡於象矣；設卦，則意盡於情偽矣；繫辭，則意盡於言矣。至是而書不能盡者盡之，言不能盡者盡之，而孰謂聖人之意終不可見也哉？抑言一也，而於聖人之意有盡有不盡者，何哉？曰：聖人之言，語上語下，其致不同也；而《易》則性命之書，徹上下者也。性命不易言，而《易》之陰陽具有性命之理，故不得而隱也。雖然，性命之理，聖人亦言其所可言者耳。
translation_en:
…transformations have no fixed pattern. Containing movement within stillness, they reach the utmost refinement of all under Heaven; lodging the subtle within the manifest, they reach the utmost profundity of all under Heaven. Whatever in the sages’ minds is difficult to describe is thus displayed in the images. Is this not how they fully express their meaning? Yet this is not all. From images come hexagrams: the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—are all present, and the six positions take shape in accordance with their times. Times have their waning and waxing, thereby revealing the incipient workings of good and evil; positions may be appropriate or inappropriate, thereby distinguishing the fine boundary between remorse and humiliation. The principles of things and affairs, by which each in turn prevails through its constancy, are all encompassed within the hexagrams. Is this not how they fully express what is genuine and what is false? Yet even this is not all. From images and hexagrams come statements: the hexagram judgments speak of the whole, while the line statements speak of a single aspect. Making the manifest subtle and bringing the hidden to light, they can fully express principles not yet actualized; vast and comprehensive, they can encompass inexhaustible applications. The teachings through which the sages show people everything without concealment are likewise all accessible in these statements. Is this not how they give full expression to their words?

Thus, by establishing images, they fully express their meaning in images; by setting out hexagrams, they fully express their meaning concerning the genuine and the false; by appending statements, they fully express their meaning in words. At this point, what writing cannot fully express is fully expressed, and what words cannot fully express is fully expressed. Who, then, could claim that the sages’ meaning ultimately cannot be apprehended? Yet words are alike in being words: why do some fully express the sages’ meaning while others do not? The answer is that the sages’ words differ in their purport according to whether they address higher or lower matters. The Book of Changes, however, is a book of human nature and Heaven’s decree, penetrating both the higher and the lower. Human nature and Heaven’s decree are not easily spoken of, yet the yin and yang of the Book of Changes contain their principles in full, so these cannot remain concealed. Nevertheless, even concerning the principles of human nature and Heaven’s decree, the sages speak only of what can be spoken.

書

帝曰：「臣作朕股肱耳目。予欲左右有民，汝翼；予欲宣力四方，汝為；予欲觀古人之象，日月星辰、山龍華蟲作會，宗彝、藻、火、粉米、黼黻絺繡，以五采彰施于五色作服，汝明；予欲聞六律、五聲、八音，在治忽，以出納五言，汝聽。」

林光祖

同考試官編修邢批：「虞廷一體之義，發揮親切，而結以君道歸諸天道，尤占識大之學矣，宜錄以式多士。」

同考試官編修歐陽批：「典則莊重，而敘事有法。虞廷君臣相與氣象，讀此作可想見矣。子其抱臣隣之志者乎！」
translation_en:
…As for commanding trust without speaking, that rests with the person himself.

Book of Documents

The emperor said: “My ministers serve as my legs and arms, my ears and eyes. When I wish to aid and guide the people, you must assist me. When I wish to extend my efforts throughout the four quarters, you must act for me. When I wish to view the symbolic designs of the ancients—the sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, and pheasants depicted in painting; and ancestral sacrificial vessels, water plants, fire, grains of rice, axe patterns, and paired bow patterns embroidered on fine cloth, with the five hues displayed in five-colored garments—you must make their significance clear. When I wish to hear the six pitch standards, the five notes, and the eight classes of instrumental sound, discerning good government or neglect through the issuing and receiving of words in the five musical modes, you must listen.”

Lin Guangzu

Associate Examiner Xu, Acting Director, comments: “Essays on the Documents of Yu do not lack words, but most strain to draw in extraneous material and fall far short of a style that is concise, clear, substantial, and profound. This composition alone excels.”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Examining Editor, comments: “This composition all but exhausts the meaning of ministers as their ruler’s close helpers. For this reason it has been selected for inclusion.”

Associate Examiner Xing, Junior Compiler, comments: “The principle that ruler and ministers at the court of Yu formed one body is expounded with aptness and immediacy. The conclusion, which traces the Way of the ruler back to the Way of Heaven, particularly shows learning marked by broad insight [?]. It should be included as a model for the many candidates.”

Associate Examiner Ouyang, Senior Compiler, comments: “Exemplary and dignified, it also presents its subject in an orderly manner. Reading this composition, one can envision the spirit of fellowship between ruler and ministers at the court of Yu. Surely you cherish the aspiration to serve as your ruler’s close helper!”

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
考試官左庶子江批詞簡意盡
聖君責大臣以一體之義而必詳其事焉盖君
臣一體以相成者也則夫政教禮樂之事不於
大臣是責而何哉帝舜望禹以弼直而此則申
言臣所以為鄰之義也意謂君之於臣也以相
臨固有不可易之分以相成寔有不容已之義
誠以君尊也尊者體要猶之元首也臣卑也卑
者用勞猶之股肱耳目也故予以一人之股肱
而運用乎天下力固弗給矣臣其作予之股肱
===
乎以一人之耳目而視聽乎天下用必弗周矣
臣其作予之耳目乎何則君有政教所以興理
也予欲左右有民而教思之無窮庶乎從欲以
治也翼而行之惟汝是資焉予欲宣力四方而
容保之無疆庶乎胥匡以生也代而敷之惟汝
是賴焉是則所以作予之股肱而運用乎天下
殆有餘力矣君有禮樂所以宣化也予欲觀象
作服以日月星辰山龍華蟲焉而繪于衣以宗
彝藻火粉米黼黻焉而繡于裳彰施以采色之

聖君責大臣以一體之義，而必詳其事焉。盖君臣一體以相成者也，則夫政教禮樂之事，不於大臣是責而何哉？帝舜望禹以弼直，而此則申言臣所以為鄰之義也。意謂君之於臣也，以相臨，固有不可易之分；以相成，寔有不容已之義。誠以君尊也，尊者體要，猶之元首也；臣卑也，卑者用勞，猶之股肱耳目也。故予以一人之股肱而運用乎天下，力固弗給矣，臣其作予之股肱乎？以一人之耳目而視聽乎天下，用必弗周矣，臣其作予之耳目乎？何則？君有政教，所以興理也。予欲左右有民，而教思之無窮，庶乎從欲以治也；翼而行之，惟汝是資焉。予欲宣力四方，而容保之無疆，庶乎胥匡以生也；代而敷之，惟汝是賴焉。是則所以作予之股肱而運用乎天下，殆有餘力矣。君有禮樂，所以宣化也。予欲觀象作服，以日月星辰、山、龍、華蟲焉而繪于衣，以宗彝、藻、火、粉米、黼、黻焉而繡于裳，彰施以采色之

Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “The wording is concise and the meaning fully expressed.”

The sage ruler charges his great ministers with the duty arising from their forming one body with him, and necessarily specifies the tasks involved. Ruler and ministers form one body and bring one another to fulfillment. To whom, then, should responsibility for government, instruction, rites, and music be assigned, if not to the great ministers? Emperor Shun expected Yu to assist him and keep him upright; here he further explains the meaning of a minister’s being his close companion. The sense is that, in the ruler’s relationship with his ministers, their respective positions of authority entail distinctions that cannot be altered, while their mutual fulfillment entails a duty that cannot be set aside. For the ruler is exalted, and the exalted comprehends the essentials, like the head; ministers are subordinate, and subordinates exert themselves in service, like the limbs, ears, and eyes.

Thus, if I employ the limbs of one person alone to act throughout all under Heaven, my strength will assuredly be insufficient. Will you ministers serve as my limbs? If I use the ears and eyes of one person alone to hear and see throughout all under Heaven, their reach will surely be inadequate. Will you ministers serve as my ears and eyes? Why is this so? The ruler has government and instruction as the means of establishing order. I wish to assist and guide the people, with inexhaustible concern for their instruction, hoping thereby to govern as I desire; it is upon you alone that I depend to aid me and carry this out. I wish to extend my efforts throughout the four quarters, embracing and protecting the people without limit, hoping that they may sustain one another in life; it is upon you alone that I rely to act in my stead and extend these efforts. In this way you serve as my limbs in acting throughout all under Heaven, and there will surely be strength to spare.

The ruler has rites and music as the means of spreading moral transformation. I wish to examine the emblematic figures and make ceremonial garments: to have the sun, moon, stars, mountain, dragon, and pheasant painted on the upper garment, and the ancestral sacrificial vessels, waterweed, fire, grains of rice, axe pattern, and paired angular pattern embroidered on the lower garment, displaying them through the multicolored …

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
文致嚴於等威之辨盖惟汝是資也其尚有以
明之邪予欲聞樂審治以六律而和乎五聲以
五聲而被之八音于以出納夫五言于以稽察
夫治忽盖惟汝是托也其亦有以聽之邪是則

translation_en:
…patterns, strictly distinguishing the gradations of rank and dignity. It is upon you that I rely: will you not make these clear? I wish to hear music and examine the state of government, using the six pitch standards to harmonize the five notes and giving expression to those notes through the eight classes of instruments. Through these, utterances in the five modes are received and issued, and good government and disorder are scrutinized. It is to you that I entrust this: will you also attend to it by listening? Thus, by serving as my ears and eyes and hearing and seeing throughout the realm, you will surely leave no circumstances unnoticed.

Viewed in this light, the head functions through its animating spirit: such is the way of the ruler. The limbs, ears, and eyes function through bodily form: such is the way of the minister. If Yu can take upon himself the responsibility of serving as the limbs, ears, and eyes, while honoring his ruler as the head, how could he fail to fulfill the duty of a close minister to assist and correct his lord? From this we further understand that the way of the ruler is precisely the Way of Heaven. Heaven does not speak, yet the myriad transformations proceed, merely because the five phases and four seasons diffuse its vital energy; nevertheless, Heaven never ceases its profound and majestic operation. The ruler does not toil, yet all accomplishments flourish, merely because the various offices and numerous officials discharge their duties; nevertheless, the ruler likewise never ceases his reverent and enlightened activity. Shun was praised for governing through nonaction: surely this was the reason! Hence the saying: “The ruler of men is like Heaven moving above.”

“Duke, may you assist me for countless millions of years in revering Heaven’s favor.” He bowed with hands clasped and knocked his head to the ground, speaking forthrightly [?].

Associate Examiner Zhang, an Examining Editor, comments: Its dignified manner aptly suits this topic; hence it is included.
Associate Examiner Xing, a Compiler, comments: It depicts the dealings between the Zhou ruler and his minister with subtlety and thoroughness. This is an excellent composition; include it.
Associate Examiner Ouyang, a Compiler, comments: Its explanation of King Cheng’s intention in replying to the Duke of Zhou is closely attuned to his meaning. Its form is elegant and correct, and its language brilliant and lucid. It is among the finest essays interpreting the Book of Documents and should be included as a model.

The worthy king praises his great minister’s intention in establishing the capital at Luo and respectfully responds to his admonition. The Duke of Zhou’s establishment of the capital at Luo was intended to match Heaven’s favor without end; his report of the divination made clear wherein the ruler’s proper course lay. “A minister’s love for his ruler is profound, and therefore his planning for the state reaches far into the future. Could your construction of Luo, my duke, have been merely a plan for one man’s ease and enjoyment? Truly, it was to receive the feudal lords at court and bring peace to all regions. Heaven’s mandate to our Zhou is indeed a blessing. You determined the directions and established the proper positions, building the royal city as a place for assemblies and audiences, and enabling me reverently to live up to that blessing: surely you sought to sustain its growing fullness. 之滋至也亦無窮。由今日以至萬億年，而宜君宜王者恒於斯焉。多方之厭德無斁，則殷命之簡畀也亦無斁。歷萬億年如今日，而有幹有年者恒於斯焉。是雖一時之締造，而弘可大之規；雖一人之謀猷，而延可久之業。公之望於我者，不亦至矣乎？
夫周公之意之美，固王之所亟嘉，而其告卜之辭，則尤王之所致敬者也。何也？營洛之舉，作之者天也；紹天以示人者，卜也；主之者，君也；輔君以承天者，公也。公惟兩示乎洛食，則知宅中圖大而嚴統御之方者，其道不可以不思；居重馭輕而迓和恒之休者，其責不可以不盡。於是乎拜手焉，以致其恭也；稽首焉，以成其禮也。盖禮有所宜，雖以成王加之而不為屈；道有所任，雖以周公受之而不為嫌。然則有周君臣之際，不亦可想見其盛矣哉？
雖然，作洛者武王之志，周公成之，而召公寔先經理之。今成王獨歸諸周公，何哉？誠以武周之心一也，周召之德同也。歸美于周公，則上契武王之心，下協
translation_en:
…will likewise bring Heaven’s blessings in ever greater abundance without end. From this day through countless ages, here there will always be one fit to be lord and king. If the many regions never tire of finding satisfaction in his virtue, neither will the bestowal of the great mandate upon the chosen ruler ever cease. Through countless ages, as today, here there will always be one possessed of ability and length of years. Thus, though the founding was accomplished at one particular time, it enlarged a plan capable of greatness; though the strategy was devised by one man, it perpetuated an undertaking capable of enduring. Were not the Duke’s hopes for me most far-reaching?
The excellence of the Duke of Zhou’s intentions was certainly something the king eagerly praised, but it was especially the Duke’s report of the divination that elicited the king’s reverence. Why? It was Heaven that initiated the undertaking of building Luo; divination transmitted Heaven’s will and revealed it to men; the ruler presided over the undertaking; and the Duke assisted the ruler in carrying out Heaven’s will. The Duke showed that the divination had twice favored Luo. The king thus knew that he must reflect upon the Way of establishing himself at the center, planning for greatness, and giving due rigor to the methods of sovereign rule; and that he must fully discharge his responsibility to occupy the position of central authority, govern the subordinate regions, and welcome the blessings of lasting harmony. Accordingly, he bowed with his hands joined to express his reverence, and bowed his head to the ground to complete the ceremony. Ritual has its proper requirements: even for King Cheng to offer such honors was no abasement. The Way assigns responsibilities: even for the Duke of Zhou to receive such honors was no cause for misgiving. Can we not thus imagine the flourishing relations between ruler and minister under the Zhou?
Nevertheless, building Luo was King Wu’s intention. The Duke of Zhou brought it to completion, while the Duke of Shao had actually first planned and organized it. Why, then, did King Cheng attribute it solely to the Duke of Zhou? Truly, it was because King Wu and the Duke of Zhou were of one mind, and the Dukes of Zhou and Shao shared the same virtue. …toward the common people and officials is evidence of manifest virtue. How fitting that through this he should win Heaven’s favor and receive its care! This is why the ancestral impersonator answers the poem Wild Ducks (Fu yi). The meaning is this: the ruler is the one whom Heaven treats with particular generosity. Heaven is generous to the ruler, and the ruler’s virtue enables him gloriously to receive Heaven’s gifts. Could Heaven’s loving mandate ever reach an end? Thus, the noble ruler of our poem Admirable Joy (Jia le) diligently cultivates his virtue in continuing illumination: his radiant brilliance shines forth, grandly matching the constant spectacle of Heaven and Earth. His Way originates in great manifestation: with doubled brightness he adheres to rectitude, shining like the sun and moon illuminating all below. How manifest is the king’s virtue! Thus, in fitting his conduct to the common people, he brings them peace and draws them near, moves them and brings them into harmony; he consults those outside the court and governs in accordance with their wishes. In fitting his conduct to officials, he makes their counsels enlightened and their assistance harmonious; he consults those at court, and all share a single virtue. The common people are Heaven’s heart; officials perform Heaven’s work on its behalf. Once he acts fittingly toward both common people and officials, he has fulfilled Heaven’s intention. How could he fail to receive blessings from Heaven?

We see Heaven protecting and assisting him, assisting and commissioning him, granting him peace and granting him goodness. The One Man establishes the supreme standard, and every favorable circumstance gathers around him. Heaven shows him how to act and how to conduct affairs; the Lord on High favors him, and the hundred spirits acknowledge him as their lord. Yet Heaven’s care does not end there. His virtue is fitting in every respect, and so too are all his blessings. Boundless is the beneficence: the favor that brings peace to our sovereign is only now arriving and has not ceased. His virtue is constant, and the mandate is likewise constant. These abundant blessings, bestowed for ten thousand years, remain ever new despite the passage of time. Ah! Such is the complete protection Heaven affords our ruler. All this is brought about by his manifest virtue. Could anyone other than the noble ruler of Admirable Joy enjoy such things? translation_en:
…to treat him as a divine being. Yet the hymn “Wild Ducks and Gulls” (Fu yi) also carries the generous rites of hospitality to their utmost extent. Why is this? It is simply that the king’s heart, in honoring his ancestors and revering his lineage, gives full expression to its sincerity in every respect. The poet of “Gracious Joy” (Jia le) therefore borrows Heaven’s voice to respond to him, and is also deeply solicitous of the succeeding king’s worthiness. How consummate this loyalty and love are! To approach the illustrious ancestors with manifest sincerity and to receive manifest favor from the Lord on High follow the same Way. Readers who consider this together with the poem “Heaven Protects” (Tian bao) will be still more convinced.
“From those kings Cheng and Kang, who possessed the four quarters: how discerning was their illumination!”
Zhang Jiyuan.
Associate Examiner Zhou, Chief Supervising Secretary, comments: “The exposition is clear and ample, neither hurried nor sluggish. It achieves a gentle, sincere, and generous manner, sufficient to serve as a model for those who interpret the Odes.”
Associate Examiner Wang, Examining Editor, comments: “The ‘illumination’ spoken of in the topic is essential substance revealed through its operation; it is explained through the manifestations of good government. Few writers expound the meaning of a hymn in this way!”
Associate Examiner Yuan, Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: “Cheng and Kang manifested their luminous virtue in their achievements in government: this is the topic’s fundamental meaning. This essay develops it fully and richly. It should be selected to head the work of the many candidates.”
Associate Examiner Peng, Hanlin Academy Compiler, comments: “The topic is fundamentally upright and grand. In treating discerning scrutiny, the author shows no harsh countenance [?]. The composition is dignified and its language luxuriant. This essay alone displays these qualities; it should be selected as a model.”
Associate Examiner Shen, Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler, comments: “It portrays flourishing virtue, and its writing and reasoning are clear and fluent. This is precisely how the meaning of a hymn should be expounded.”
Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor, comments: “Amid its elaborate cadences, there is an unfettered spirit.”

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
周人頌二王之君天下而克明其德也夫君德
莫大乎至明也成康以之其君天下也宜哉此
周人祀先之詩盖謂天祚周業代有令王故執
競以開後武王之功莫尚矣成康繼世而有天
下其德不有可言者乎自今觀之席燕翼之休
而得統於武成固基天之命而奄有九有矣承
貽謀之慶而繼體於成康亦荷天之寵而君臨
萬邦矣夫履帝位而不疚者徵諸德臨天下而
不眩者存乎明二王之為君何如哉盖日月照
===
臨先王以明而出治也彼則有以善繼之而致
乎緝熈之學聰明作后先王以明而統天也彼
則有以善述之而對乎光訓之詒是以明德所
發天地昭焉於謨訓則賁如也於法象則粲如
也所謂天子之光將無微不達矣夫孰得而掩
之德輝所動上下察焉以群工則辨治也以庶
物則咸熈也所謂大君之智盖無遠弗届矣其
明不亦著乎是則成康紹天之明而纘先業於
不忘則克享天心而垂裕後昆遠矣周人之升

translation_en:
The people of Zhou praised the two kings for ruling all under Heaven and being able to make their virtue manifest. Of a ruler’s virtues, none is greater than perfect illumination. Kings Cheng and Kang possessed it: how fitting that they should rule all under Heaven! This poem, used by the people of Zhou in sacrificing to their ancestors, means that Heaven blessed the enterprise of Zhou, so that each generation had an excellent king. Thus, for steadfast strength in opening the way for his successors, King Wu’s achievement was unsurpassed. Cheng and Kang succeeded to the throne and possessed all under Heaven: surely their virtue, too, deserves to be spoken of?

Viewed from the present, Cheng enjoyed the blessings of provision made for descendants and inherited the succession from Wu; he firmly established Heaven’s mandate and possessed all the nine regions. Kang received the blessings of plans bequeathed to posterity and succeeded Cheng; he too bore Heaven’s favor and ruled over the myriad states. To occupy the imperial throne without fault is verified through virtue; to preside over all under Heaven without becoming confused depends upon illumination. What, then, were these two kings like as rulers?

As the sun and moon shine down, the former kings brought forth good government through their illumination. These two kings ably continued their work and attained the learning that sustains and extends brightness. Being discerning and perceptive, the former kings became rulers and, through their illumination, governed in accord with Heaven. These two kings ably carried on their work and responded to the luminous instructions bequeathed to them. Thus, wherever their luminous virtue issued forth, Heaven and Earth shone: in counsels and instructions it was splendid; in standards and exemplars it was brilliant. What is called the radiance of the Son of Heaven reached even the smallest things. Who could obscure it?

Wherever the radiance of their virtue exerted its influence, those above and below perceived it clearly: the assembled officials discharged their duties, and all things flourished. What is called the wisdom of the great ruler reached even the most distant places. Was its illumination not manifest? Thus Cheng and Kang continued Heaven’s illumination and carried forward their predecessors’ enterprise without forgetting it. …singing in the ancestral temple indeed had good reason! I have observed that the rulers of Zhou upheld illustrious virtue from generation to generation. It was fitting that their blessed tenure should extend beyond the allotted span [?]. Yet, looking further back to Xia and Shang, their civilizing instructions shone brilliantly; under Tang and Yu, there were reverent enlightenment and profound wisdom. Thus we know that the essential principles of government under the emperors and kings of antiquity never went beyond illustrious virtue. Could the manifestations of their loftiness and breadth, and the consummate achievements of their sagely and wondrous transforming influence, possibly have arisen by chance? Ah! Here we may discern how emperors and kings transmitted and preserved their rule.

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
得不即其事以貶之哉且桃丘何為而弗遇也
衛侯棄魯而為齊鄭之從也于是乎有郎之戰
惡曹之盟焉君子曰衛之失信一至此哉吾聞
桃丘之會約在衛也久要之言固非漫然之諾
桃丘之地近在衛也邦域之中初何遠涉之虞
衛苟知此肯中變以從齊鄭邪奈何執德不恒
甘食言而罔恤因人起釁乃棄志以相從以故
魯也行李徒勤莫遂儀文之接衛也兵戎是逞
遽剪兄弟之歡是誰之過與人徒知于郎之戰
===
率賦以仇人者列國之罪同也而不知衛之背
信其罪實有浮焉者不然其何事于戰邪人徒
知惡曹之盟要言以同歃者列國之惡均也而
不知衛之失信其惡實有甚焉者不然又胡為
乎盟邪故經於桃丘書曰弗遇者盖惡之也其
戰于郎直書曰來盟于惡曹俱奪其爵者盖甚
之也而衛失信之罪於是乎不可掩矣抑魯桓
之罪王法所當治者衛雖棄之可也乃深貶之
者何盖春秋惇信明義之書也齊鄭業已助桓

punctuated: 得不即其事以貶之哉？且桃丘何為而弗遇也？衛侯棄魯而為齊鄭之從也，於是乎有郎之戰、惡曹之盟焉。君子曰：「衛之失信，一至此哉！」吾聞桃丘之會，約在衛也，久要之言，固非漫然之諾；桃丘之地，近在衛也，邦域之中，初何遠涉之虞？衛苟知此，肯中變以從齊鄭邪？奈何執德不恒，甘食言而罔恤，因人起釁，乃棄志以相從！以故魯也，行李徒勤，莫遂儀文之接；衛也，兵戎是逞，遽剪兄弟之歡。是誰之過與？人徒知于郎之戰，率賦以仇人者，列國之罪同也，而不知衛之背信，其罪實有浮焉者。不然，其何事于戰邪？人徒知惡曹之盟，要言以同歃者，列國之惡均也，而不知衛之失信，其惡實有甚焉者。不然，又胡為乎盟邪？故經於桃丘書曰「弗遇」者，盖惡之也；其戰于郎，直書曰「來」，盟于惡曹，俱奪其爵者，盖甚之也。而衛失信之罪，於是乎不可掩矣。抑魯桓之罪，王法所當治者，衛雖棄之可也，乃深貶之者何？盖春秋惇信明義之書也，齊鄭業已助桓
translation_en: …could it fail to censure him through its account of these events? Moreover, why was there no meeting at Taoqiu? Because the Marquis of Wei abandoned Lu and followed Qi and Zheng. Hence came the battle at Lang and the covenant at E’cao. The gentleman says: “Could Wei’s breach of faith have reached such a point!” I have heard that responsibility for the agreement to meet at Taoqiu lay with Wei. The words of that longstanding agreement were surely no casual promise. Taoqiu, moreover, lay nearby in Wei; within its own territory, what concern could there have been about a distant journey? Had Wei understood this, would it have changed course midway to follow Qi and Zheng? Why did it fail to remain constant in virtue, willingly break its word without concern, and, when others provoked a quarrel, abandon its own purpose to follow them? Consequently, Lu’s envoys labored in vain, unable to carry out the ceremonial exchange, while Wei indulged in warfare, abruptly severing the amity between brother states. Whose fault was this? People know only that, in the battle at Lang, the participating states bore equal guilt for leading their levies into hostilities against another; they do not realize that Wei’s betrayal of trust made its guilt greater still. Otherwise, what business had it joining the battle? People know only that, in the covenant at E’cao, the participating states were equally culpable for binding themselves by pledges and jointly smearing their lips with sacrificial blood; they do not realize that Wei’s breach of faith made its wrongdoing more serious still. Otherwise, why did it enter the covenant? Thus, when the Classic writes “did not meet” concerning Taoqiu, it expresses condemnation. In recording the battle at Lang, it simply writes “came”; in recording the covenant at E’cao, it likewise withholds their ranks. This expresses still stronger condemnation. Wei’s guilt in breaking faith thereby becomes impossible to conceal. Yet the crimes of Duke Huan of Lu warranted punishment under royal law, so Wei could properly have abandoned him. Why, then, is it censured so severely? Because the Spring and Autumn Annals is a book that upholds good faith and makes righteousness clear. Qi and Zheng had already assisted Duke Huan…

text:
□惡矣今不能明大義以興師而乃於私忿是
徵牲歃是務尚為知類也哉春秋貶之聖人之
情見矣
冬楚人伐黃〔僖公十有一年〕

同考試官檢討林批明暢可錄
考試官左庶子江批氣鬯詞蔚
觀春秋紀與國被患而伯主怠義之罪見矣蓋
===
國非同盟則於恤患之義猶可諉也楚之伐黃
也而桓其可諉乎假義之烈於是乎隳矣吾聞
春秋紀約而志詳故外諸侯相滅不書伐者為
其非同盟之國耳黃非齊桓之同盟乎當桓之
圖伯也楚方荐食于上國桓將合諸侯而懲之
則恐其與之并力于我也由是偕黃盟貫以斷
右臂之勢會於陽穀以定掎角之謀而黃也慕
義之心專雖觸強夷而不顧從華之志篤乃棄
世好而不辭得非以桓之信義方隆而己之緩
