觀春秋紀與國被患，而伯主怠義之罪見矣。蓋國非同盟，則於恤患之義猶可諉也。楚之伐黃也，而桓其可諉乎？假義之烈，於是乎隳矣。吾聞春秋紀約而志詳，故外諸侯相滅不書伐者，為其非同盟之國耳。黃非齊桓之同盟乎？當桓之圖伯也，楚方荐食于上國。桓將合諸侯而懲之，則恐其與之并力于我也。由是偕黃盟貫，以斷右臂之勢；會於陽穀，以定掎角之謀。而黃也慕義之心專，雖觸強夷而不顧；從華之志篤，乃棄世好而不辭。得非以桓之信義方隆，而己之緩
translation_en:
…□ evil [?]. Now, unable to uphold the great principles of righteousness by raising an army, they instead seek redress for private anger and concern themselves with sacrificial animals and blood-smeared covenant oaths. Can they still be said to understand what belongs to the same moral category? The Spring and Autumn Annals censures them, and the Sage’s sentiments are thereby revealed.

“In winter, the men of Chu attacked Huang.” 〔Eleventh year of Duke Xi〕
By Song Xian.
Associate Examiner Zhao, Acting Director, comments: “It skillfully brings out the crucial point in the Sage’s reproach of Duke Huan of Qi.”
Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor, comments: “Clear and fluent; worthy of inclusion.”
Examiner Jiang, Left Secretariat Supervisor, comments: “Its expressive force flows freely, and its language is rich.”

When we observe how the Spring and Autumn Annals records an allied state suffering calamity, the hegemon’s guilt in neglecting his righteous duty becomes apparent. If a state were not a fellow member of the covenant, one might still evade the duty to relieve its distress. But when Chu attacked Huang, could Duke Huan evade that duty? Here the achievements he had won by borrowing the mantle of righteousness collapsed.

I have heard that the Spring and Autumn Annals is concise in its records but detailed in its purport. Thus, when rulers of states other than Lu destroy one another’s states, it does not record the preceding attacks, simply because those states were not fellow members of the covenant. Was Huang not a covenant ally of Duke Huan of Qi? When Duke Huan was seeking hegemony, Chu was repeatedly devouring the states of the central realm. Duke Huan intended to unite the feudal lords and chastise Chu, but feared that Huang would join forces with Chu against his own side. Accordingly, he joined Huang in a covenant at Guan, to sever Chu’s right arm, and met at Yanggu, to settle a strategy of coordinated attacks from different directions.

Huang’s devotion to righteousness was single-minded: even when it incurred the hostility of powerful outsiders, it paid no heed. Its determination to follow the civilized states was firm: it did not shrink from abandoning generations of friendly relations. Was this not because Duke Huan’s good faith and righteousness were then flourishing, and because, in its own times of respite…

急有恃邪今茲楚也興伐黄之師為當齊之計
強弱不支民倒懸矣而引手之急能無望於宗
盟眾寡莫禦勢阽危矣而褰裳之援切有傒於
霸主使桓公而追惟管仲之言再申召陵之義
率彼同盟悉心以從事爰整其旅戮力以周旋
則黄難可紓而楚氛攸熄矣夫何簡書已至而
援師不出卒之楚烈益熾而黄社告墟彼方朝
夕以急而此猶宴安之懐彼固腹心是投而此
則秦越以視藉之也而卒弃之與之也而曷庇
===
之黄亦何賴於我而自賈其禍至是與君子以
是知桓之不復宗諸侯矣春秋於黄滅特書伐
者見黄以同盟来告而齊卒莫能救也是故桓
之興也始於救邢之勤而其既也隳于滅黄之
役其救邢也以用管仲之言而其不救黄也以
弗恤管仲之見然則桓之伯業卒係于仲之一
身人君用賢始終之效亦足鑒矣夫
禮記
夫歌者直己而陳德也動己而天地應焉

punctuated:
急有恃邪？今茲楚也，興伐黄之師，為當齊之計。強弱不支，民倒懸矣，而引手之急，能無望於宗盟？眾寡莫禦，勢阽危矣，而褰裳之援，切有傒於霸主。使桓公而追惟管仲之言，再申召陵之義，率彼同盟，悉心以從事，爰整其旅，戮力以周旋，則黄難可紓，而楚氛攸熄矣。夫何簡書已至，而援師不出？卒之楚烈益熾，而黄社告墟。彼方朝夕以急，而此猶宴安之懐；彼固腹心是投，而此則秦越以視。藉之也，而卒弃之；與之也，而曷庇之？黄亦何賴於我，而自賈其禍至是與？君子以是知桓之不復宗諸侯矣。春秋於黄滅特書伐者，見黄以同盟来告，而齊卒莫能救也。是故桓之興也，始於救邢之勤；而其既也，隳于滅黄之役。其救邢也，以用管仲之言；而其不救黄也，以弗恤管仲之見。然則桓之伯業，卒係于仲之一身。人君用賢始終之效，亦足鑒矣夫！

禮記

夫歌者，直己而陳德也，動己而天地應焉。
translation_en:
…in emergencies, had someone on whom to rely? Now Chu raised an army to attack Huang as part of its plan to counter Qi. The weak could not withstand the strong, and the people suffered as though hanging upside down: in their urgent need for a helping hand, how could they fail to look to the leader of their covenant? Outnumbered, they could offer no resistance, and their situation was perilous: they earnestly awaited the hegemon’s aid, hastening to them with robes hitched up. Had Duke Huan recalled Guan Zhong’s words and reaffirmed the righteous purpose of the meeting at Shaoling, led his allies in wholehearted action, drawn up his forces, and exerted their combined strength to meet the crisis, Huang’s distress could have been relieved and Chu’s threatening advance quelled. Why, then, did no relieving army set out, even after the written appeal had arrived? In the end, Chu’s violence blazed still more fiercely, and Huang’s altars of state were reduced to ruins. While Huang faced danger morning and night, Qi still cherished its ease; while Huang entrusted itself to Qi with complete sincerity, Qi regarded it with the indifference of Qin toward Yue. Having relied upon Huang, Qi ultimately abandoned it; having allied with it, why did Qi not protect it? What benefit did Huang derive from relying upon us, that it should have brought such calamity upon itself? From this, the gentleman knows that Duke Huan could no longer preside over the feudal lords.

The Spring and Autumn Annals specifically records an “attack” in its account of Huang’s destruction to show that Huang, as a fellow member of the covenant, came to report its distress, yet Qi ultimately failed to rescue it. Thus Duke Huan’s rise began with his diligent efforts to rescue Xing, while his final decline came with the campaign that destroyed Huang. He rescued Xing because he followed Guan Zhong’s advice; he failed to rescue Huang because he disregarded Guan Zhong’s views. Duke Huan’s achievement as hegemon thus depended, in the end, upon Guan Zhong alone. The consequences of whether a ruler employs worthy men consistently from beginning to end surely offer a sufficient lesson!

Book of Rites

“As for singing, it is a means of setting oneself upright and giving expression to one’s virtue. It moves oneself, and Heaven and Earth respond…”

雖各有宜也而其始亦奚以遠求哉於己取之
而已矣蓋身以德立身正則德成德以歌發德
著則歌永故或持其靜定之操或守其恭儉之

樂師論聲歌本諸德，而有以極其功化之大焉。蓋歌成於德，則其本立矣；其功化之極也，固其感通自然之應與！師乙之答子貢如此。且聲歌雖各有宜也，而其始亦奚以遠求哉？於己取之而已矣。蓋身以德立，身正則德成；德以歌發，德著則歌永。故或持其靜定之操，或守其恭儉之度，凡所以修厥身者無不豫；或養其寬裕之性，或充其剛毅之才，凡所以成乎己者靡不周。則直方之道既無所疑於躬，而德輝之動自不能隱於歌矣。由是和順足以成其英華之發，性天有以闡其流行之幾，則其功化豈但已哉？吾見
translation_en:
…the four seasons are harmonious, the stars follow their proper order, and all things are nourished.

Hu An

Associate Examiner Gao, Acting Vice Director, comments: “The two words ‘rectify oneself’ provide a remarkably firm foundation. Your ability to elucidate them must come from attentive inquiry into your inner self.”

Associate Examiner Chen, Supervising Secretary, comments: “This composition is harmonious, measured, pure, and correct. Surely its author can give expression to his own virtue!”

Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Mentor, comments: “The language and spirit are as expansive as spring.”

The music master discusses how singing is rooted in virtue and can thereby bring its transforming influence to its fullest greatness. For when song arises from virtue, its foundation is established. The utmost reach of its transforming influence is surely the spontaneous response produced by sympathetic resonance! Such was Music Master Yi’s answer to Zigong. Although different kinds of singing each have their appropriate application, why seek their source far away? One need only draw upon oneself.

For the person is established through virtue: when the person is upright, virtue is perfected. Virtue finds expression through song: when virtue becomes manifest, song gives it sustained utterance. Thus, whether maintaining a disposition of stillness and composure or observing a standard of reverence and frugality, one leaves nothing unprovided for in cultivating oneself. Whether nurturing a generous and accommodating nature or fully developing one’s capacity for firmness and resolution, one leaves nothing incomplete in perfecting oneself. Once the way of uprightness and rectitude is securely embodied in oneself, the stirring radiance of virtue cannot remain concealed in song.

Through this, harmony and accord suffice to bring one’s finest qualities into expression, while one’s Heaven-endowed nature can reveal the subtle springs of its continuous activity. How, then, could the transforming influence of song stop there? I see…

text:
法象莫大乎天地也而天地於我乎應焉貞觀
之道其範圍之矣變通莫大乎四時也而四時
於我乎和焉錯行之運其彌綸之矣仰以觀乎
星辰之紀有以見其理也而何有於忒乎遠以
觀乎萬物之賾有以見其育也而何有於害乎
是知歌本諸身則其體立德顯諸歌則其用行
君子安可不知所先務而徒求宜於歌也邪抑
嘗考諸虞典而有以知師乙之言之有自也舜
以典樂命夔而其教胄子者必始之以直寬剛
===

述其功則又有所謂鳳儀獸舞之盛焉其因古
昔聖王作樂之本與學者合而觀之然後知師
乙之言有所自而直己之功不可緩也
故明乎其節之志以不失其事則功成而
德行立

故明乎其節之志，以不失其事，則功成而德行立。

translation_en:
…No models are greater than Heaven and Earth, yet Heaven and Earth respond to me: the Way of their constant manifestation is encompassed herein. No transformations are greater than those of the four seasons, yet the four seasons harmonize with me: their alternating movements are comprehensively ordered herein. Looking upward to observe the ordered courses of the stars, one can see their proper regulation—how could there be any deviation? Looking far afield to observe the mysteries of the myriad things, one can see their flourishing—how could there be any harm? Thus we know that when song is rooted in oneself, its substance is established; when virtue is manifested through song, its functioning takes effect. How could the gentleman fail to recognize what he must attend to first and merely seek what is fitting in song?

Moreover, I have examined the Canon of Yu and thereby come to understand that Music Master Yi’s words have a source. Shun charged Kui with directing music. In teaching the sons of the nobility, Kui necessarily began with uprightness, generosity, firmness, and simplicity, proceeded to poetry, song, tones, and pitch standards, and culminated in harmony between spirits and human beings. When Kui himself described his achievements, there was also the magnificent spectacle of phoenixes appearing in stately bearing and beasts dancing. Was this because he followed the foundation upon which the sage kings of antiquity made music? Students must consider these accounts together; only then will they understand that Music Master Yi’s words have a source, and that the work of making oneself upright cannot be delayed.

“Thus, by understanding the intent of its musical measures and not failing in the activity, achievement is completed and virtuous conduct established.”

Wang Yizhong

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Supervising Secretary: “The exposition is clear and fluent. This composition, too, aspires to …”

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
功德者與
考試官左庶子江批詞有音節可誦
惟因射而盡其義斯效大矣甚矣德業之備於
射也明其節之義而效獲焉射之道其重矣哉
且天子諸侯卿大夫士之射也曰騶虞貍首曰
采蘋采蘩射行而詩以應是之謂節也曰備官
時會曰循法修職詩歌而義以存是之謂志也
誠使射者之於節也因辭以會其意而不徒為
聞見之知由聲以析其旨而必究夫精微之蘊
===
則志之所趨者定矣於是以志而見諸用也隨
分以迪夫常體至理於修為之間因責以盡其
實服妙道於彌綸之際則事之所行者力矣夫
如是殆見其發之為勛業也加諸天下國家者
雖不同而各懋乎勳庸之盛文明以普可大之
業斯著焉蘊之為德行也具於君臣上下者雖
不一而各臻夫褒道之旋純粹以精日新之德
斯備焉盖功者事之積也德行者功之本也顧
有事舉而功弗成功成而德行弗立者哉有志

則志之所趨者定矣於是以志而見諸用也隨
分以迪夫常體至理於修爲之閒因責以盡其
實服妙道於彌綸之際則事之所行者力矣夫
如是殆見其發之爲勛業也加諸天下國家者
雖不同而各懋乎勳庸之盛文明以普可大之
業斯著焉藴之爲德行也具於君臣上下者雖
不一而各臻夫履道之旋純粹以精日新之德
斯備焉盖功者事之積也德行者功之本也顧
有事舉而功弗成功成而德行弗立者哉有志
punctuated:
功德者與？
考試官左庶子江批：詞有音節，可誦。
惟因射而盡其義，斯效大矣。甚矣，德業之備於射也！明其節之義而效獲焉，射之道其重矣哉！且天子、諸侯、卿、大夫、士之射也，曰《騶虞》《貍首》，曰《采蘋》《采蘩》，射行而詩以應，是之謂節也；曰備官、時會，曰循法、修職，詩歌而義以存，是之謂志也。誠使射者之於節也，因辭以會其意，而不徒為聞見之知；由聲以析其旨，而必究夫精微之蘊，則志之所趨者定矣。於是以志而見諸用也，隨分以迪夫常，體至理於修為之間；因責以盡其實，服妙道於彌綸之際，則事之所行者力矣。夫如是，殆見其發之為勛業也，加諸天下國家者雖不同，而各懋乎勳庸之盛，文明以普，可大之業斯著焉；蘊之為德行也，具於君臣上下者雖不一，而各臻夫褒道之旋，純粹以精，日新之德斯備焉。盖功者，事之積也；德行者，功之本也。顧有事舉而功弗成，功成而德行弗立者哉？有志
translation_en:
…one who aspires to achievement and virtue?
Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “The language has rhythm and cadence and lends itself to recitation.”
Only by fully realizing the moral significance of archery can its effects become great. How fully virtue and accomplishment are embodied in archery! When one understands the meaning of its musical measures and achieves their effects, how weighty the Way of archery becomes! When the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, grand masters, and gentlemen practice archery, they use the songs “Zouyu,” “Lishou,” “Gathering Duckweed,” and “Gathering Southernwood.” The shooting proceeds in accord with the poems: this is what is called its musical measure. Providing a full complement of officials, attending audiences at the appointed times, following established rules, and fulfilling official duties—these meanings are preserved in the singing of the poems: this is what is called their intent. If archers truly apprehend the meaning of these measures through their lyrics, rather than merely acquiring knowledge through hearing and seeing, and analyze their purport through their sounds, thoroughly investigating their subtle implications, then the direction of their aspirations will be settled. When they then put those aspirations into practice, following the constant norms according to their allotted stations and embodying ultimate principle in their self-cultivation and conduct, fulfilling the substance of their responsibilities and practicing the wondrous Way in comprehensively ordering affairs, they will act with vigor.
In this way, when these aspirations issue forth as meritorious achievements, their application to the realm, the state, or the family may differ, yet each person will strive for outstanding accomplishments. As cultured enlightenment spreads everywhere, undertakings capable of greatness will become manifest. When these aspirations are stored within as virtuous conduct, their embodiment in ruler and minister, superior and subordinate, may differ, yet each will attain the fulfillment of the exalted Way [?]. Through purity and refinement, virtue renewed daily will become complete. Achievement is the accumulation of deeds; virtuous conduct is the foundation of achievement. Could there indeed be deeds carried out without achievement being accomplished, or achievement accomplished without virtuous conduct being established? Those who aspire…

於功德者盍於射焉求之夫射一藝而已然大
義存焉古之人以之正己以之擇士以之則安
則譽於天下者重夫義也故曰事之盡禮樂而

translation_en:
…those intent upon achievement and virtue—why should they not seek them in archery? Archery is but a single art, yet great moral principles reside in it. The ancients used it to rectify themselves and to select worthy men; through it they attained peace and renown throughout the realm, because they valued its moral principles. Thus it is said: “Among activities that fully embody ritual and music and can be practiced repeatedly to establish virtuous conduct, none equals archery. Hence the sage kings devoted themselves to it.” Otherwise, it would merely be an art. How could it then serve to reveal virtue? Surely this is why the moral principles of archery are valued!
Second Session
Discourse
“Enduring Continuance Is the Means by Which Things Are Brought to Completion”
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Chief Supervising Secretary: Candidates can generally discuss the achievements of utmost sincerity, readily writing several thousand words; yet their patchwork borrowings and strained connections are thoroughly tiresome. In precise and penetrating understanding, sound and correct argumentation, and exceptional spirit and scope, none compares with this essay [?]. It is therefore selected for inclusion as a model.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Examining Editor: The virtue of Heaven and the kingly Way fundamentally admit no distinction between outer and inner, or between prior and subsequent: they are one all-pervading Way. It is precisely through this that a true king, by enduring continuance, brings things to completion and becomes a counterpart to Heaven and Earth. Close examination reveals the profundity of this composition; it contains not a single empty expression. Its author has devoted his mind to inward cultivation, and so it is selected for inclusion.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Compiler: Bringing things to completion through enduring continuance is simply a matter of setting this process in motion through utmost sincerity. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
誠而精實明暢畧無斧鑿痕是必深於性學者首薦何忝
同考試官編修彭批天地聖人用處作者類能
言之至於不二不息所以為三才樞紐者實難措詞是
作邃旨精深根極底裏其有見於天人之撰者乎
同考試官修撰沈批至誠功用作者類多汗漫
獨此篇根極要領發揮精到雖數言而中庸全書具在
是矣非老成深見何以得此錄之用為天下式
考試官左庶子江批此題義理淵微舉中庸一
篇大要包括殆盡所謂體用一原顯微無間之旨於
===
此見之顧塲中士子類多掇拾陳言漫語綴緝滿篇
殊為可厭披閲困頓中忽得此卷豁然如遊昭曠濯
清風矣高薦之且錄之以示窮理之學
聖人所以參天地而成其化者亦唯運之以不
息之心而已矣心之不息者非他也誠也天下
之道誠則不息有息則非誠矣誠也者命之源
也命也者性之本也性也者心之理也心也者
化之所繇出也合性與命而繇心以出化一誠
之所貫也是故誠則不待存而自無不存矣無

===
清風矣喝薦之且録之以示窮理之學
聖人所以參天地而成其化者亦唯運之以不
息之心而已矣心之不息者非他也誠也天下
之道誠則不息有息則非誠矣誠也者命之源

punctuated:
誠而精實明暢，畧無斧鑿痕，是必深於性學者，首薦何忝？

同考試官編修彭批：天地聖人用處，作者類能言之。至於不二不息所以為三才樞紐者，實難措詞。是作邃旨精深，根極底裏，其有見於天人之撰者乎？

考試官左庶子江批：此題義理淵微，舉中庸一篇大要包括殆盡。所謂體用一原、顯微無間之旨，於此見之。顧塲中士子類多掇拾陳言，漫語綴緝滿篇，殊為可厭。披閲困頓中，忽得此卷，豁然如遊昭曠、濯清風矣。高薦之，且錄之，以示窮理之學。

Associate Examiner Peng, Compiler, comments: Most writers can discuss the workings of Heaven, Earth, and the sage. Yet it is truly difficult to express how being undivided and unceasing constitutes the pivot of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity. This composition penetrates deeply into the subtle meaning and reaches its innermost foundations. Might its author have discerned the workings of Heaven and humanity?

Associate Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler, comments: Writers discussing the efficacy of utmost sincerity are generally diffuse and unrestrained. This essay alone reaches the essential foundations and develops them with precision. Though it contains only a few words, the entire Doctrine of the Mean is present in them. Without mature judgment and profound insight, how could one achieve this? It is recorded here to serve as a model for all under Heaven.

Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor, comments: The principles underlying this topic are profound and subtle; it embraces almost all the main purport of the Doctrine of the Mean. Here one sees the meaning of the saying that substance and function have a single source, and that the manifest and the subtle admit of no separation. Yet most candidates in the examination hall merely gather stale expressions and fill their essays with loosely stitched-together remarks, which is exceedingly tiresome. Exhausted by reading, I suddenly came upon this paper: at once I felt as though I were wandering in a bright, open expanse, bathed in a pure breeze. I recommend it highly and also record it here to illustrate the learning that investigates principle to its utmost.

The means by which the sage stands alongside Heaven and Earth and brings their transforming work to completion is simply to carry it forward with an unceasing mind. What makes the mind unceasing is nothing other than sincerity. In the Way of all under Heaven, sincerity entails ceaselessness; if there is any cessation, it is not sincerity. Sincerity is the source of Heaven’s endowment; Heaven’s endowment is the foundation of human nature; human nature is the principle of the mind; and the mind is that from which transformation proceeds. Bringing human nature and Heaven’s endowment together, and producing transformation through the mind, all are permeated by the one sincerity. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
□存則自無不應矣無不存且應則常存常應
而其化自無不悠且久矣夫惟其化之悠且久
也則物之囿于其化者又惡得而有弗成者哉
是故自其誠之有常也之謂不息自其化之有
成也之謂悠久而其所以爲誠之體則一也天
下之物皆誠之實體而至誠者亦自其實體而
成之耳是道也天得之以覆萬物地得之以載
萬物聖人得之以成萬物而萬物得之以覆載
於天地而成於聖人也其道一也故曰悠久所
===
以成物今夫天下皆知聖人成物之化矣而不
知其所以成之者誠之運悠且久也皆知聖人
誠之運之悠且久矣而不知其所以悠且久者
誠之體自不息也曷不觀諸天地乎今夫天靜
專動直而大生焉今夫地靜翕動闢而廣生焉
此其成物之功何如也然而不能以速成也彼
其氣序之流行也其屈伸則相感往来則相通
所以播而成物者盖冲然其悠且久也至其貞
觀之理確然而示人以易也隤然而示人以簡

translation_en:
…present everywhere [?], it naturally responds to everything. Being present everywhere and responding to everything, it is constantly present and constantly responsive, and its transforming influence naturally extends far and endures long. Precisely because its transforming influence extends far and endures long, how could anything within its scope fail to attain completion? Thus, viewed in terms of the constancy of sincerity, this is called “unceasing”; viewed in terms of the completion achieved by its transforming influence, it is called “far-reaching and enduring.” Yet what constitutes the substance of sincerity is one and the same. All things under Heaven are concrete embodiments of sincerity, and one possessed of utmost sincerity merely brings them to completion on the basis of their concrete substance. Heaven obtains this Way and thereby covers the myriad things; Earth obtains it and thereby bears them; the sage obtains it and thereby brings them to completion. The myriad things obtain it and are thereby covered and borne by Heaven and Earth and brought to completion by the sage. The Way is one and the same. Thus it is said: “Being far-reaching and enduring is how it brings things to completion.”
Now, everyone under Heaven knows the transforming influence by which the sage brings things to completion, but they do not know that what enables him to complete them is the far-reaching and enduring operation of sincerity. Everyone knows that the operation of the sage’s sincerity extends far and endures long, but they do not know that it does so because the substance of sincerity is itself unceasing. Why not observe this in Heaven and Earth? Heaven, when still, is concentrated; when moving, it is direct, and thus gives birth on a great scale. Earth, when still, gathers inward; when moving, it opens outward, and thus gives birth far and wide. How great is their accomplishment in bringing things to completion! Yet they cannot accomplish this hastily. As their vital force flows through its successive phases, its contraction and expansion stimulate one another, and its coming and going communicate with one another. What enables it to spread abroad and bring things to completion is its tranquil, far-reaching, and enduring operation. As for the principle manifest in their constancy, Heaven steadfastly shows people ease, and Earth compliantly shows people simplicity…

息之心也所謂誠也物得之以自成而受成於
天地焉者也向使天地而匪誠則其運且息矣
天地而自息其運則乾坤亦幾乎毀矣而尚何

群然而仰成於聖人者為物亦衆矣而聖人者
欲參天地而不成之則其為化亦豈可以旦夕
而幾也乎是故聖人於此亦惟運其不息之心

translation_en:
…it is also enduring and unchanging, wholly unified and constant. This is the unceasing heart of Heaven and Earth: what is called sincerity. Things obtain it to fulfill themselves, thereby receiving their fulfillment from Heaven and Earth. Were Heaven and Earth without sincerity, their operations would cease. If Heaven and Earth themselves ceased their operations, Qian and Kun—the creative and receptive powers—would come close to destruction. How, then, could they still bring things to fulfillment? By observing Heaven and Earth, we can understand the sage.

Among Heaven and Earth, the things that together look to the sage for fulfillment are numerous indeed. Yet if the sage wishes to form a triad with Heaven and Earth but does not bring them to fulfillment [?], how could his transforming work be expected to succeed in a single morning or evening? Thus, in this, the sage merely puts his unceasing heart into operation. This heart is the very substance of sincerity; it is that by which Heaven and Earth bring things to fulfillment, and which things obtain to fulfill themselves.

Precisely because things obtain it yet cannot bring their fulfillment to completion, there are achievements that even Heaven and Earth cannot accomplish unaided. Hence things cannot but look to the sage for fulfillment. The sage’s heart communicates fully with his nature; his nature communicates fully with his allotted mandate; and his mandate communicates fully with Heaven. Thus his heart, which brings things to fulfillment, is itself necessarily unceasing. How, then, could the sage form a triad with Heaven and Earth and complete their transforming work without setting it in motion through his own unceasing heart?

And what, indeed, is this ceaselessness of the sage’s heart? Vigilance and apprehension are the foundation of sincerity, and the sage is never without vigilance and apprehension. Watchfulness over oneself when alone is the subtle inception of sincerity, and the sage is never without such watchfulness. Profound reverence, and Heaven [?]…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
已者誠之至也而聖人則無不恭而無所已也
此皆其誠之必至而非有所勉焉者是故其行
之而為達德也推之而為達道也布之而為九
經也立之而為三重也散之而為三千三百也
錯之而為容為執為敬為別也形之而為著為
明為動為變也盖自其居室之近而達之乎華
夏蠻貊之遠自其言行之庸而察之乎天地之
大皆其成物之事也則亦皆其不息之心而運
之也而安得不悠且久邪故今自其外而觀之

正而勿助也其居也有容不隘而不溢也是何

其虛也至一而其應自直也其體也至信而其
達自順也其靜也至常而其動自定也是又何
如其久也所以幹乎其悠也又自其合内外而
觀之則盛德大業體用一原時出而無窮也天
德王道顯微無間敦裕而不已也是悠也久也

translation_en:
…ceasing [?] is the culmination of sincerity; yet the sage is reverent in everything and never ceases. All these are necessary fulfillments of his sincerity, involving no forced effort. Thus, when he puts it into practice, it becomes the universally applicable virtues; when he extends it, it becomes the universally applicable ways; when he distributes it, it becomes the nine guiding principles; when he establishes it, it becomes the three weighty matters; when he deploys it in detail, it becomes the three thousand and three hundred rules of ritual. In its varied applications, it becomes proper bearing, proper holding of objects, reverence, and distinctions; in its manifestation, it becomes conspicuousness, clarity, the power to move others, and transformation. From the proximity of his own dwelling it reaches to the distant lands of Huaxia and the Man and Mo peoples; from ordinary speech and conduct it becomes manifest throughout the vastness of Heaven and Earth. These are all his work of bringing things to fulfillment, and all are set in motion by his unceasing mind. How, then, could this fail to be far-reaching and enduring?

Now, viewed from without, his extension of it has an order: he neither contends nor hastens. His waiting proceeds by degrees: he neither fixes upon an expected result nor forces its growth. His abiding has capaciousness: it is neither cramped nor overflowing. How far-reaching this is! This is how he gives effect to its endurance. Viewed from within, his emptiness is supremely unified, and his responses are naturally upright; his underlying substance is supremely trustworthy, and its expression is naturally harmonious; his stillness is supremely constant, and his activity is naturally settled. How enduring this also is! This is how he sustains its far-reaching scope.

Viewed, further, in the union of inner and outer, his abundant virtue and great accomplishments have substance and function issuing from a single source, appearing as circumstances require and never exhausted. Heavenly virtue and the kingly Way admit no separation between the manifest and the subtle; they are substantial and ample, and never cease. This far-reaching scope and this endurance are simply set in motion by the sage’s unceasing mind. Even the sage himself does not…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
知其為悠且久也是故其積之也博厚而不可
極其發之也高明而不可窮始也聖人不過盡
吾之誠以成已之性而其既也則萬物亦各正
其性而受成于聖人之誠矣是何也久於其道
而天下化成言而民莫不信也行而民莫不悅
也見而民莫不敬也達德刑而民作孚也達道
立而民興行也九經正而民報効也三重建而
民寡過也三千三百之禮範圍而曲成民自不
賞而勸不怒而威也然此其感應之間猶有所
===
待耳及夫無待而成則亦殺之弗怨利之弗庸
民日遷善而不知為之者矣夫是以尊親通乎
蠻貊位育極乎天地雖百世以俟聖人而不惑
矣然而聖人不息之心固猶夫初也故曰聖人
所以參天地而成其化亦惟運其不息之心而
已矣雖然聖人誠者也其不息也不思而不勉
也未至於聖人而思有以誠之當如何曰擇善
其端也固執其實也為已而知幾其立心之始
也而程子又曰其要只在謹獨夫能謹獨則心

知其為悠且久也。是故，其積之也，博厚而不可極；其發之也，高明而不可窮。始也，聖人不過盡吾之誠，以成已之性；而其既也，則萬物亦各正其性，而受成于聖人之誠矣。是何也？久於其道，而天下化成。言而民莫不信也，行而民莫不悅也，見而民莫不敬也。達德刑而民作孚也，達道立而民興行也，九經正而民報効也，三重建而民寡過也。三千三百之禮，範圍而曲成，民自不賞而勸，不怒而威也。然此其感應之間，猶有所待耳。及夫無待而成，則亦殺之弗怨，利之弗庸，民日遷善而不知為之者矣。夫是以尊親通乎蠻貊，位育極乎天地，雖百世以俟聖人而不惑矣。然而聖人不息之心，固猶夫初也。故曰：聖人所以參天地而成其化，亦惟運其不息之心而已矣。

雖然，聖人，誠者也；其不息也，不思而不勉也。未至於聖人，而思有以誠之，當如何？曰：擇善，其端也；固執，其實也；為已而知幾，其立心之始也。而程子又曰：「其要只在謹獨。」夫能謹獨，則心
translation_en:
…know that his activity is far-reaching and enduring. Thus, what he accumulates is broad and substantial beyond all measure; what he manifests is lofty and luminous beyond all limit. At first, the sage merely realizes his own sincerity fully, thereby bringing his own nature to fulfillment. In the end, however, all things also attain the proper realization of their respective natures and receive their fulfillment through the sage’s sincerity. Why is this? By enduring in his Way, he transforms and perfects all under Heaven. When he speaks, none among the people fail to trust him; when he acts, none fail to delight in him; when he appears, none fail to revere him. When the universally applicable virtues are exemplified, the people become trustworthy; when the universally applicable relationships are established, the people are stirred to practice them; when the nine guiding principles of government are set right, the people respond with service; when the three weighty institutions are established, the people commit few errors. The three hundred major and three thousand minor rules of ritual encompass everything and bring each particular to fulfillment. The people are naturally encouraged without rewards and held in awe without any display of anger. Yet this interaction between influence and response still depends upon something. When fulfillment comes without such dependence, even those put to death bear no resentment, and those benefited give him no credit. The people advance daily toward goodness without knowing who brings this about. Thus, reverence and affection for him extend even to the Man and Mo peoples; his work of setting things in their proper places and nourishing them reaches throughout Heaven and Earth. Even if he were to await a sage a hundred generations hence, he would have no doubts. Yet the sage’s unceasing heart remains just as it was at the beginning. Hence it is said: the means by which the sage stands alongside Heaven and Earth and completes their transforming work is simply the exercise of his unceasing heart.

Nevertheless, the sage is inherently sincere; his ceaseless activity requires neither deliberation nor effort. What, then, should someone do who has not yet attained sagehood but seeks a means of becoming sincere? The answer is: choosing the good is the starting point; holding firmly to it is the substance of the undertaking; cultivating oneself and discerning the first stirrings of things is the beginning of establishing one’s resolve. Master Cheng further said: “The essential point lies solely in vigilance when alone.” If one can maintain vigilance when alone, then the heart…

punctuated:
統性命，通極於誠，始於成已，終が成物。及其至也，亦將與天地參矣。
表
擬侍講學士宋濂等進《皇明寶訓》表
尤瑛
同考試官署郎中許批：恭惟我皇祖《寶訓》一書，中間綱紀兼總，直與典謨並傳。子能摸擬先臣類輯進呈之意，而詞復爾雅，故錄。
同考試官檢討張批：我聖祖耿光大烈，實賴此《寶訓》一書昭示無極。此作乃能揄揚盛美，而詞復渾雅。刻之，不獨以其駢儷之工也。
同考試官編修邢批：我聖祖嘉言善行，載在《寶訓》，所以垂憲萬世者。子能具述先臣忠愛之意，揄揚極盡，且典則而典麗，莊敬而文，表之佳者也，錄之。
translation_en:
…unifies one's nature and destiny and reaches the utmost in sincerity, beginning with perfecting oneself and ending with perfecting things [?]. Upon reaching its highest attainment, one will also stand alongside Heaven and Earth.

Memorial

A memorial modeled on Academician Expositor-in-Waiting Song Lian and others presenting the Precious Instructions of the August Ming (Huang Ming Baoxun).

By You Ying.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Acting Bureau Director: Reverently considering this book, the Precious Instructions of our imperial ancestor, it comprehensively encompasses the guiding principles and detailed rules of government and will be transmitted alongside the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents. You have successfully represented our predecessor officials' intentions in compiling, arranging, and presenting it; moreover, your language is refined and correct. I therefore select it for inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Examining Editor: The radiant glory and great achievements of our sagely progenitor truly depend upon this book, the Precious Instructions, to be made manifest for all time. This composition successfully extols his magnificent virtues, and its language is both rounded and elegant. It is being printed for more than just its skillful parallel phrasing.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, Compiler: The excellent words and good deeds of our sagely progenitor are recorded in the Precious Instructions, thereby bequeathing a model for all generations. You have fully expressed our predecessor officials' loyal devotion and extolled his virtues to the utmost. Moreover, the writing accords with classical standards and possesses classical elegance; it is solemn and reverent, yet accomplished in expression. This is an excellent memorial. Let it be included.

Plans bequeathed provide for descendants; ministers and people look up to a model for a hundred generations. The continuity between founding and preserving the dynasty depends upon the complete rectitude of its plans and achievements. Its brilliance joins that of the Kui and Bi constellations; its auspicious signs accord with the River Chart and Luo Writing. punctuated: 溥博淵泉而時出，會車書于一統，舞干羽于兩階。前後逾二十年，詔諭凡四十類。由渡江而至御極，絲綸藹仁義之言；自敬天以及制夷，綱紀總帝王之範。臣濂等謬叨甄拔，均沐寵私。學本愧于三長，愚莫效乎一得。給尚方之筆札，青簡難窮；飽大官之殽羞，素餐是懼。管窺穹昊，況思圖繪以何能？蠡測滄溟，敢云酌飲而自足？惟上厪重瞳之睿覽，抑先導義例之津涯。倬乎雲漢之光，言幾五萬；煥乎文章之美，傳並六經。伏願聖壽無疆，勳業同天地之悠久；皇圖有永，本支瞻
translation_en:
…vast and deep as a flowing spring, manifesting itself in due season, unifying carriage tracks and writing throughout the realm, and having the dance with shields and feathers performed between the two stairways. Spanning more than twenty years, the imperial edicts and instructions comprise forty categories. From the crossing of the Yangzi to the accession to the throne, the imperial pronouncements abound in words of benevolence and righteousness; from revering Heaven to governing the foreign peoples, their guiding principles encompass the exemplary standards of emperors and kings.

Your servants Lian and the others have undeservedly received selection and advancement, all alike enjoying Your Majesty’s favor. Our learning falls short of the three qualifications of a historian, and in our ignorance we cannot offer even a single useful insight. Supplied with brushes and writing materials from the Imperial Manufactories, we could scarcely exhaust the record even on bamboo slips; sated with delicacies from the imperial kitchen, we fear that we eat without earning our keep. We view the vast heavens through a narrow tube: how could we presume to depict them? We measure the boundless sea with a gourd: dare we claim that a mere draught suffices?

We would only trouble Your Majesty’s sagely gaze to examine this work, first offering a means of approaching its principles of compilation. Resplendent as the light of the Milky Way, its words number nearly fifty thousand; radiant in literary beauty, it shall be transmitted alongside the Six Classics. We humbly wish that Your Majesty’s sacred lifespan may be boundless, and that your achievements may endure as long as Heaven and Earth; that the imperial enterprise may last forever, and that the main and collateral branches of the imperial house may look upon…

第一問

translation_en:
…the renewed splendor of the sun and moon. Your servants Lian and the others have respectfully compiled, by subject, the Precious Instructions of the August Ming (Huang Ming baoxun) in five juan, and submit it together with this memorial for Your Majesty’s attention.

Third Session
Policy Essays
First Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Chief Supervising Secretary: “Reverence is the foundation of imperial governance. Since our imperial ancestor established the supreme standard, successive sage sovereigns have carried it forward, and today it flourishes especially abundantly. This essay excels at expounding it. Its author has evidently been deeply steeped in the transforming influence of the sage sovereign; this is more than mere literary skill.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler: “From antiquity, emperors and kings have upheld a single Way in succession: this reverence alone. Our sage founder initiated it in former times, and His Majesty has inherited and continued it thereafter. The transmission of this teaching of the mind flourishes to a degree unmatched in past or present. You have been able to bring it to the fore at the outset and discuss it; you may thus be close to understanding the intention behind the great sage’s establishment of institutions [illegible phrase: 於□]. Select this essay for inclusion.”

How could it be compared with the modest prosperity of the Tang house, which had only the good government of the Zhenguan reign? Yet the Essentials of Government circulated throughout the realm because Wu Jing wielded his brush at that time. Now, in compiling this Daily Calendar, the ministers have followed the ancient method of arranging events by year, assembling the record for presentation to the throne. Your servant Lian has presumptuously written a preface at the beginning. Ashamed of my shallow learning, I have failed to give full expression to its glories. Yet an edict has just ordered that it be preserved in secrecy, in a golden coffer within a stone chamber, so those below in remote places have been unable to behold this magnificence. It should therefore be compiled by subject and disseminated throughout the realm. Undeservedly receiving Your Majesty’s gracious recognition, I was specially granted approval. Following the imperial instructions, I have arranged and transcribed the material by category, awaiting further additions from subsequent records.

The Way transmitted among emperors and kings since antiquity, and the source of their method of cultivating the mind, have a long history indeed. In its simplest and most essential form, does it not consist in the endeavor to revere virtue? Reverence is where virtue gathers, the substance of the mind, and the source from which government proceeds. The government of emperors and kings is rooted in the mind, and the means by which they govern their minds is rooted in reverence. Since antiquity this has been unalterable. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
祖訓精誠錄近質以
皇上敬一箴其真有見於
制作之妙傳心之微而思有以對揚其盛美
乎請敬陳之昔在唐虞授受典謨孔彰始
以精一之言繼以執中之訓精者敬以擇
也一者敬以守也而中則敬之極功也當
時雖不言敬而敬之源始矣故放勳則欽
明允恭重華則温恭允塞斯則能敬之實
而其作歌則勅天時幾昌言則慎憲屢省
===
斯則持敬之功至其儆戒無虞敬修可願
上下協恭則又保敬之道此二帝所以允
蹈敬德而開心學之宗者也禹受舜而王
則兢業懋德慎修思永以敬而入聖湯纘
夏而興則顧諟明命欽崇天道以敬而反
身文武繼商而作則無斁之保敬勝之吉
又皆以敬而永命此三王所以休迪前聖
而傳心學之法者也是故肇人文之盛以
啟後王莫過於二帝垂典則之訓以貽後

punctuated:
《祖訓》、《精誠錄》，近質以皇上《敬一箴》，其真有見於制作之妙、傳心之微，而思有以對揚其盛美乎？請敬陳之。
昔在唐虞，授受典謨，孔彰，始以精一之言，繼以執中之訓。精者，敬以擇也；一者，敬以守也；而中則敬之極功也。當時雖不言敬，而敬之源始矣。故放勳則欽明允恭，重華則温恭允塞，斯則能敬之實；而其作歌則勅天時幾，昌言則慎憲屢省，斯則持敬之功。至其儆戒無虞，敬修可願，上下協恭，則又保敬之道。此二帝所以允蹈敬德，而開心學之宗者也。
禹受舜而王，則兢業懋德，慎修思永，以敬而入聖；湯纘夏而興，則顧諟明命，欽崇天道，以敬而反身；文武繼商而作，則無斁之保，敬勝之吉，又皆以敬而永命。此三王所以休迪前聖，而傳心學之法者也。是故肇人文之盛，以啟後王，莫過於二帝；垂典則之訓，以貽後
translation_en:
…the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun) and the Record of Utmost Sincerity (Jingcheng lu), and testing these against the more recent Admonition on Reverence and Oneness (Jingyi zhen) by His Majesty. Have you not truly perceived the marvelous character of these imperial compositions and the subtlety of the transmission of the mind, and sought thereby to extol their magnificent excellence? Allow me respectfully to set forth my explanation.
In ancient times, under Tang and Yu, the transmission and reception of rule were abundantly illuminated in the Canon and Counsels. First came the words concerning refinement and oneness, followed by the injunction to hold fast to the Mean. Refinement means choosing through reverence; oneness means maintaining one's hold through reverence; and the Mean is the ultimate achievement of reverence. Although reverence was not explicitly named at that time, its source was already established. Thus Fangxun, that is, Yao, was reverent, discerning, sincere, and respectful; Chonghua, that is, Shun, was gentle and respectful, with sincerity pervading him. These were the actual manifestations of their capacity for reverence. In composing his song, Shun urged attentiveness to Heaven's mandate, to proper timing, and to the first stirrings of events; in offering excellent counsel, his minister urged caution regarding established standards and repeated self-examination. These were the efforts by which reverence was maintained. As for remaining watchful when there was no cause for alarm, reverently cultivating what was worthy of aspiration, and joining in respect from the highest to the lowest, these were further ways of preserving reverence. This is how the Two Emperors truly practiced reverent virtue and founded the tradition of learning of the mind.
Yu received rule from Shun and became king: vigilant and diligent, he exerted himself in virtue, cultivated himself carefully, and gave thought to the enduring future. Through reverence he attained sagehood. Tang succeeded the Xia and rose to power: he kept the luminous mandate constantly before him and reverently honored the Way of Heaven. Through reverence he examined himself. Wen and Wu succeeded the Shang and arose: through unwearying preservation and the good fortune that comes when reverence prevails, they too prolonged their mandate through reverence. This is how the Three Kings nobly followed the earlier sages and transmitted the method of learning of the mind. Thus, in initiating the flourishing of human culture and opening the way for later kings, none surpassed the Two Emperors; in handing down teachings embodying constant standards to bequeath to later…

裔，莫備于三王。自是以還，漢唐宋之君，學不知敬，既於聖人之道有所未聞；而敬不知本，其於聖人之心，又安有所得也哉？逮我皇明，高皇帝有克明濬哲之德，有日躋緝熈之心，固已邁王而並帝矣。文皇繼承，時則有《聖學心法》之書。有統言者，義難分述，君臣二篇是也；有專言者，事各有指，學問以下是也。

translation_en:
…descendants, none were more comprehensive than the Three Kings. From that time onward, the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song pursued learning without understanding reverence, and thus remained uninstructed in aspects of the Way of the sages. Moreover, in their reverence they did not understand its foundation: how, then, could they have attained any understanding of the sages’ minds? With the advent of our august Ming, Emperor Gao possessed the virtue of luminous discernment and profound wisdom, and a mind that advanced daily toward ever greater brilliance. He had assuredly surpassed the Three Kings and equaled the Two Emperors. Emperor Wen succeeded him, and in his time there appeared the book Methods of the Mind in Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa). Some chapters speak comprehensively, their principles being difficult to expound separately: these are the two chapters on rulers and ministers. Others speak of particular matters, each with its own subject: these are the chapters beginning with “Learning and Inquiry.”
There are five human relationships; that the book speaks only of ruler and minister, and father and son, is indeed because, as a book for emperors and kings, it has a particular purpose in bequeathing a model. For succession from one generation through ten thousand generations, the Way of father and son is of great weight; for one man to govern and nurture all regions, the Way of ruler and minister is urgent. This is why the book concentrates on these two relationships. Yet when it speaks of the governance of the inner palace, it includes the Way of empresses and consorts, and thus does not omit the relationship between husband and wife. When it speaks of harmony among kin, it includes the Way governing the nine degrees of kinship, and thus does not omit the relationship between elder and younger. When it speaks of the Way of ministers, the officials are friends to one another, so that relationship, too, is not omitted. This is why the book encompasses all five. This book carries forward, from the past, …

聖祖，旣對揚而有光；下啓神裔，又垂裕而罔極。蓋嘗伏讀《聖祖精誠錄》與《祖訓》矣，一則首以敬天之篇，一則先以創守之訓，是聖敬之布在方冊者，皇祖已開其先矣。又嘗伏誦皇上聖製《敬一》之箴矣，曰敬則妙乎心傳，曰一則純乎天理，是聖敬之見於著作者，皇上又闡其蘊矣。

…the Sagely Ancestor, it has gloriously acknowledged and proclaimed his legacy; in opening the way for his divine descendants, it has also bequeathed blessings without limit. I have humbly read the Record of the Sagely Ancestor’s Utmost Sincerity (Shengzu jingcheng lu) and the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun). The one opens with a chapter on revering Heaven, the other with instructions on founding and preserving the dynasty. Thus, the Imperial Ancestor had already taken the lead in setting forth sagely reverence in written works. I have also humbly recited Your Majesty’s imperially composed Admonition on Reverence and Oneness (Jingyi). Its word “reverence” expresses the subtlety of the transmission of the mind; its word “oneness” expresses the purity of Heaven’s principle. Thus, Your Majesty has further elucidated the profound meaning of sagely reverence as expressed in writing.
Accordingly, when the Methods of the Mind discusses the way of the ruler, it necessarily begins with learning: this speaks to the effort required to cultivate reverence. It next treats revering Heaven: this speaks to the essential point of cultivating reverence. One who can be reverent can take Heaven and the ancestors as models. The work has four main divisions and twenty-nine subsidiary sections; in essence, all concern reverence and learning, and express the wish to provide for descendants. Thus, the preface to Methods of the Mind in Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa) begins by speaking of those who establish the dynasty and transmit its succession …

君經歷艱難，終言世世修德，無敢或懈。其始終一於敬，有如是者。大哉，敬乎！帝王學之，至皇祖而益明，文皇述之，至皇上而大著。自此與天地無疆，皆是道也。是以東宮育德，仰瞻帝躬，至教固有所承矣。然而祖宗之製，固為聖子神孫發也。他日以備出閣講讀，正所以衍此道於無疆者，又何疑邪？若夫唐之帝範，此特聖人盛德之至，取其篇名之義耳，何啻天壤而可倫乎？謹對。

第二問
translation_en:
… ruler’s experience of hardship, and ends by speaking of cultivating virtue generation after generation, never daring to slacken. Such is its unwavering commitment to reverence from beginning to end. Great indeed is reverence! Emperors and kings studied it; with the Imperial Ancestor it became still clearer. Emperor Wen transmitted it; with Your Majesty it has become fully manifest. Henceforth, for as long as Heaven and Earth endure, all will follow this Way. Thus the Crown Prince, nurturing his virtue and looking reverently to Your Majesty’s own person, assuredly has a source from which to receive the highest teaching. Yet the works of the imperial ancestors were indeed composed for their sagely sons and divine grandsons. To provide them in due course for the Crown Prince’s lectures and readings upon his coming out to the outer apartments is precisely the means of perpetuating this Way without end. What further doubt can there be? As for the Tang work Model for Emperors (Difan), it is merely that the sage, in the fullness of his abundant virtue, has adopted the meaning of its title. The difference between them is greater even than that between Heaven and Earth: how could they be compared? Respectfully submitted in reply.

Second Question

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
周士佐
同考試官署郎中許批心法並用內外咸舉此
成周所以有道之長子能援古條答宛然在目至我
朝立國延休配周遠過與我
皇上覲揚光大高出隆古之意且敷揚有體忠懇無窮錄之不直取其

聖祖

旨其甞究心於治化之源而有得者歟

Zhou Shizuo

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Acting Director: Cultivation of the mind and methods of government are employed together, and internal and external affairs are both addressed: this is why the perfected Zhou order so long possessed the Way. You draw on antiquity and answer point by point, bringing it vividly before our eyes. As for our dynasty’s founding and the perpetuation of its blessings, matching and far surpassing Zhou [?], and our Emperor’s purpose of gloriously manifesting and enlarging this legacy [?], rising far above high antiquity, you expound these matters with appropriate form and inexhaustible loyal sincerity. In selecting this essay, we value more than its literary qualities alone.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Examining Editor: To take sincerity of intention and anxious diligence as the foundation for accomplishing the great enterprise of ordering the realm has been the way by which emperors and kings have achieved good government since antiquity. It is likewise through this that our Sagely Progenitor and our Emperor have surpassed the Three Dynasties and risen to the level of Tang and Yu. This composition alone expounds and elucidates the matter fully, leaving none of its meaning unexplained. Surely its author has devoted himself to investigating the source of good government and moral transformation, and gained insight into it?

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, Compiler: Most candidates can speak of cultivating internal affairs and repelling external threats. But this policy essay explains fully and in detail the actual sincerity of intention and anxious diligence involved; it plainly does not treat these as mere methods alone. In the learning required to order the realm, whom could we choose but you?

Comment by Associate Examiner Ouyang, Compiler: Poems such as “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao) and “Gathering Ferns” (Caiwei) embody the spirit and lifeblood of Zhou’s kingly enterprise. Policies for cultivating internal affairs and repelling external threats all issue from this source. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
聖祖
皇上之神功大業同符先王尤為有見乎其潜心王道者乎
考試官左庶子江批天保采薇諸詩乃古帝王
經綸之道合內外而一之者故儒先每每稱之子能剖
析此義至於我
皇上聖德神功同符
聖祖而上躋古帝王之盛者尤能揄揚以風來世亦可以占子經綸之蘊
矣是用錄之
帝王經綸之迹布在方冊廣大精密賾然
===
而莫可究者其文也而其憂勤惻怛本諸
心以達諸政以致諸其民人盎然而有不
可解之情其實也得其實則其文舉矣不
得其實而惟其文之慕則亦徒法而已也
其何以幾帝王之盛乎哉執事策士而及
此是将以俊傑望士也顧愚何足以知此
雖然亦嘗觀之詩而得其槩矣請述以對
昔者有周盛時文武成康聖賢繼作周召
畢榮篤棐夾輔內而宅俊登庸民物煕皞

聖祖、皇上之神功大業，同符先王，尤為有見乎！其潜心王道者乎！

考試官左庶子江批：天保、采薇諸詩，乃古帝王經綸之道合內外而一之者，故儒先每每稱之。子能剖析此義，至於我皇上聖德神功同符聖祖，而上躋古帝王之盛者，尤能揄揚，以風來世，亦可以占子經綸之蘊矣。是用錄之。

帝王經綸之迹，布在方冊，廣大精密，賾然而莫可究者，其文也。而其憂勤惻怛，本諸心，以達諸政，以致諸其民人，盎然而有不可解之情，其實也。得其實，則其文舉矣；不得其實，而惟其文之慕，則亦徒法而已也。其何以幾帝王之盛乎哉？執事策士而及此，是将以俊傑望士也。顧愚何足以知此？雖然，亦嘗觀之詩而得其槩矣，請述以對。昔者有周盛時，文武成康，聖賢繼作；周召畢榮，篤棐夾輔。內而宅俊登庸，民物煕皞，
translation_en:
…the divine achievements and great undertakings of the Sagely Ancestor and His Majesty as matching those of the former kings: this shows exceptional insight! Surely he has devoted himself deeply to the Way of Kings!

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor: The poems “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao), “Gathering Ferns” (Caiwei), and others embody the ancient emperors’ and kings’ way of ordering the realm, uniting internal and external affairs as one. Thus earlier Confucian scholars repeatedly praised them. You have analyzed this meaning clearly. As for how His Majesty’s sagely virtue and divine achievements match those of the Sagely Ancestor and rise to the heights attained by the ancient emperors and kings, you have been especially able to celebrate them so as to instruct future generations. This also allows us to discern your reserves of ability to order the realm. For this reason, this answer has been selected for inclusion.

The traces of the emperors’ and kings’ ordering of the realm are recorded in books. Vast and comprehensive, precise and meticulous, so profound that they cannot be fully fathomed—these are its outward forms. But their anxious diligence and heartfelt solicitude, rooted in their hearts, extended to their government, and brought to bear upon their people, overflowing with a feeling that could never be dispelled—this is its substance. Grasp that substance, and the outward forms can all be put into effect. Fail to grasp that substance and merely admire the outward forms, and these remain nothing more than laws and methods alone. How could one thereby approach the greatness of the emperors and kings? In setting a policy question for candidates that addresses this matter, you gentlemen evidently expect outstanding talent from us. Yet how could someone as ignorant as I be capable of understanding it? Nevertheless, I have examined the Book of Odes and gained some general understanding of it. Allow me to set this out in reply.

In the flourishing age of Zhou, Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang succeeded one another as sages and worthies; the dukes of Zhou, Shao, Bi, and Rong faithfully assisted and supported them. Within the realm, men of outstanding talent were placed in office and advanced to service, and the people and all living things flourished in harmony…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
外而九夷八蠻罔不通道其治盖極其盛
矣自今觀之其治内也於鹿鳴吾得其燕
惠焉於四牡於皇華吾得其使臣焉於常
棣吾得其親親焉於伐木吾得其故舊不
遺焉此其恩意之聯屬悃愊之浹孚所謂
如元首股肱一體之相須如家人父子一
堂之相與今讀其詩尚可想見也是以實
勝者也其諸敦本辨族選材叙位之制如
封建學校之類之見於周禮者其文非不
===
較然著也今試取而行之其能感人動物
如彼其盛矣乎其治外也於采薇吾得其
遣役焉於出車吾得其勞帥焉於杕杜吾
得其勞戍焉此其憂傷勞苦之情體恤軫
愛之至所謂說以使民而民忘其勞說以
犯難而民忘其死今讀其詩亦可想見也
是亦以實勝者也其諸井邑車甸眚伐壇
削之制如井田軍旅之類之見於周禮者
其文非不犁然設也今試取而行之其又

…and abroad, the Nine Yi and Eight Man all maintained intercourse with the realm. Its governance had surely reached the height of flourishing. Looking back from the present, we see its domestic governance: in “The Deer Call” (Lu ming), I discern its gracious hospitality at banquets; in “The Four Stallions” (Si mu) and “The Splendid Flowers” (Huang hua), its treatment of ministers sent on missions; in “The Cherry Tree” (Chang di), its affection for kin; and in “Felling Trees” (Fa mu), its refusal to neglect old friends. Here were bonds of kindness and goodwill, and sincerity that permeated all and inspired mutual trust. This is what is meant by the head and limbs depending on one another as parts of a single body, and by fathers and sons associating as members of one household beneath one roof. Even today, reading these poems, we can still picture it. This was a triumph of substance. As for its institutions for strengthening fundamental bonds, distinguishing lineages, selecting talent, and assigning ranks—such things as the establishment of fiefs and schools, recorded in the Rites of Zhou—their formal arrangements were certainly clearly set forth. Yet if we were now to adopt and implement them, could they move people and stir all beings as profoundly as in that flourishing age?

As for its governance of external affairs: in “Gathering Bracken” (Cai wei), I discern how it dispatched men on military service; in “Sending Out the Chariots” (Chu che), how it honored commanders for their toil; and in “The Solitary Pear Tree” (Di du), how it honored returning garrison soldiers. Here were feelings of sorrow and concern for hardship, and the utmost sympathy and loving care. This is what is meant by employing the people with gladness so that they forget their toil, and leading them into danger with gladness so that they forget the prospect of death. Reading these poems today, we can likewise picture it. This too was a triumph of substance. As for its institutions concerning well-field and settlement units, chariot levies and dian districts, and punitive measures of chastisement, attack, and territorial reduction [?]—such things as the well-field system and military organization, recorded in the Rites of Zhou—their formal arrangements were certainly clearly laid down. Yet if we were now to adopt and implement them, could they in turn…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
能感人動物如彼其盛矣乎是何也情見
乎詩而制存於禮得於其禮而不得於其
詩者徒法也苟得於其詩則其實舉矣何
有於內何有於外何有於修且攘之莫舉
邪夫固周之所以盛也明是而漢而唐而
宋吾惑焉彼其幾於攘也而內日以虛幾
於修也而外日以不振甚則雜夷為治弁
其內外而失之極矣尚惡足言哉洪惟我
朝
===
太祖高皇帝再開天宇汛掃腥穢
成祖文皇帝三犁虜庭廓清氛孽

punctuated: 能感人動物，如彼其盛矣乎？是何也？情見乎詩，而制存於禮。得於其禮而不得於其詩者，徒法也。苟得於其詩，則其實舉矣。何有於內？何有於外？何有於修且攘之莫舉邪？夫固周之所以盛也。明是，而漢而唐而宋，吾惑焉。彼其幾於攘也，而內日以虛；幾於修也，而外日以不振。甚則雜夷為治，弁其內外，而失之極矣，尚惡足言哉！洪惟我朝太祖高皇帝再開天宇，汛掃腥穢；成祖文皇帝三犁虜庭，廓清氛孽；神聖繼作，謨烈重光。以關雎、麟趾之心，而行立政、周官之法。其在外也，節鎮外連，督府內制，屯戍萬里，守在四夷。濯靈赫聲，如風霆之流行；保大定功，如嶽鎮之底奠。蓋自有周以還，未之能過矣。其在內也，藩郡將尉以聯其族，部寺院司以辨其職，司府州縣以比其屬，鄉學國雍以明其教，則壤辨方
translation_en:
…could they move people and stir living things with such magnificent effect? Why is this so? Feelings appear in the Odes, while institutions are preserved in the Rites. To grasp what is in the Rites without grasping what is in the Odes is to possess mere regulations. If one grasps what is in the Odes, their substance is fully realized. What difficulty then remains in domestic affairs? What difficulty in external affairs? How could either internal cultivation or the repulsion of outsiders fail to be accomplished? This, indeed, was why Zhou flourished. Understanding this, I find the Han, Tang, and Song perplexing. When they came close to repelling outsiders, they grew daily weaker within; when they came close to internal cultivation, their power abroad declined daily. At worst, they brought barbarians into their government and confused [?] the internal and external realms, going utterly astray. What more is there worth saying of them?
Reflecting reverently upon our dynasty: Taizu, the Gao Emperor, opened heaven’s domain anew and swept away its foul pollution; Chengzu, the Wen Emperor, three times plowed through the enemy’s courts and cleared away their baleful influence. Divine and sagely rulers arose in succession, renewing the brilliance of their plans and achievements. With the spirit of “The Ospreys” (Guanju) and “The Qilin’s Hoof” (Linzhi), they put into practice the methods of “Establishing Government” (Lizheng) and “The Officers of Zhou” (Zhouguan).
In external affairs, the regional military commands link together beyond the capital, while the Chief Military Commissions exercise control from within. Military colonies and garrisons extend for ten thousand li, and defensive positions lie among the barbarians on all four sides. Their manifest might and resounding renown spread like wind and thunder; their preservation of greatness and consolidation of achievements are as firmly grounded as the great guardian mountains. Since the time of Zhou, nothing has surpassed this.
In domestic affairs, princely and commandery establishments, Generals, and Commandants bind together the imperial clan; Ministries, Courts, Offices, and Bureaus distinguish official duties; provincial Commissions, Prefectures, Subprefectures, and Counties organize subordinate jurisdictions; local schools and the Imperial University make instruction clear; and the grading of soils and differentiation of regions…

綿絡如江海之流轉盖自有周以還亦未
之能及矣
列聖紹休茂隆無替迨我
皇上神功聖德益有以覲揚而光大之以修則
盡倫而盡制以攘則克懷而克威是以重
熙累洽迅邁渙敷積之而益博厚發之而

以正其貢，體統尊嚴，如天日之照臨；氣勢綿絡，如江海之流轉。盖自有周以還，亦未之能及矣。列聖紹休，茂隆無替。迨我皇上，神功聖德，益有以覲揚而光大之。以修則盡倫而盡制，以攘則克懷而克威。是以重熙累洽，迅邁渙敷，積之而益博厚，發之而益高明，盖將上下與天地同流矣。猗歟休哉！而執事者尤欲責之以萬一之獻，愚固游於大化、順帝則而弗知者也，尚何能言？

translation_en:
…to regulate their tribute. The hierarchy is august and dignified, like heaven and the sun shining down; its vital force extends without interruption, like the circulating waters of rivers and seas. Indeed, since the Zhou, nothing has equaled it. Successive sage emperors carried forward this excellence, sustaining its flourishing grandeur without decline. Under our present Emperor, divine achievements and sagely virtue have further exalted and magnified it. In cultivating internal order, he fully realizes human relationships and institutions; in repelling external threats, he can both win allegiance and inspire awe. Thus brilliance follows brilliance and harmony accumulates upon harmony; his influence advances swiftly and spreads far. As it accumulates, it grows ever broader and deeper; as it manifests itself, it grows ever loftier and brighter. Indeed, above and below, it will flow together with Heaven and Earth. Ah, how splendid! Yet you who preside over this examination still ask me to offer some contribution, however slight. I am merely one who lives within this great transforming influence and follows the Emperor’s standards without being conscious of them. What, then, can I say?
I have heard that Ji Zha of Wu asked to observe the rites of Zhou, and the Grand Astrologer of Lu had the songs of the Two Southern Sections, the Airs of the States, the Elegantiae, and the Eulogies performed for him. The Song scholars Guishan and Kaoting discussed the poems up through “Heaven Preserves” (Tianbao) and those from “Gathering Bracken” (Caiwei) onward. One said, “What the former kings undertook was rooted in sincerity of intention.” The other said, “The rule of Kings Wen and Wu began in anxious diligence and ended in ease and joy.” This is truly the great foundation upon which emperors and kings order the realm; and our founding ancestors and successive sage emperors, together with our…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
皇上已試之明効也愚尚何能言哉不然則季
札亦何取於詩而安內攘外之道要亦不
外於鹿鳴諸什而得之是必有說矣請以
是終幸執事進而教之
第三問
瞿景淳
同考試官都給事中周批據事論事不必皆同得
尚友法而體裁即又迥出
同考試官檢討王批吾子品擬如此於以當世
===
知所行不惑矣
同考試官編修袁批古人心事不同惟類情者
能一之子能劑量不爽可謂有真見矣
同考試官編修彭批論世者非素有權度鮮
不眩于異同子能就事論事真千古斷案矣
同考試官修撰沈批古人事未易折衷此作
根據詳明議論渾厚是可與論其世也
考試官左庶子江批人物一策正欲觀諸士處心制
事之微而因以占諸它日子能隨事折衷不隨不亢

皇上已試之明效也愚尚何能言哉不然則季
札亦何取於詩而安內攘外之道要亦不
外於鹿鳴諸什而得之是必有說矣請以
是終幸執事進而教之
第三問
瞿景淳
同考試官都給事中周　批〔據事論事不必皆同得尚友法而體裁卽之適出〕
同考試官檢討王　批〔吾子品擬如此於以當世〕
===
同考試官編修袁　批〔古人心事不同惟類情者知所行不惑矣〕
同考試官編修彭　批〔論世者非素有權度鮮能一之子能劑量不爽可謂有真見矣〕
同考試官修撰沈　批〔古人事未易折衷此作不眩于異同子能就事論事真千古斷案矣〕
考試官左庶子江　批〔人物一策正欲觀諸士處心制根據詳明議論渾厚是可與論其世也〕
事之微而因以占諸它日子能隨事折衷不隨不亢
punctuated:
皇上已試之明効也。愚尚何能言哉？不然，則季札亦何取於詩？而安內攘外之道，要亦不外於鹿鳴諸什而得之，是必有說矣。請以是終，幸執事進而教之。

第三問
瞿景淳

同考試官都給事中周批：據事論事，不必皆同，得尚友法，而體裁即又迥出。

同考試官檢討王批：吾子品擬如此，於以當世，知所行不惑矣。

同考試官編修袁批：古人心事不同，惟類情者能一之。子能劑量不爽，可謂有真見矣。

同考試官編修彭批：論世者非素有權度，鮮不眩于異同。子能就事論事，真千古斷案矣。

同考試官修撰沈批：古人事未易折衷，此作根據詳明，議論渾厚，是可與論其世也。

考試官左庶子江批：人物一策，正欲觀諸士處心制事之微，而因以占諸它日。子能隨事折衷，不隨不亢，
translation_en:
…the manifest efficacy already demonstrated by His Majesty. What more can I, in my ignorance, say? Otherwise, what would Jizha have found of value in the Odes? The way to secure peace within and repel threats from without is, in essence, also to be found within the “Deer Call” (Lu ming) group of odes. There must surely be an explanation for this. Allow me to conclude here; I hope that you, Sir, will favor me with further instruction.

Third Policy Question
Qu Jingchun

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Chief Supervising Secretary: You discuss each matter on its own evidence, without insisting that all cases be alike. You have grasped the method of befriending the ancients, and the form and organization of your essay are also outstanding.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Examining Editor: With such appraisals and comparisons, you will know how to act when confronting the affairs of your own age, without being perplexed.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Compiler: The intentions and actions of the ancients differed; only someone who discerns affinities in their circumstances and feelings [?] can bring them into a coherent whole. Your weighing and measuring are unerring: you may indeed be said to possess true insight.

Comment by Associate Examiner Peng, Compiler: Unless those who discuss past ages have long cultivated standards of judgment, few escape bewilderment at similarities and differences. You can discuss each matter on its own terms. This is truly a definitive judgment for all ages.

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler: It is no easy matter to reach balanced judgments on the deeds of the ancients. This essay is detailed and clear in its supporting evidence, and substantial and measured in its argument. Its author is someone with whom one can discuss their times.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction: This policy question concerning historical figures was intended precisely to reveal the subtleties of the candidates’ intentions and their handling of affairs, and thereby to judge their future conduct. You can reach balanced judgments appropriate to each matter, neither following others blindly nor taking an obstinately contrary stance…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
權度蓋精切矣中行君子其在子乎是用高薦
君子之於天下也本之貞固以立其幹通
之權變以達其施而天下之能事畢矣何
也所貴乎君子者貴其同而能異也夫惟
匪貞既無以自異而匪變又無以大同於
是乎矯以為亢則亂常而拂倫詭以為隨
又習非而徇俗是二者皆非也君子弗由
也君子之所由者惟同而能異是故圓神
不倚而舉世不敢以為隨獨立不懼而舉
===
世不敢以為亢以是而通天下之志而成
天下之務蓋沛乎其順矣又何疑於其跡
之同弗同請因執事之問而陳之今夫周
公之吐握延賢以相成王而當天下之任
也彼孫抃之薦唐介為侍御史或謂抃未
之識則曰抃豈求識臺官者正以避市恩
之嫌耳若德宗時謁禁方嚴執政至闔門
謝客而裴度之拜相也則建請還第延訪
士夫以濟時艱此其心雖未必周公之誠

君子之於天下也本之貞固以立其幹通

也君子之所由者惟同而能異是故圓神
不倚而舉世不敢以爲隨獨立不懼而舉
===
世不敢以爲亢以是而通天下之志而成
天下之務盖沛乎其順矣又何疑於其跡
之同弗同請因執事之問而陳之今夫周
公之吐握延賢以相成王而當天下之任
也彼孫抃之薦唐介爲侍御史或謂抃未
之識則曰抃豈求識臺官者正以避市恩
之嫌耳若德宗時謁禁方嚴執政至闔門
謝客而裴度之拜相也則建請還第延訪
士夫以濟時艱此其心雖未必周公之誠
punctuated:
權度蓋精切矣！中行君子，其在子乎？是用高薦。

君子之於天下也，本之貞固以立其幹，通之權變以達其施，而天下之能事畢矣。何也？所貴乎君子者，貴其同而能異也。夫惟匪貞，既無以自異；而匪變，又無以大同。於是乎矯以為亢，則亂常而拂倫；詭以為隨，又習非而徇俗。是二者皆非也，君子弗由也。君子之所由者，惟同而能異。是故圓神不倚，而舉世不敢以為隨；獨立不懼，而舉世不敢以為亢。以是而通天下之志，而成天下之務，蓋沛乎其順矣，又何疑於其跡之同弗同？請因執事之問而陳之。

今夫周公之吐握，延賢以相成王，而當天下之任也。彼孫抃之薦唐介為侍御史，或謂抃未之識，則曰：「抃豈求識臺官者？」正以避市恩之嫌耳。若德宗時，謁禁方嚴，執政至闔門謝客；而裴度之拜相也，則建請還第延訪士夫，以濟時艱。此其心雖未必周公之誠
translation_en:
…Your judgment is indeed precise and penetrating! Might you be a gentleman who follows the mean? For this reason I recommend you highly.

In dealing with the world, the gentleman takes steadfast rectitude as his foundation, establishing his governing principles, and employs flexible judgment to put them into practice. Thus he accomplishes all that can be accomplished in the world. Why is this? What is valued in the gentleman is his ability to accord with others while also differing from them. Without rectitude, he has no means of distinguishing himself; without adaptability, he has no means of achieving broad concord. Yet if he affects aloofness, he disrupts enduring norms and violates proper human relationships; if he dissimulates in order to conform, he becomes habituated to error and panders to convention. Both courses are wrong, and the gentleman follows neither. His course is simply to accord with others while remaining capable of differing. Thus, adaptable and discerning without partiality, he cannot be regarded by anyone as a mere follower; standing alone without fear, he cannot be regarded by anyone as overbearing. Through this he brings the aspirations of the world into accord and accomplishes its affairs, proceeding freely and smoothly. Why, then, should there be doubt over whether his outward conduct accords with that of others? Allow me to explain in response to your question.

Now the Duke of Zhou would spit out his food and hold his unbound hair to receive worthy men, assisting King Cheng and bearing responsibility for the world. When Sun Bian recommended Tang Jie as Attendant Censor, someone remarked that he did not know Tang personally. He replied, “Am I someone who seeks acquaintance with censorial officials?” His purpose was precisely to avoid the suspicion of buying gratitude. In Emperor Dezong’s time, restrictions on visits were so strict that those governing even shut their doors and declined guests. Yet when Pei Du was appointed chief councilor, he proposed that he be allowed to return to his residence and receive and consult scholar-officials, so as to overcome the difficulties of the age. Although their intentions may not necessarily have possessed the Duke of Zhou’s sincerity…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
而其恪共則可尚矣祁奚之舉親舉賢以
答晉侯而嗣中軍之任也若王旦之薦寇
準為樞密使上謂準嘗短卿則曰臣位久
多闕正益見其無隱之忠耳至神宗時吕
正獻毎因公議數列安石而正獻之執政
也則多所汲引獨於其子不用此其心雖
不及祁奚之公而其直諒亦可嘉矣察吏
治者所以奠民庸也故范文正為叅政毎
見監司之不才者輒一筆勾之盖有得于
===
周官弊治之義矣而韓公億見諸路攟摭
官吏小過者輒不懌曰奈何錮人於聖世
是又虞廷宥過之仁焉顧一則亟於元惡
一則原於小眚跡雖異也而其心何嘗有
不同集衆思者所以廣忠益也故司馬光
之榜客位請以奏牘聞朝廷書狀規過失
盖有契于孔明之心矣而李文靖常言在
位無補惟中外所陳利害一切報罷則又
曹參寧一之風焉顧一則用之飾蠱一則

答晉侯而嗣中軍之任也若王旦之薦寇

見監司之不才者輒一筆勾之蓋有得于
===
周官敎治之義矣而韓公億見諸路擿擿
官吏小過者輒不懌曰宗何錮人於聖世
是又虞廷宥過之仁焉顧一則亟於元惡
一則原於小眚跡雖異也而其心何嘗有
不同集衆思者所以廣忠益也故司馬光
之榜客位請以奏牘閭朝廷書狀規過失
蓋有契于孔明之心矣而李文靖常言在
位無補惟中外所陳利害一切報罷則又
曹參寧一之風焉顧一則用之餙蠱一則
punctuated:
而其恪共則可尚矣。祁奚之舉親舉賢，以答晉侯而嗣中軍之任也，若王旦之薦寇準為樞密使，上謂準嘗短卿，則曰：「臣位久，多闕，正益見其無隱之忠耳。」至神宗時，吕正獻毎因公議數列安石，而正獻之執政也，則多所汲引，獨於其子不用。此其心雖不及祁奚之公，而其直諒亦可嘉矣。

察吏治者，所以奠民庸也。故范文正為叅政，毎見監司之不才者，輒一筆勾之，盖有得于周官弊治之義矣。而韓公億見諸路攟摭官吏小過者，輒不懌，曰：「奈何錮人於聖世？」是又虞廷宥過之仁焉。顧一則亟於元惡，一則原於小眚，跡雖異也，而其心何嘗有不同？

集衆思者，所以廣忠益也。故司馬光之榜客位，請以奏牘聞朝廷、書狀規過失，盖有契于孔明之心矣。而李文靖常言在位無補，惟中外所陳利害，一切報罷，則又曹參寧一之風焉。顧一則用之飾蠱，一則
translation_en:
…yet their reverent diligence deserves esteem. Qi Xi recommended both a kinsman and a worthy man in response to the Marquis of Jin’s inquiry about succession to the command of the Central Army. Similarly, when Wang Dan recommended Kou Zhun as Military Affairs Commissioner, the emperor said that Kou Zhun had spoken disparagingly of him. Wang replied: “Your servant has long held office and has many shortcomings. This only makes his loyalty in concealing nothing all the more evident.” In Emperor Shenzong’s time, Lü Zhengxian repeatedly invoked public opinion to enumerate Anshi’s faults [?]. Yet when Zhengxian held executive office, he promoted many men, while declining to employ Anshi’s son. Although his intentions fell short of Qi Xi’s impartiality, his uprightness and sincerity likewise deserve praise.

Scrutinizing officials’ administration serves to secure the people’s livelihood. Thus, when Fan Wenzheng served as Participant in Determining Governmental Matters, whenever he encountered an incompetent surveillance official, he struck out his name with a single stroke of the brush. He had evidently grasped the meaning of assessing administration in the Offices of Zhou. Yet Lord Han Yi was invariably displeased when he saw men in the various circuits picking out officials’ minor faults. He said: “Why bar men from office in an age of sage rule?” This, in turn, embodied the benevolence of Shun’s court in pardoning inadvertent offenses. One was urgent in dealing with grave wrongdoing; the other made allowances for minor errors. Though their actions differed, how could their underlying intentions ever have been different?

Gathering the thoughts of many serves to broaden the benefits of loyal counsel. Thus Sima Guang posted a notice in his reception hall asking visitors to submit memorials informing the court and written statements correcting faults. He evidently shared Kongming’s intentions. Yet Li Wenjing often said that he made no contribution while in office, merely rejecting all proposals concerning advantages and disadvantages submitted from within and outside the capital. This, in turn, reflected Cao Can’s practice of maintaining peace and unity. One, however, employed his approach to remedy decay, while the other…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
用之保泰時則殊矣而其忠何嘗有不一
以任官言之萊公之却例簿誠識體之言
也故曰宰相用人安用例若必例則一執
簿吏足矣若仲淹之圖上百官則以矯夷
簡之專耳不然豈以公之賢而踵光庭之
敝邪以事君言之文潞公復中書每侍對
而禮甚恭盖老臣之體也故曰某以耆舊
禮不得不恭若伊川為說書每侍講而色
甚莊則以任賓師之道耳不然豈以頤之
===
賢而昧孟軻氏之訓邪是則身之所履既
殊而道之所錯遂異亦惟其時義之當焉
耳且本之貞固既不至於徇人達之變通
又不至於失己是以公是公非與天下共
義好義惡惟皇極游卓然而立於君子之
塗也由此其選與故曰君子亦仁而已矣
何必同
第四問
畢鏘

簿〔吏〕足矣若仲淹之圖上百官則以矯夷

禮不得不恭若伊川為說書每侍講雷色
甚莊則以任賓師之道耳不然豈以頤之
===
賢而昧孟軻氏之訓邪是則身之所履既
殊而道之所錯遂異亦惟其時義之當焉
耳且本之貞固既不至於徇人達之變通
又不至於失己是以公是公非與天下共
義好義惡惟皇極遵卓然而立於君子之
塗也由此其選與故曰君子亦仁而已矣
何必同
第四問
畢鏘
punctuated:
用之保泰，時則殊矣，而其忠何嘗有不一？以任官言之，萊公之却例簿，誠識體之言也。故曰：「宰相用人，安用例？若必例，則一執簿吏足矣。」若仲淹之圖上百官，則以矯夷簡之專耳。不然，豈以公之賢而踵光庭之敝邪？以事君言之，文潞公復中書，每侍對而禮甚恭，盖老臣之體也。故曰：「某以耆舊，禮不得不恭。」若伊川為說書，每侍講而色甚莊，則以任賓師之道耳。不然，豈以頤之賢而昧孟軻氏之訓邪？是則身之所履既殊，而道之所錯遂異，亦惟其時義之當焉耳。且本之貞固，既不至於徇人；達之變通，又不至於失己。是以公是公非，與天下共；義好義惡，惟皇極游。卓然而立於君子之塗也，由此其選與？故曰：「君子亦仁而已矣，何必同？」

第四問
畢鏘
translation_en:
…the other employed it to preserve peace and prosperity. Their circumstances differed, but how could their loyalty ever have been anything but one?

To speak of appointing officials: when the Duke of Lai, Kou Zhun, rejected the register of precedents, his words truly showed an understanding of the essentials. He said: “When a chief councilor appoints men, what need has he of precedents? If precedents must be followed, a single clerk holding a register would suffice.” As for Fan Zhongyan’s presentation of a chart of the officials, this was simply to correct Lü Yijian’s monopolization of authority. Otherwise, how could a man as worthy as Fan have perpetuated the abuses of Pei Guangting?

To speak of serving the ruler: when Wen Yanbo, Duke of Lu, returned to the Secretariat, he was exceptionally respectful in his ceremonial conduct whenever he attended an imperial audience. This befitted a veteran minister. He said: “As an old servant of the dynasty, I cannot but be respectful in my observance of ceremony.” When Cheng Yi, known as Yichuan, served as an Expositor, however, he maintained a very solemn expression whenever he attended to lecture. This was simply because he assumed the role of an honored guest and teacher. Otherwise, how could a man as worthy as Yi have failed to understand the teachings of Meng Ke?

Thus, when the situations in which men find themselves differ, the ways in which they apply the Way also differ. All that matters is that they accord with what is right for the occasion. Moreover, by grounding themselves in steadfast rectitude, they avoid merely accommodating others; by extending this through adaptability, they avoid losing themselves. Thus they share with all under Heaven an impartial judgment of right and wrong; their likes and dislikes accord with righteousness, and they move solely within the bounds of the sovereign norm. They stand firmly on the path of the gentleman. Are these, then, to be counted among the elect [?]? Hence the saying: “Gentlemen need only be benevolent. Why must they be alike?”

Fourth Question
Bi Qiang

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
同考試官署郎中趙批漢以來説禮名家歷歷
若指諸掌而以大成之學歸之朱子三禮之傳議論甚
正末欲以朱子修復之意折衷於
聖明之朝是善衛聖道弼
聖治者
同考試官檢討林批三禮一策士子鮮能究
心此作考據精詳卓然有見乎其貫經世之學者乎
考試官左庶子江批策善條答篇首數言尤
見造理之學
===
蓋聞禮者性命之成體者也其形而下也
布於三千三百之賾也是之謂器其形而
上也極於無聲無臭之微也是之謂道道
不息者也而其器之寓諸經也則不能無
顯晦之時矣是故儒先之於禮也有傳經
之功焉有衛經之功焉凡以愛禮而明道
也執事發策承學而有及於此愚有以窺
執事愛禮之心矣請述以對夫禮何從出
哉出於天者也昔者帝王繼天出治質文

考試官左庶子江批：策善條答，篇首數言，尤見造理之學。
蓋聞禮者，性命之成體者也。其形而下也，布於三千三百之賾也，是之謂器；其形而上也，極於無聲無臭之微也，是之謂道。道不息者也，而其器之寓諸經也，則不能無顯晦之時矣。是故儒先之於禮也，有傳經之功焉，有衛經之功焉，凡以愛禮而明道也。執事發策承學，而有及於此，愚有以窺執事愛禮之心矣。請述以對。夫禮何從出哉？出於天者也。昔者帝王繼天出治，質文
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Zhao, Acting Director, comments: The renowned authorities on ritual since the Han are presented distinctly, as though pointing to things in one’s palm. The essay credits Master Zhu’s transmission of the Three Ritual Classics with bringing this learning to its culmination; its arguments are thoroughly sound. At the end, it proposes taking Master Zhu’s intentions for their restoration and establishing an appropriate settlement under our sagely and enlightened court. This is skillfully defending the Way of the sages and assisting sagely government.
Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor, comments: Few candidates can devote thorough attention to a policy essay on the Three Ritual Classics. This composition offers precise and detailed textual investigation and outstanding insight. Does its author not possess a comprehensive command of the learning of statecraft?
Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction, comments: The policy essay answers the questions well, point by point. The few opening statements particularly reveal learning that penetrates principle.
I have heard that ritual is the fully realized embodiment of human nature and Heaven’s mandate. In its aspect below physical form, it extends throughout the intricacies of the three thousand and the three hundred ritual observances: this is called concrete embodiment. In its aspect above physical form, it reaches the utmost subtlety, without sound or scent: this is called the Way. The Way never ceases, yet its concrete embodiments, as lodged in the Classics, inevitably have periods of manifestation and obscurity. Thus, in their work on ritual, earlier Confucian scholars rendered service both by transmitting the Classics and by defending them. All this arose from cherishing ritual and seeking to illuminate the Way. In posing policy questions to those pursuing learning, you, honored examiners, have touched upon this subject, allowing me, in my ignorance, to glimpse your devotion to ritual. Permit me to set forth my reply. From where does ritual emerge? It emerges from Heaven. In ancient times, emperors and kings succeeded Heaven in bringing forth orderly government, and simplicity and refinement…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
相推而禮行焉盖至周而大備故曰周禮
其禮儀威儀三千三百所以品節民用而
錯綜官常者則曰儀禮二者聖人之經也
至于禮記則或錄舊禮之文或述變禮之
由而其中又多儀禮之疏義故特謂之傳
是三禮者果何自而傳哉自夫河洛效靈
圖書象出鳳鳥秘瑞刪述功成聖人經世
之具已萃於六經之文矣然韓起聘魯見
易象春秋始嘆周禮之在魯孟子論王制
===
謂諸侯去籍至於申商滅棄禮法典籍大
壞則禮經之缺在春秋戰國已然而不特
灰於秦政之烈矣天右斯文漢除挾律於
是遺書間出而魯高堂生傳儀禮十七篇
與古文經出淹中者篇目相合然皆止於
士大夫禮其朝覲會同郊祀大饗遂逸而
莫攷河間獻王購集所得諸禮凡百三十
篇獨周禮晚出李氏獻之秘府然五官僅
存而冬官遂逸厥後戴德刪八十五為大

punctuated:
相推而禮行焉。盖至周而大備，故曰《周禮》。其禮儀威儀三千三百，所以品節民用而錯綜官常者，則曰《儀禮》。二者，聖人之經也。至于《禮記》，則或錄舊禮之文，或述變禮之由，而其中又多《儀禮》之疏義，故特謂之傳。是三禮者，果何自而傳哉？自夫河洛效靈，圖書象出，鳳鳥秘瑞，刪述功成，聖人經世之具已萃於六經之文矣。然韓起聘魯，見《易》象、《春秋》，始嘆周禮之在魯。孟子論王制，謂諸侯去籍。至於申商滅棄禮法，典籍大壞，則禮經之缺，在春秋戰國已然，而不特灰於秦政之烈矣。
天右斯文，漢除挾律，於是遺書間出，而魯高堂生傳《儀禮》十七篇，與古文經出淹中者篇目相合。然皆止於士大夫禮，其朝覲會同、郊祀大饗，遂逸而莫攷。河間獻王購集所得諸禮，凡百三十篇。獨《周禮》晚出，李氏獻之秘府，然五官僅存，而冬官遂逸。厥後戴德刪八十五為大
translation_en:
…simplicity and refinement succeeded one another, and ritual was practiced. It attained its full development under the Zhou, hence the title Rites of Zhou (Zhou li). The three hundred rules of ceremony and three thousand rules of deportment, which regulated the people’s conduct and coordinated the standing duties of officials, are set forth in the Ceremonies and Rites (Yi li). These two are classics of the sages. As for the Record of Rites (Li ji), some passages record the wording of ancient rites, while others explain why rites were changed; it also contains many explanations of the meaning of the Ceremonies and Rites. Thus it is specifically called a commentary. How, then, were these Three Ritual Texts transmitted? From the time when the Yellow River and the Luo River manifested their numinous powers, the Diagram and Writing appeared in symbolic forms, and the phoenix concealed its auspicious signs [?], the work of editing and exposition was completed, and the sages’ instruments for ordering the world were gathered into the texts of the Six Classics. Yet only when Han Qi visited Lu on a diplomatic mission and saw the images of the Changes and the Spring and Autumn Annals did he exclaim that the rites of Zhou were preserved in Lu. When Mencius discussed royal institutions, he said that the feudal lords had removed the records. By the time Shen Buhai and Shang Yang destroyed and discarded ritual norms, the canonical records had suffered great devastation. Thus the ritual classics were already incomplete during the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods; their destruction was not solely the result of the flames unleashed by the harsh rule of Qin.
Heaven protected this cultural tradition, and the Han abolished the law prohibiting possession of books. Lost writings then began to reappear from time to time. Master Gaotang of Lu transmitted seventeen chapters of the Ceremonies and Rites, whose chapter titles matched those of the classic in ancient script that emerged at Yanzhong. Yet these all concerned only the rites of gentlemen and grand masters. The rites for court audiences and assemblies, suburban sacrifices, and great ceremonial feasts had consequently been lost and could no longer be investigated. The various ritual texts purchased and collected by the Prince Xian of Hejian totaled 130 chapters. The Rites of Zhou alone emerged late, when a member of the Li family presented it to the imperial repository. Yet only its five sections on offices survived; the Offices of Winter had been lost. Subsequently, Dai De edited the material into eighty-five chapters to form the Greater…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
戴禮戴聖刪四十六為小戴記而馬融傳
小戴之學足以明堂月令等篇其為四十
九是為禮記鄭玄受馬融之學為三禮疏
先王典章煩縟之數各有訓攷而離經始
合矣此漢儒傳經之畧也且周官之考工
記不類經文儀禮之王朝禮又多遺缺聖
人經世之大典鬱而弗明是以漢武以為
黷亂不經何休以為六國陰謀世莫有傳之
者獨劉歆知其為周公致太平之迹乃用
===
之以輔莽唐太宗知其為聖人之作而不能
用之以致治他尚何說哉至于韓愈大
賢亦苦儀禮之難讀而謂今誠無所用則
禮經之不行盖自劉歆輩誣之而不獨壞
於王安石棄經之失矣逮于有宋諸儒輩
出篤信遺經講明理學淳熙有俞廷椿復
古之編嘉熈有王次點補遺之作丘葵訂
二家以為成書吳澄集三禮以為考註其
羽翼之功固皆有可言者而大儒朱熹則
