戴禮，戴聖刪四十六為《小戴記》，而馬融傳小戴之學，足以《明堂》《月令》等篇，其為四十九，是為《禮記》。鄭玄受馬融之學，為三禮疏，先王典章煩縟之數，各有訓攷，而離經始合矣。此漢儒傳經之畧也。
且《周官》之《考工記》不類經文，《儀禮》之王朝禮又多遺缺，聖人經世之大典鬱而弗明。是以漢武以為黷亂不經，何休以為六國陰謀，世莫有傳之者。獨劉歆知其為周公致太平之迹，乃用之以輔莽。唐太宗知其為聖人之作，而不能用之以致治，他尚何說哉？至于韓愈大賢，亦苦《儀禮》之難讀，而謂今誠無所用，則禮經之不行，盖自劉歆輩誣之，而不獨壞於王安石棄經之失矣。
逮于有宋，諸儒輩出，篤信遺經，講明理學。淳熙有俞廷椿《復古》之編，嘉熈有王次點《補遺》之作，丘葵訂二家以為成書，吳澄集三禮以為考註。其羽翼之功，固皆有可言者，而大儒朱熹則
translation_en:
…the Rites of the Elder Dai. Dai Sheng reduced the material to forty-six chapters to form the Record of the Younger Dai. Ma Rong transmitted the learning of the Younger Dai and supplemented it with such chapters as “Hall of Enlightenment” and “Monthly Ordinances,” bringing the total to forty-nine: this became the Record of Rites. Zheng Xuan received Ma Rong’s learning and composed commentaries on the Three Ritual Classics. The elaborate prescriptions of the former kings’ institutions and regulations each received explanation and examination, and the scattered classics were at last brought together. This is a brief account of how Han scholars transmitted the classics.
Moreover, the “Record of Artificers” in the Offices of Zhou does not resemble the text of the classic, while the court rites in the Ceremonies and Rites have many omissions. The sages’ great canons for ordering the world thus remained obscured and poorly understood. Accordingly, Emperor Wu of Han regarded the work as confused and contrary to canonical norms, and He Xiu regarded it as a conspiracy of the Six States; no one in the world transmitted it. Liu Xin alone recognized it as a record of how the Duke of Zhou brought about supreme peace, yet used it to assist Wang Mang. Emperor Taizong of Tang knew it was the work of a sage, but could not use it to achieve good government. What more need be said of others? Even so worthy a man as Han Yu found the Ceremonies and Rites difficult to read and said that it truly had no use in his day. Thus, the failure to put the ritual classics into practice began, it would seem, with their misrepresentation by men such as Liu Xin; their ruin was not due solely to Wang Anshi’s error in abandoning the classic.
By the Song dynasty, Confucian scholars appeared in succession, firmly believing in the surviving classics and elucidating the learning of principle. During the Chunxi era, Yu Tingchun compiled Restoration of Antiquity; during the Jiaxi era, Wang Cidian wrote Supplement to the Omissions. Qiu Kui revised the works of these two scholars into a completed book, while Wu Cheng brought together the Three Ritual Classics to produce critical annotations. Their contributions in supporting these texts certainly all merit discussion; as for the great scholar Zhu Xi, he …

天啟聖明，大昌景運。祖宗建極，表章六經，一道德以同風，定章程以作士。百七十餘年以來，鴻儒碩學作楨王國，而經生學士亦皆襃然抱藝以求實用。猗歟盛哉！顧愚竊有見焉。朱子曰：「六經之道同歸，而禮樂之用為急。」故其在當時有修復三禮劄疏，惓惓懇懇，為具陳於上而不
translation_en:
…restored the rites of the royal court and other rites, and entrusted the two categories of mourning and sacrifice to his disciple Huang Gan, who carried on and completed the work, entitled Comprehensive Explanation (Tongjie). Wang Kekuan subsequently followed its established method to supplement its omissions. Thus a text that had remained incomplete for a thousand years was brought together and consolidated through their efforts, and the many doubts concerning it were also resolved. Such, in outline, were the efforts of Song scholars to defend the Classics. Nevertheless, those who transmit the Classics transmit their wording. As earlier critics of Han scholars said, “When commentaries and subcommentaries appeared, the meaning of the Classics became obscured.” Thus those who transmit the Classics cannot escape the risk of impairing them. Those who defend the Classics defend their Way. As earlier critics of Song scholars said, “They offered much discussion but achieved little.” Thus those who defend the Classics may likewise fail to put them effectively into practice. Consequently, true Confucians have not appeared, and scarcely anything has been heard of government like that of the ancient emperors and kings.
Heaven has brought forth a sagely and enlightened ruler, greatly advancing our glorious fortunes. The imperial ancestors established the supreme standard, honored and elucidated the Six Classics, unified moral teaching to bring customs into accord, and established regulations to cultivate scholars. For more than 170 years, eminent Confucians and learned scholars have served as pillars of the realm, while students of the Classics and men of learning have also proudly borne their scholarly attainments in pursuit of practical application. Ah, how flourishing! Yet I venture, in my ignorance, to offer an observation. Master Zhu said, “The Ways of the Six Classics converge upon the same end, but putting rites and music into practice is the most urgent task.” Thus, in his own day, he submitted memoranda and memorials on restoring the Three Ritual Classics, earnestly and insistently setting the matter out in full before the throne, but did not…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
獲行盖真儒衞道之功固有待於
今日禮樂盛明之世矣恭惟
皇上以天縱之資邁日新之德履中樂和會道
器於一身明天察地貫性命而成則是於
王朝享覲大禮固已兼統而會萃之矣若夫
民風士俗古鄉三物之禮所以養其德性
而秩之倫彞者似猶未淪浹於海宇豈三
禮之訓未盡昭布邪執事倘不以愚言為
狂即以朱子之意上徹
===
聖明折衷全禮彙為一經分列科試俾海隅鯫
生皆獲誦習聖經之全以觀
盛世之化將見敷錫之下因聖人之遺經而
務求聖人之至意因聖人之至意而務得
性命之全體下以率訓於
皇極上以弼治於太和俾諸儒衞翼之功獲收
實用而我
列聖表章之制一惟
皇上統總而大成之不其偉與若夫會通彙粹

translation_en:
…put into practice. Indeed, the work of true Confucians in defending the Way has awaited this present age, when rites and music flourish in enlightened splendor. I respectfully consider that Your Majesty, endowed by Heaven and advancing in virtue renewed each day, treads the path of centrality and delights in harmony. You unite the Way and its concrete embodiments in your own person, comprehend Heaven and discern Earth, and penetrate human nature and Heaven’s mandate to establish standards. Thus, in the great rites of offerings and audiences at the royal court, you have already comprehensively brought these together.

As for popular customs and the habits of scholars, the ancient district rites taught three categories of attainment—virtues, conduct, and arts—to nurture people’s moral nature and order their enduring human relationships. These seem not yet to have thoroughly permeated the realm. Could it be that the teachings of the Three Ritual Classics have not yet been fully and clearly disseminated? If you, honored examiner, do not deem my humble words rash, convey Master Zhu’s intention to His enlightened Majesty: critically reconcile the complete body of ritual writings, compile them into a single classic, and assign its divisions within the examinations. Then even humble students in the remotest coastal regions may recite and study the entirety of the sages’ canonical writings and witness the transforming influence of this flourishing age.

We shall then see that, as these blessings spread, people will use the classics left by the sages to strive to grasp the sages’ deepest intent, and through that intent strive to comprehend the full substance of human nature and Heaven’s mandate. Below, they will follow the instruction of the imperial standard; above, they will assist governance in achieving supreme harmony. Thus the labors of Confucian scholars in defending and supporting the Way will yield practical results. The institutions through which our successive sage emperors honored and brought the classics to prominence will be comprehensively united and brought to full fruition by Your Majesty alone. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
謹之於事定之後者也盖先事而不定則
失之疎臨事而不决則失之懾後事而不
慮則失之玩以是而處常且猶不免於擾
患而况於制狄哉故曰毋恃其不来恃吾
有以待之是智勇而嚴之說也請因明問
而敬陳之夫夷狄之患自古有之雖以殷
周之盛亦所未免顧其撻伐之威以翼商
邑而服諸侯者為之地而其順治威嚴之
治乃所以成薄伐之績也自漢以還叛服
===
不常則有可疑矣盖高文盛時皆屢挫於
應虜而宣元之間漢幾頓矣而虜乃稱臣
焉是其狡啓於治朝非吾力之不足也彼
之勢趨於強也厭忱於季世非吾力之有
餘也彼之勢趨於弱也迄唐而宋勢且寖
長盖至胡元而極矣
天啓我
明
太祖高皇帝一起而殲之殆盡

不常則有可疑矣盖高文盛時皆屢歷於
應虜而宣元之間漢幾頓矣而虜乃稱臣
焉是其發啓於治朝非吾力之不足也彼
之勢趨於强也獻忱於季世非吾力之有

長盖至胡元而極矣

punctuated:
謹之於事定之後者也。盖先事而不定，則失之疎；臨事而不决，則失之懾；後事而不慮，則失之玩。以是而處常，且猶不免於擾患，而况於制狄哉？故曰：「毋恃其不来，恃吾有以待之。」是智勇而嚴之說也。請因明問而敬陳之。
夫夷狄之患，自古有之。雖以殷周之盛，亦所未免。顧其撻伐之威，以翼商邑而服諸侯者，為之地；而其順治威嚴之治，乃所以成薄伐之績也。自漢以還，叛服不常，則有可疑矣。盖高文盛時，皆屢挫於應虜；而宣元之間，漢幾頓矣，而虜乃稱臣焉。是其狡啓於治朝，非吾力之不足也，彼之勢趨於強也；厭忱於季世，非吾力之有餘也，彼之勢趨於弱也。迄唐而宋，勢且寖長，盖至胡元而極矣。天啓我明，太祖高皇帝一起而殲之殆盡。
translation_en:
…to remain vigilant after affairs have been settled. For failing to settle matters beforehand is an error of negligence; failing to act decisively when events arise is an error of timidity; and failing to consider matters afterward is an error of complacency. With such conduct, one cannot avoid troubles even in ordinary circumstances—how much less when controlling the northern barbarians! Thus it is said: “Do not rely on their not coming; rely on our having the means to meet them.” This expresses the meaning of wisdom, courage, and vigilance. Allow me respectfully to elaborate in response to your illuminating question.
The threat from the barbarians has existed since antiquity. Even Yin and Zhou at their height could not escape it. Yet the might of their punitive campaigns, which protected the city of Shang and brought the feudal lords into submission, laid the foundation; and their orderly and stern governance enabled them to achieve success in those campaigns. From the Han onward, the barbarians alternated unpredictably between rebellion and submission, presenting grounds for perplexity. In the flourishing reigns of Gaozu and Emperor Wen, the Han repeatedly suffered setbacks in confronting them; yet between the reigns of Emperors Xuan and Yuan, when the Han was nearly exhausted, the barbarians declared themselves its subjects. Their cunning aggression under well-governed courts arose not because our strength was insufficient, but because their power was growing. Their acquiescence [?] in the dynasty’s declining years arose not because our strength was abundant, but because their power was weakening. Through the Tang and into the Song, their power gradually increased, reaching its height under the barbarian Yuan. Heaven brought forth our Ming, and Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, rose and all but annihilated them.

text:
成祖文皇帝又從而三犁其庭斯時也非不可
翦此而後朝食也然而
皇仁天覆假之喙息乃今孽遺滋蔓擾我邊陲
賴我
皇上聰明神武上繼
二聖祖之烈赫然而
命將出師設總督之憲臣以一其權擇專閫之
虎帥以董其旅司農之錢穀支發不貲司
空之軍器申飭必再其所以惓惓於制虜
===

聖武布昭邊鄙不聳者已再易年第戎心叵測
出沒靡常則撤備而不虞與備之而勞費
誠有如執事之所慮者也顧今日之勢以
守為戰即勞且費亦有不得而惜者何也
愚所謂嚴之之說是也且昔蘇洵亦嘗曰
凡戰之道未戰養其力將戰養其氣既戰

其財豈非嚴為之備以守而為戰也乎夫

translation_en:
Emperor Wen, Chengzu, followed this by thrice plowing through their encampments. At that time, it was certainly possible to annihilate them before taking the morning meal. Yet imperial benevolence, all-encompassing as Heaven, granted them a breathing space. Now these surviving evildoers have multiplied and spread, harassing our frontiers. Fortunately, our Emperor, wise and divinely martial, carries forward the achievements of the two sagely founding ancestors. With awe-inspiring resolve, he appointed commanders and dispatched armies, installed a censorial official as Supreme Commander to unify authority, and selected fierce generals entrusted with independent regional command to direct the troops. The Minister of Revenue has disbursed money and grain in immense quantities, while the Minister of Works has repeatedly issued strict instructions concerning military equipment. In his unremitting concern to subdue the northern foes, the Emperor has surely settled his plans and made his decisions firmly.

Thus his sagely martial prowess has been manifest everywhere, and the borderlands have remained free from alarm for two years already. Yet the intentions of the barbarians are unfathomable, and their appearances and disappearances follow no constant pattern. To withdraw defenses and be caught unprepared, or to maintain them at great cost in labor and resources: this is indeed the dilemma you have raised. Given the present circumstances, however, defense must serve as warfare. Even where this entails toil and expense, there are things on which we cannot afford to economize. Why? This is what I mean by dealing with them rigorously. Moreover, Su Xun once said: “The way of warfare is this: before fighting, nurture strength; when about to fight, nurture morale; after fighting, nurture financial resources.” Once the fighting is over, one might expect to be free of further trouble. Yet he still wished to nurture financial resources. Was this not precisely to make rigorous preparations against the enemy, using defense as a means of warfare? Now, …

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
欲以守而為戰則養財之道舍屯田鹽法
之外亦無可講矣何也昔趙充國之留屯
湟中韓重華之墾田代北是皆以守而為
戰者也而其迹皆在今山陜之域顧今皆
鞠而為莽矣況夫近日五堡之復可以廣
新屯
國初河西之屯可以尋舊績是亦不可以復
講矣乎且管敬仲之佐齊也以鹽筴而致
霸劉晏通兩淮之鹺而唐之中興寔賴之
===
今之法固猶夫法也而文具則多矣況夫
餘鹽之榷可轉而給邊私鹽之逸可收以
佐餉是又可以弗講乎或謂今鹽法尚可
理而屯田則未易以復者然則今之勞且
費將終不能以有濟乎無已則有簡兵之
說乎愚聞之兵貴精不貴多兵多則冗徒
足以耗食今之兵方患其不多而顧又苦
其冗何也弗簡之故也無多之名而有冗
之實所以坐耗其食而弗知也且兵無事

punctuated: 欲以守而為戰，則養財之道，舍屯田鹽法之外，亦無可講矣。何也？昔趙充國之留屯湟中，韓重華之墾田代北，是皆以守而為戰者也，而其迹皆在今山陜之域，顧今皆鞠而為莽矣。況夫近日五堡之復，可以廣新屯；國初河西之屯，可以尋舊績，是亦不可以復講矣乎？且管敬仲之佐齊也，以鹽筴而致霸；劉晏通兩淮之鹺，而唐之中興寔賴之。今之法固猶夫法也，而文具則多矣。況夫餘鹽之榷，可轉而給邊；私鹽之逸，可收以佐餉，是又可以弗講乎？或謂今鹽法尚可理，而屯田則未易以復者，然則今之勞且費，將終不能以有濟乎？無已，則有簡兵之說乎？愚聞之，兵貴精，不貴多；兵多則冗，徒足以耗食。今之兵，方患其不多，而顧又苦其冗，何也？弗簡之故也。無多之名，而有冗之實，所以坐耗其食而弗知也。且兵無事
translation_en:
…If defense is to serve as warfare, then, as means of sustaining financial resources, there is nothing to discuss beyond military agricultural colonies and the salt administration. Why is this? In former times, Zhao Chongguo kept troops farming in Huangzhong, and Han Chonghua reclaimed fields in Daibei. Both used defense as a means of warfare, and the sites of their activities all lie within present-day Shanxi and Shaanxi. Yet today these have all become overgrown wilderness. Moreover, the recent recovery of the five forts offers an opportunity to expand new agricultural colonies, while the colonies established in Hexi at the beginning of our dynasty provide earlier achievements to trace. Should these measures not be considered anew? Furthermore, when Guan Jingzhong assisted the state of Qi, he secured its hegemony through salt policy; Liu Yan facilitated the salt trade of the Lianghuai region, and the restoration of the Tang truly depended upon it. Today's regulations are fundamentally still those regulations, but much has become mere paperwork. Moreover, revenue from the monopoly on surplus salt could be transferred to provision the frontier, and illicit salt that escapes control could be brought under it to supplement military supplies. Can these matters go unexamined?

Some say that the salt administration can still be put in order today, but that military agricultural colonies cannot readily be restored. Does this mean, then, that our present toil and expenditure will ultimately achieve nothing? If there is no other recourse, might we consider selecting and reducing the troops? I have heard that troops are valued for their quality, not their numbers; excessive numbers create redundancy and merely consume provisions. At present, we worry that our troops are too few, yet also suffer from their redundancy. Why? Because they have not been properly selected. Though they are not considered numerous, they are redundant in fact; thus they idly consume provisions without our recognizing it. Moreover, when troops have nothing to do…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
而食則不可使聚聚則不可使無事而食
此二者相勝而不可以並行是故以守為
戰之兵尤不可不簡也是非愚言也倡勇
敢練材實蘇軾蓋嘗言之矣亦非徒軾言
也募驍勇飭訓練李抱真蓋嘗行之矣今
誠能倣而行之練之既精畜之既豫於是
乎隸之以屯田有事則戰無事則耕是簡
兵者乃所以益兵也以是而守而亦何勞
且費之足慮乎哉愚書生也而談兵知必
===
見迂矣然而不敢嘿也謹以是復

punctuated: 而食，則不可使聚；聚，則不可使無事而食。此二者相勝，而不可以並行。是故以守為戰之兵，尤不可不簡也。是非愚言也，倡勇敢，練材實，蘇軾蓋嘗言之矣；亦非徒軾言也，募驍勇，飭訓練，李抱真蓋嘗行之矣。今誠能倣而行之，練之既精，畜之既豫，於是乎隸之以屯田，有事則戰，無事則耕，是簡兵者乃所以益兵也。以是而守，而亦何勞且費之足慮乎哉？愚書生也，而談兵，知必見迂矣。然而不敢嘿也，謹以是復。
translation_en: …and consume provisions while idle, they must not be kept assembled; if they are assembled, they must not be allowed to consume provisions while idle. These two considerations counteract each other and cannot both be put into practice at once. Thus, troops whose way of fighting is to hold defensive positions must especially be carefully selected. This is not merely my own humble opinion: Su Shi once spoke of encouraging the brave and training men of genuine ability. Nor did it remain merely Su Shi’s proposal: Li Baozhen once put into practice the recruitment of valiant men and the enforcement of training. If we could now truly follow these examples, train the troops to proficiency, and make advance provision for their support, we could then assign them to military agricultural colonies. When hostilities arose, they would fight; when there were none, they would farm. Selecting troops would thus be a means of strengthening the army. With such troops holding our defenses, what need would there be to worry about toil and expense? I am but a scholar, yet I speak of military affairs; I know that I shall surely be deemed impractical. Nevertheless, I dare not remain silent. I respectfully submit this in reply.

His Majesty thereupon commanded your servant Rubi, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction, to preside over the examination. Thus it is said: “Yao attained the central measure of Heaven and Earth.” Was this not a flourishing of cosmic fortune? At that time, ministers who assisted the unfolding of that fortune—those who presided over the hundred affairs, administered rites and music, brought waters and lands into order, or taught planting and cultivation—were dignified and numerous, taking one another as models. All received the transforming influence and assisted in governance, together ushering in harmonious and glorious rule. How splendid it was!

His grand counsels and mighty achievements shine throughout Heaven and Earth, resplendent across past and present; they cannot readily be recounted in full. As for his Admonition on Reverent Unity (Jingyi zhen) and his annotations to the Five Admonitions (Wuzhen), all under Heaven vie to circulate and recite them. The method of cultivating the mind embodied therein profoundly grasps the essence of what has been transmitted and received since Yao. Thus the transforming influence of the Way flows abundantly, and literary and moral instruction spreads in every direction. After so long a period of nurturing and inspiration, none throughout the realm, to the seas and beyond, fail to follow and obey. Even insects, plants, and trees may hope for his abundant beneficence and bask in his radiance—how much more those who are alike subjects of the Emperor! translation_en:
…a sagely age—an opportunity encountered once in a thousand years. Now your names have been entered in this record, and you will soon present your answers at the Palace Examination in the court of the sagely Son of Heaven. From this time forward, may you purify your hearts, attend to your administrative duties, display your talents, and undertake affairs, together assisting our Ming dynasty in its boundless, magnificent achievements. Might there emerge among you men like the nine ministers and twelve regional governors of Yao’s time?

Your servant reverently bows with hands clasped and head to the ground, and places this preface at the beginning of the record. Your servant has heard that no system for selecting scholars was more comprehensive than that of the Zhou. Our Ming dynasty, in consulting antiquity and establishing its institutions, has likewise taken the Zhou as its model. Never have well-established roots failed to produce abundant blossoms; when the roots have been uprooted, we certainly have never seen them capable of flowering. translation_en:
…to His Majesty. Ah! How has such an abundance of talent come about? Truly, human talent and the fortunes of the age depend upon one another for their fulfillment. Thus, the emperors of Tang and Yu had men such as Yu, Ji, and Gao Yao, endowed with the talent to assist emperors; the kings of Yin and Zhou had men such as Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao, endowed with the talent to assist kings. The primal essence of Heaven and Earth and the transformative achievements of sages and divine rulers coalesce when gathered and inspire trust when diffused: there is an inherent principle governing their workings. From the Han onward, however, these gradually declined.
Our Emperor alone, endowed by Heaven with divine sagacity, arose in response to the fortunes of the age. He clarified human relationships and fully established institutions, thereby setting the supreme standard for humanity. He has indeed traced the Way of the ancient emperors and kings back to its source and inherited its succession. From time to time, he has also disseminated admonitions and instructions to advance literary and moral education, thereby further taking up…

translation_en:
…the benevolence of the imperial ancestors and successive sage sovereigns in nurturing talent for posterity, making it ever deeper and more generous. The Book of Changes says, “Over time, transformation is accomplished.” Surely this is that very time! Thus the gathering together of primordial vital essence and the spreading of sagely transformation that inspires trust, witnessed in remote antiquity, are witnessed once again today. It is therefore fitting that these should manifest themselves in such an abundance of talented men.
Yet although this abundance of talent is revealed through literary composition, what makes it abundant is not literary accomplishment alone, but sincerity. Sincerity means virtuous conduct and attainment in the Way and the arts. Only when sincerity and ability are united can one speak of true talent. Thus loftiness and brilliance, breadth and depth, are rooted in purity and singleness of purpose; assisting Heaven and Earth in establishing their proper places and nurturing all things rests upon equilibrium and harmony. This is the teaching of establishing sincerity, and the talents of those who assisted the emperors and kings of antiquity were indeed, on this basis…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
之命臣等之掄材也亦姑即
其文叩其所謂志節器識之
可進於是者而取之而其竟
進與否則有用材者操其繩
尺以擬諸其後也然則諸士
之與茲選也可榮也不亦可
懼乎哉諸士而善用其懼則
===
將進而追古名佐致吾
皇於二帝三王之上而臣益有餘
榮否則即材也猶失選也而
臣之為懼焉者亦終能釋乎
哉爰是忠告為諸士勸惟諸
士其懋諸
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼

皇於二帝三王之上而〔臣〕益有餘
榮否則即材也猶矣選也而
〔臣〕之爲懼焉者亦終能釋乎
哉爰是忠告爲諸士勸惟諸
士其懋諸
奉議大夫左春坊左庶子兼
punctuated:
之命。臣等之掄材也，亦姑即其文，叩其所謂志節器識之可進於是者而取之。而其竟進與否，則有用材者操其繩尺，以擬諸其後也。然則諸士之與茲選也，可榮也，不亦可懼乎哉？諸士而善用其懼，則將進而追古名佐，致吾皇於二帝三王之上，而臣益有餘榮。否則，即材也，猶失選也，而臣之為懼焉者，亦終能釋乎哉？爰是忠告，為諸士勸，惟諸士其懋諸！
奉議大夫、左春坊左庶子兼
translation_en:
…were designated as such on this basis. In selecting talent, we your servants can, for the present, only examine the candidates’ writings, probing their aspirations, integrity, capacity, and discernment, and choosing those capable of advancing toward this ideal. Whether they ultimately do advance will be for those who employ their talents to assess afterward, with measuring line and rule in hand. Thus, for you gentlemen to be included in this selection is an honor; but is it not also cause for apprehension? If you make good use of that apprehension, you will advance to emulate the renowned ministers of antiquity and raise our Emperor above the Two Emperors and Three Kings; and I, your servant, will enjoy still further reflected honor. Otherwise, even if you possess talent, the selection will nevertheless have been mistaken. Could the apprehension I feel on this account ever finally be dispelled? I therefore offer this faithful counsel to encourage you gentlemen. May you exert yourselves!
Grand Master for Court Discussion, Left Vice Supervisor of Instruction in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently …

Officials in Charge of the Examination

Zhang Bi, Grand Master for Assisting in Governance and Minister of Rites, concurrently Academician of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Chongxiang; he was from Shishou County, Huguang, and became a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) in the xinwei year (1511).

Sun Cheng’en, Grand Master for Thorough Counsel and Right Vice Minister of Rites, administering the Household Administration of the Heir Apparent and concurrently serving as Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Zhenfu; he was from Huating County, Zhili, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinwei year (1511).

Examiner

Jiang Rubi, Grand Master for Counsel and Left Mentor of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Senior Compiler of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Maojing; he was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and became a metropolitan graduate in the xinsi year (1521).

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子曰事君敬其事而後其食
詩曰不顯惟德百辟其刑之是故君子篤
恭而天下平詩云予懷明德不大聲以
色子曰聲色之於以化民末也詩曰德
輶如毛毛猶有倫上天之載無聲無臭
至矣
使禹治之禹掘地而注之海驅蛇龍而放
===
之葅水由地中行江淮河漢是也險阻
既遠鳥獸之害人者消然後人得平土
而居之
易
同人柔得位得中而應乎乾曰同人
澤上有水節君子以制數度議德行
子曰書不盡言言不盡意然則聖人之意
其不可見乎子曰聖人立象以盡意設
卦以盡情偽繫辭焉以盡其言

第壹塲

易
同人柔得位得中而應乎乾曰同人
澤上有水節君子以制數度議德行
子曰書不盡言言不盡意然則聖人之意
其不可見乎子曰聖人立象以盡意設
卦以盡情僞繫辭焉以盡其言
punctuated:
第壹場

四書

子曰：「事君，敬其事而後其食。」

詩曰：「不顯惟德，百辟其刑之。」是故君子篤恭而天下平。詩云：「予懷明德，不大聲以色。」子曰：「聲色之於以化民，末也。」詩曰：「德輶如毛。」毛猶有倫。「上天之載，無聲無臭。」至矣！

使禹治之。禹掘地而注之海，驅蛇龍而放之葅。水由地中行，江淮河漢是也。險阻既遠，鳥獸之害人者消，然後人得平土而居之。

易

同人，柔得位得中而應乎乾，曰同人。

澤上有水，節。君子以制數度，議德行。

子曰：「書不盡言，言不盡意。」然則聖人之意，其不可見乎？子曰：「聖人立象以盡意，設卦以盡情偽，繫辭焉以盡其言。」
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Confucius said: “In serving a ruler, attend reverently to your duties and put your emolument afterward.”

The Book of Odes says: “How illustrious is his virtue! The many lords take it as their model.” Thus, through earnest reverence, the gentleman brings peace to all under Heaven. The Odes says: “I cherish bright virtue, without loud proclamations or imposing displays.” Confucius said: “In transforming the people, proclamations and outward displays are of secondary importance.” The Odes says: “Virtue is light as a hair.” Yet a hair still admits of comparison. “The workings of Heaven above have neither sound nor scent.” This is the utmost!

He charged Yu with bringing it under control. Yu dug channels through the earth and directed the waters into the sea; he drove out snakes and dragons and banished them to the marshes [?]. The waters flowed through channels in the earth: these were the Jiang, Huai, He, and Han rivers. Once dangers and obstructions had been removed and the birds and beasts that harmed people had disappeared, people could occupy the level land and dwell there.

Book of Changes

Fellowship with Others: the yielding line obtains its proper place, occupies the central position, and responds to Qian; hence it is called Fellowship with Others.

Water above a lake: Limitation. The gentleman accordingly establishes measures and limits and deliberates upon virtuous conduct.

Confucius said: “Writing does not fully convey speech, and speech does not fully convey meaning.” Does this mean, then, that the meaning of the sages cannot be apprehended? Confucius said: “The sages established images to convey their meaning fully, arranged the hexagrams to express fully what is genuine and what is false, and appended statements to convey their words fully.”

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
乾以君之坤以藏之
書
帝曰臣作朕股肱耳目予欲左右有民汝
翼予欲宣力四方汝爲予欲觀古人之
象日月星辰山龍華蟲作會宗彝藻火
粉米黼黻絺繡以五采彰施于五色作
服汝明予欲聞六律五聲八音在治忽
以出納五言汝聽
終始惟一時乃日新
===
會其有極歸其有極曰皇極之敷言是彝
是訓于帝其訓凡厥庶民極之敷言是
訓是行以近天子之光曰天子作民父
母以爲天下王
公其以予萬億年敬天之休拜手稽首誨
言
詩
如金如錫如圭如璧
彼有不穫穉此有不斂穧彼有遺秉此有

From those kings Cheng and Kang, who possessed all the lands in the four quarters: how discerning was their understanding!

Spring and Autumn Annals

In the ninth month, on the dingmao day, the son Tong was born. (Sixth year of Duke Huan.) The Viscount of Wu sent Zha on a diplomatic visit. (Twenty-ninth year of Duke Xiang.)

In autumn, the duke went to meet the Marquis of Wei at Taoqiu, but the meeting did not take place. In winter, in the twelfth month, on the bingwu day, the Marquis of Qi, the Marquis of Wei, and the Earl of Zheng came to fight at Lang. (Tenth year of Duke Huan.) In spring, in the first month, men of Qi, Wei, and Zheng concluded a covenant at Ecao. (Eleventh year of Duke Huan.)

In winter, men of Chu attacked Huang. (Eleventh year of Duke Xi.)

The Duke of Song attacked Zhu. (Nineteenth year of Duke Zhao.) The Viscount of Chu, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Sui, and the Baron of Xu besieged Cai. (First year of Duke Ai.)

問：自唐虞授受，開萬世心學之原，爰及三代，典則詒謀，相守一道。至秦漢以降，則代有不同，其于古心學亦皆有得否邪？我成祖文皇帝編輯《聖學心法》一書，又親為之序，乃有取於唐之《帝範》，何歟？且人倫有五，但言君臣父子，而不及其餘；有專言者，有統言者，其說可得聞乎？抑不知于我太祖高皇帝所著《祖訓》《精誠錄》，及今上皇帝御製《敬一箴》，同乎否邪？皇太子正位東宮有年矣，他日岐嶷大成，出閤講學，其亦可以此書進讀，用少裨作聖之功乎？願敬陳之，將以轉聞於上。

translation_en:
Fifth Question

Question: The transmission of rule from Yao to Shun opened the source of the learning of the mind for all ages. Through the Three Dynasties, their standards and plans bequeathed to posterity upheld a single Way. From the Qin and Han onward, however, each dynasty differed. Did they nevertheless all attain some understanding of the ancient learning of the mind? Our Emperor Wen, Chengzu, compiled the book Essential Methods of Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa) and personally wrote its preface. Why did he draw upon the Tang work Models for Emperors (Difan)? Moreover, there are five human relationships, yet he discusses only ruler and minister, father and son, without treating the others. Some statements address particular matters, while others encompass the whole: may we hear an explanation of this? We also wonder whether this work accords with the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun) and Record of Utmost Sincerity (Jingcheng lu), written by our Emperor Gao, Taizu, and the Admonition on Reverent Oneness (Jingyi zhen), composed by His Majesty the present Emperor.

The Imperial Heir Apparent has occupied his rightful position in the Eastern Palace for some years. When, in days to come, his precocious gifts reach full development and he comes forth from his inner apartments to receive instruction, might this book also be presented for his reading, to contribute in some small measure to his attainment of sagehood? We ask that you respectfully set forth your views, which will be conveyed to His Majesty.

translation_en:
… invariably cite the perfected Zhou order. The traces of its ordering of the realm—such as the establishment of fiefs, the well-field system, schools, and military forces—are recorded in great detail in the Rites of Zhou. Yet earlier Confucian scholars repeatedly praised it by referring instead to the poems up to and including “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao), concerning the ordering of internal affairs, and those from “Gathering Vetch” (Caiwei) onward, concerning the ordering of external affairs. Why is this? Some say that its point of departure was rooted in sincerity of intention; others say that it began with anxious diligence. Were these really two different ways? Or did what they called ritual alone lack these qualities? The reasons for developments since the Han can be discussed; concerning the Song, earlier Confucian scholars frequently left judgments. Did they truly understand what they were speaking of?
Our sagely founding ancestor inaugurated the dynasty, and Chengzu succeeded to the imperial throne. Their brilliant glory and great achievements assuredly bequeathed peace for ten thousand generations. Successive sage sovereigns carried forward this excellence, flourishing ever more greatly without decline. Now our reigning Emperor, through his divine achievements and sagely virtue, has still further displayed and exalted [?] this legacy and enlarged its glory. Indeed, he has already surpassed Zhou and risen to the flourishing heights of Tang and Yu, the ages of Yao and Shun. We wonder whether you gentlemen, in the sincerity of your humble offerings—as of celery or the warmth of the sun—have even one contribution in ten thousand to present. Please discuss this fully; those charged with conducting this examination wish to hear your views.

賢，禮也。或不求識一面臺官，或請還第見士大夫，其握沐吐哺之義否邪？薦士，公也。或多所汲引，其子不用；或我薦彼攻，益見忠直，其舉親舉讐之義否邪？察吏治者，或曰：「昆虫草木皆欲得所，柰何錮人于聖世？」或者不然，謂一家一路所繫不同，此其言孰當？集衆思者，或榜客位，以奏牘聞朝廷，書狀規過失；或者不然，謂無補於國，惟所陳利害一切報罷，此其事孰優？任官一也，何却例簿與上百官圖之殊見？事君一也，何起布衣侍講甚莊與耆舊侍對甚恭之異禮？夫尚友論世，天下士也，即當其任，其曷依歸焉？
問：六籍之闕也久矣，而禮為甚。禮有三：《周禮》，其綱也；《儀禮》，其經也；《禮記》，其傳也。粤自漢興，訪求遺書，《周禮》五官出而冬官逸，《儀禮》十七篇出而朝覲、會同、郊饗等禮逸。《禮記》雜出於漢儒，而或為八十五
translation_en:
…the worthy is a matter of ritual propriety. Yet one man did not seek even a single meeting with a censor, while another requested permission to return to his residence to receive scholar-officials. Do these accord with the principle exemplified by grasping one’s unwashed hair and spitting out one’s food to receive worthy men? Recommending men for office is a matter of impartiality. Yet one man advanced many others while his own son remained without an appointment; another recommended a man who then criticized him, thereby displaying still greater loyalty and uprightness. Do these accord with the principle of recommending both relatives and enemies? Among those who scrutinized officials’ administration, one said: “We wish even insects, plants, and trees to find their proper place; how can we bar men from office in a sage’s age?” Another disagreed, saying that the interests involved in a single household and an entire circuit were different. Which statement was appropriate? Among those who gathered the views of many, one posted a notice in his reception area, reported to the court by memorial, and used written communications to admonish against faults [?]. Another disagreed, saying that this brought no benefit to the state, and simply rejected all the proposals submitted concerning advantages and disadvantages. Which course was superior? Appointing officials was their common task: why, then, the divergent views represented by rejecting the register of precedents and submitting a chart of the hundred officials? Serving the ruler was their common task: why, then, the different forms of propriety—one summoned from commoner status conducting himself with great dignity while lecturing before the ruler, another, a venerable senior, displaying great deference when answering the ruler’s questions? You are scholars of the realm who befriend the ancients and consider the ages in which they lived. If you yourselves held these responsibilities, what would you take as your guide?
Question: The Six Classics have long been incomplete, and the ritual texts especially so. There are three ritual works: the Rites of Zhou supplies their framework, the Ceremonies and Rites their canonical prescriptions, and the Record of Rites their commentary. From the rise of the Han, searches were made for surviving books. The five offices of the Rites of Zhou were recovered, but the Office of Winter was lost. Seventeen chapters of the Ceremonies and Rites were recovered, but the rites for court audiences, assemblies of rulers, suburban sacrifices, sacrificial feasts, and the like were lost. The Record of Rites emerged in assorted forms from the Han scholars, with one version comprising eighty-five…

text:
篇或爲四十九篇其離合異同之故可
考而知歟抑不知出於何代獻於何人
而其人之傳之也何自豈秦燼顧未之
及歟昔之讀周禮者往往疑信相半儀
禮則昔賢亦苦其難讀謂於今誠無所
用此其人之意見何不同如是歟然而
復古補遺考註等編則又思以羽翼周

===
又有因其成法而爲經禮補逸者要之
皆有裨於禮學也子諸士亦嘗肄之而
能言其意歟願詳以告以觀經世之學
問夷狄之患自古有之雖殷周之盛所未
免也顧其自治及所以禦之者何如耳
自漢以下叛服不常或於治朝則見侵

translation_en:
…chapters, or as forty-nine chapters. Can the reasons for their division and combination, their differences and similarities, be ascertained through investigation? Or is it unknown in what age they emerged, to whom they were presented, and from what source their transmitters received them? Could it be that the Qin book-burning had after all failed to reach them? Those who read the Rites of Zhou in former times often mingled doubt and belief in equal measure. As for the Ceremonies and Rites, earlier worthies likewise found it difficult to read, declaring that it truly had no use in their own day. Why did their opinions differ so greatly? Yet compilations such as Restoring Antiquity, Supplementing Omissions, and Critical Annotations sought to support and elucidate the Rites of Zhou. As for the Ceremonies and Rites, a great Confucian scholar of the Song once reconstructed the rites of the royal court, the regional states, households, villages, and schools, entrusting the two remaining categories of rites to his disciples. Others followed his established method to compile Supplementing Lost Portions of the Canonical Rites. In sum, all these works contributed to the study of ritual. Have you gentlemen studied them, and can you explain their import? Please set this out in detail, so that we may assess your learning in ordering the world.

Question: The scourge of the Yi and Di has existed since antiquity; even Yin and Zhou at their height could not escape it. What matters is how a dynasty orders its own affairs and how it defends itself against them. From the Han onward, their rebellion and submission have been inconstant: sometimes they invaded and inflicted humiliation during well-governed reigns, yet voluntarily submitted as subjects in a dynasty’s declining years. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
成祖文皇帝驅逐掃蕩遠遁沙漠賴
皇仁天覆未滅其種百數十年生息滋蔓屢擾
邊陲
皇上赫然震怒命將出師畏威悔禍一歲無警
兹欲撤備恐獸心叵測去而復來備之
則勞師費財亦足慮也宜何如而可

translation_en: …and Emperor Wen, Chengzu, drove them out and swept them away, so that they fled far into the desert. Thanks to imperial benevolence, encompassing them like Heaven, their people were not exterminated. For more than a hundred years they have multiplied and spread, repeatedly disturbing the frontier. His Majesty, in mighty wrath, commanded his generals to send forth troops. Fearing his awe-inspiring power and repenting of the calamities they had brought upon themselves, they have caused no alarm for a year. Now, if we wish to withdraw our defensive preparations, we fear that their bestial hearts are unfathomable and that, having departed, they may return. Yet maintaining defenses against them exhausts the troops and consumes wealth—also grounds for concern. What course should properly be taken?

translation_en:
First Session
Four Books

Confucius said: “In serving a ruler, attend reverently to your duties and put your remuneration afterward.”

Huangfu Jin 皇甫溍

Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Chief Supervising Secretary: This develops the meaning of attending reverently to duties and putting remuneration afterward. Its language and ideas are sincere and apt; it particularly deserves to be selected for inclusion first.

Comment by Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler: It correctly distinguishes righteousness from profit, with clarity and force. It should be included to show ministers the proper standard of conduct.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, Compiler: Classical and elegant, sound and correct; worthy of inclusion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, Senior Compiler: This composition captures the righteousness required of a minister in serving his ruler. Its language is also classical and elegant; it merits selection.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Supervisor of Instruction: The language and meaning form a seamless whole.

The Sage sets forth the righteousness required of a minister in serving his ruler, in which salary is not a consideration. For a gentleman enters office to put righteousness into practice: how could he do so to seek a salary? By establishing this teaching, the Sage gives the most searching admonition to those who serve as ministers. His meaning is, presumably, that the incipient distinction between righteousness and profit is exceedingly subtle, yet the resulting divergence between public duty and private interest is vast. If one is wholly devoted to righteousness, profit does not come first; if one is wholly devoted to profit, righteousness is put afterward. Thus, in serving his ruler, a minister must regard reverent attention to his duties as righteousness, and must not make seeking a salary his foremost concern. Early and late he attends to public duties, anxiously striving…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
如有弗及敬吾官守求以盡其職焉耳矣食固
非所計也朝夕惟寅惓惓如有弗釋敬吾言責
求以盡其忠焉耳矣食固在所緩也雖祿以勸
賢也然待勸而行所行必不力君臣之倫固所
得於性分而尚有所待邪雖祿以報功也然望
報而事所事必不忠君臣之義無所逃于天地
而尚何所望邪吾知小賢受小祿大賢受大祿
以分則然也顧其機在上而不在下君子則不
以不家食為幸而方以體國為憂矣小言有小
===
利大言有大利以効則然也顧所制在人而不
在己君子則不以有祿食為榮而且以素餐為
愧矣吁一義利之間公私判焉一先後之間得
失係焉可不慎哉是故聖人之言學也曰後獲
而其言仕也曰後食凡以自盡其心也彼所謂
公養之仕者蓋有不得已焉爾非事君之常道
也是固不可不辨
詩曰不顯惟德百辟其刑之是故君子篤
恭而天下平詩云予懷明德不大聲以色

在已君子則不以有祿食爲榮而且以素餐爲
愧矣吁一義利之間公私判焉一先後之間得
失係焉可不慎哉是故聖人之言學也曰後獲
而其言仕也曰後食凡以自盡其心也彼所謂
公養之仕者蓋有不得已焉爾非事君之常道
也是固不可不辨
詩曰不顯惟德百辟其刑之是故君子篤
punctuated:
如有弗及，敬吾官守，求以盡其職焉耳矣，食固非所計也。朝夕惟寅，惓惓如有弗釋，敬吾言責，求以盡其忠焉耳矣，食固在所緩也。雖祿以勸賢也，然待勸而行，所行必不力。君臣之倫，固所得於性分，而尚有所待邪？雖祿以報功也，然望報而事，所事必不忠。君臣之義，無所逃于天地，而尚何所望邪？吾知小賢受小祿，大賢受大祿，以分則然也。顧其機在上而不在下，君子則不以不家食為幸，而方以體國為憂矣。小言有小利，大言有大利，以効則然也。顧所制在人而不在己，君子則不以有祿食為榮，而且以素餐為愧矣。吁！一義利之間，公私判焉；一先後之間，得失係焉，可不慎哉？是故聖人之言學也，曰「後獲」；而其言仕也，曰「後食」，凡以自盡其心也。彼所謂公養之仕者，蓋有不得已焉爾，非事君之常道也，是固不可不辨。

《詩》曰：「不顯惟德，百辟其刑之。」是故君子篤恭而天下平。《詩》云：「予懷明德，不大聲以色。」
translation_en:
…as though unable to accomplish enough, I attend reverently to my official charge, seeking only to discharge its duties fully; emoluments are certainly no part of my calculation. Reverent morning and evening, earnestly concerned as though unable to lay my responsibility aside, I attend reverently to my duty to speak, seeking only to fulfill my loyalty; emoluments are certainly a secondary concern. Although stipends encourage the worthy, those who wait for encouragement before acting will surely lack vigor in what they do. The relationship between ruler and minister is inherent in our allotted moral nature: what further inducement should one await? Although stipends reward achievement, those who serve in expectation of reward will surely lack loyalty in their service. The obligations between ruler and minister cannot be escaped anywhere under Heaven and on earth: what further reward should one expect? I know that lesser worthies receive smaller stipends and greater worthies larger ones: this accords with their respective stations. Yet the power to determine this rests with those above, not those below. The gentleman therefore does not count it good fortune to be supported outside his own household; rather, he concerns himself with the needs of the state. Lesser counsel brings lesser benefit, and greater counsel greater benefit: this accords with their effects. Yet the decision rests with others, not oneself. The gentleman therefore does not regard receiving a stipend as an honor; rather, he feels shame at eating without having rendered service. Ah! The distinction between righteousness and profit divides public-mindedness from private interest; the distinction between what comes first and what comes afterward determines success and failure. Can one fail to take care? Thus, when the sage speaks of learning, he says, “Put the rewards afterward”; when he speaks of holding office, he says, “Put emoluments afterward.” Both serve to make one exert one’s heart to the utmost. As for what is called taking office for public support, this arises only from unavoidable necessity; it is not the regular way of serving one’s ruler. This distinction must indeed be made clear.

The Book of Odes says: “How illustrious is his virtue! The many lords take it as their model.” Thus the gentleman is earnest in reverence, and all under Heaven is at peace. The Book of Odes says: “I cherish bright virtue, without loud voice or stern countenance.” …

Zhou Wenzuo.

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
靜虛動直之體穆然運萬化於無形夫孰得而
見之齊莊以有臨人則知之矣而其體信達順
之妙亹乎應萬幾而無迹夫孰得而知之是固
不顯其敬矣然而作孚之機存於上而刑於下
彼得於觀者自順帝則而不知也至咸之感出
乎身者加乎民凡在所臨者悉囿帝力而弗有
也其應之神也為何如著此者將何以擬諸其
形容哉嘗觀皇矣之詩云予懷明德不大聲以
色若可以言其妙矣而孔子則曰是化民之末
===
也矧曰不大猶有聲色者存固未可也又嘗觀
烝民之詩曰德輶如毛庶可以言其妙矣然自
我論之非知德之言也蓋謂之毛猶有比類者
在亦未可也其惟文王之詩曰上天之載無聲
無臭則形氣泯於俱無而神化運於不測以是
而言其妙允乎其至矣吾知其在天也四時行
焉百物生焉大德敦化不可得而見也其在聖
人也天地位焉萬物育焉不顯篤恭亦不可得
而見也是故知天則□聖人矣故曰允乎其至

…the underlying constitution of his stillness and emptiness in repose, and his uprightness in action, solemnly sets the myriad transformations in motion without visible form: who could possibly see it? People recognize his dignified gravity as he presides over them; yet the subtle workings by which he embodies trustworthiness and gives full expression to accord tirelessly respond to the myriad incipient affairs without leaving a trace: who could possibly know them? His reverence is indeed not displayed. Yet the impulse that inspires trust resides in the one above and becomes a model for those below. Those who receive it through observing him naturally follow the Supreme Lord’s rules without knowing it. The influence of his consummate responsiveness proceeds from his own person and reaches the people. All over whom he presides are encompassed by the Supreme Lord’s power, yet do not regard themselves as possessing it. How wondrous is the efficacy of his response! How, then, can the author who sets this forth find a comparison to describe it?
I have considered the words of the ode August Is the Lord (Huang yi): “I cherish luminous virtue, which makes no great display in voice or countenance.” This might seem sufficient to express its subtlety, yet Kongzi says: “These are the least of the means by which the people are transformed.” Moreover, to say “no great display” still leaves voice and countenance present; this will certainly not suffice. I have also considered the words of the ode The Multitude of the People (Zheng min): “Virtue is light as a hair.” Perhaps this might express its subtlety. Yet, as I judge it, these are not the words of one who understands virtue. For to call it a hair still leaves something with which it can be compared; this, too, will not suffice. There remain only the words of the ode King Wen (Wen Wang): “The workings of Heaven above have neither sound nor smell.” Here, form and material force both vanish into absence, while spiritual transformation operates beyond all fathoming. I know that, as it exists in Heaven, the four seasons proceed and the hundred things come into being: great virtue brings about abundant transformation, yet cannot be seen. As it exists in the sage, Heaven and Earth take their proper places and the myriad things are nurtured: his profound reverence is not displayed and likewise cannot be seen. Thus, to know Heaven is to [know?] the sage [one character illegible]. Hence it is said: “Truly it reaches the utmost…”

text:
式多士矣
考試官左庶子江批敘事中自有議論
觀聖君命臣治水而績用成見世治之一驗也
夫世之治雖由于氣化而亦人事有以成之也
觀諸聖人之治水可見矣此孟子因門人好辨
之疑而歷敘生民之故以曉之也意謂當帝堯
在位之時有洚水儆予之患時則鯀罔績矣乃
舉舜而敷治舜納麓矣復命禹以嗣興以上則
君憂臣勞而弗恤以下則父舍子用而不疑凡
===
以為天下而已由是禹也掘壅塞而注之海盖
海為百川之匯也驅蛇龍而放之葼盖葼乃水
草之鍾也疏導之功既奏地中之水自行南條
如江漢既順其性而于海乎朝宗北條如河淮
亦循其道而于海乎會同昔多險阻今則壅塞
去而滔天者平矣昔多鳥獸今則蛇龍遠而害
人者消矣夫然後降丘宅土而人無巢窟之虞

考試官左庶子江批：敘事中自有議論。
觀聖君命臣治水而績用成，見世治之一驗也。
夫世之治，雖由于氣化，而亦人事有以成之也。觀諸聖人之治水可見矣。此孟子因門人好辨之疑，而歷敘生民之故以曉之也。意謂當帝堯在位之時，有洚水儆予之患，時則鯀罔績矣。乃舉舜而敷治，舜納麓矣，復命禹以嗣興。以上則君憂臣勞而弗恤，以下則父舍子用而不疑，凡以為天下而已。由是禹也，掘壅塞而注之海，盖海為百川之匯也；驅蛇龍而放之葼，盖葼乃水草之鍾也。疏導之功既奏，地中之水自行。南條如江漢，既順其性，而于海乎朝宗；北條如河淮，亦循其道，而于海乎會同。昔多險阻，今則壅塞去而滔天者平矣；昔多鳥獸，今則蛇龍遠而害人者消矣。夫然後降丘宅土，而人無巢窟之虞，猶巳溺之者，固由巳而拯也；地平天成，而人有粒食之利，猶巳飢之者，亦由巳而食也。向非堯

Examiner Jiang, Left Associate Mentor, comments: Within the narration itself there is argument.
In observing how sage rulers commanded their ministers to control the waters and how their efforts achieved success, we see evidence of an orderly world.
Although order in the world arises from the transformations of vital energy, human effort also contributes to its achievement. This can be seen in the sages’ control of the waters. Here, because his disciples questioned his fondness for disputation, Mencius recounted the successive circumstances of human life to enlighten them. His meaning was that, when Emperor Yao occupied the throne, he faced the calamity expressed in the words, “The floodwaters warn me.” At that time Gun had achieved nothing. Yao therefore raised Shun to office to extend good governance. Shun had been sent into the great forests; Yu was then commanded to rise and carry on the work. Above, the ruler was anxious and the minister toiled without concern for himself; below, the father was dismissed and the son employed without misgivings. All this was solely for the sake of the world.
Thus Yu dug through obstructions and channeled the waters into the sea, for the sea is where the hundred rivers converge. He drove away snakes and dragons and banished them to the thickets [?], for these were places where water and vegetation gathered [?]. Once the work of dredging and channeling had succeeded, the waters within the land flowed of themselves. The southern watercourses, such as the Jiang and Han, followed their natural tendencies and paid homage to the sea; the northern watercourses, such as the He and Huai, likewise followed their courses and assembled in the sea. Formerly there had been many hazards and obstructions; now the blockages were removed and the waters that had towered to heaven were leveled. Formerly there had been many birds and beasts; now snakes and dragons were far away, and the creatures that harmed people had disappeared.
Only then could people descend from the hills and settle on the land, free from the anxieties of dwelling in nests and caves. He who felt as though he himself had caused them to drown indeed rescued them through his own efforts. The earth was put in order and Heaven’s work completed, and people enjoyed the benefit of grain to eat. He who felt as though he himself had caused them to hunger likewise fed them through his own efforts. Had Yao not…

彖傳本卦體釋同人之義，而著其有同道之益焉。甚矣，中正貫天下之道也！二五中正為應，斯固同道以相益者矣，謂之同人也宜哉！彖傳之意，盖謂天下理一而分殊，君子貴同而賤獨。同之於人，盖必有道矣。而卦之名為同人者，豈無所取乎？試以二五言之。夫二柔也，二當位且中，是柔之得其中正者也。柔得中正，則是和順以為德者本之秉彝之懿，而沉潜以為善者約於義理之衷。其在二也，虛心以受益，夫固有取善之資矣。由是而應乎乾焉，和順者麗於陽明，而相須之勢甚殷；沉潜者濟以剛克，而相與之情益篤。其與五也，比類以成行，夫固有交修之益矣。夫二五中正之應如此，而何以言同人也？盖君子之同也，不求同于人，而求同于理。曰中正而應，則其理同矣；其理同，則無所往而不同也。同之為道也，不于其迹，而于其心。曰中正而應，則其心同矣；其心同，則亦無所往而不同也。此

Comment by Examiner Wang Yi, Left Mentor: The language and tenor are refined and worthy of recitation.

The Commentary on the Judgments explains the meaning of Fellowship with Others (Tongren) through the structure of the hexagram, making manifest the benefit of sharing the same Way. How profoundly centrality and correctness pervade the Way of all under Heaven! The second and fifth lines, central and correct, stand in correspondence: they assuredly share the same Way and thereby benefit one another. How fitting that this is called Fellowship with Others! The intent of the Commentary on the Judgments is, I believe, that principle throughout the world is one, while its particular manifestations differ, and that the gentleman values fellowship and disdains isolation. Fellowship with others must indeed follow a Way. Could the hexagram have been named Fellowship with Others without a basis?

Let us consider the second and fifth lines. The second is yielding; it occupies its proper position and is also central. Thus it is a yielding line that has attained centrality and correctness. When the yielding attains centrality and correctness, the virtue of harmony and compliance is rooted in the excellence of our constant endowed nature, while goodness cultivated through quiet immersion is held to the mean of moral principle. In the second line, an open mind receives benefit: it assuredly possesses the capacity to draw goodness from others. Through this it responds to Qian. Harmony and compliance attach themselves to yang brightness, and their mutual dependence becomes most profound; quiet immersion is aided by firm self-mastery, and their mutual attachment grows still deeper. In its relationship with the fifth line, it joins with its kind to perfect its conduct: there is assuredly the benefit of mutual cultivation.

Such is the central and correct correspondence of the second and fifth lines. Why, then, is it called Fellowship with Others? The gentleman, in seeking fellowship, does not seek agreement with other people but agreement in principle. To say that the lines are central and correct and stand in correspondence means that their principle is shared. With their principle shared, nowhere can they go without being in accord. The Way of fellowship lies in the heart, rather than in outward traces. To say that the lines are central and correct and stand in correspondence means that their hearts are united. With their hearts united, likewise nowhere can they go without being in accord. This…

translation_en:
…For this unites them through the impartiality of the Great Way, something outward forms cannot adequately represent; it harmonizes them in the goodness of attaining unity, something differences of power and station cannot constrain. At court, this is what is meant by ruler and ministers joining in fellowship at court and all possessing a single virtue. Throughout the realm, this is what is meant by the myriad people joining in fellowship in the countryside and everywhere practicing your virtue. Is the meaning of Fellowship with Others not already abundantly clear? Yet fellowship means having no differences. To differ where one could be without differences incurs the harm of discord; to agree where one need not agree falls into factionalism. In essence, without difference there can be no agreement, and between agreement and difference there is scope for discretionary judgment. When the ancients adapted to changing circumstances in order to follow the Way, was it not because they examined differences and brought about agreement, possessing a distinctive insight into its depths? Thus it is said: “The way of the gentleman is sometimes to enter service and sometimes to remain in retirement, sometimes to remain silent and sometimes to speak.” Alas! Who but one who understands the Way could bring these into accord and unite them?

The Master said: “Writing does not fully express speech; speech does not fully express meaning.” Does this mean that the sages’ meaning cannot be apprehended? The Master said: “The sages established images to express their meaning fully, arranged the hexagrams to express fully the genuine and the false, and appended statements to them to express their words fully.”

The Great Commentary frames its words to probe the sages’ profound meaning, which must be discerned in their making of the Changes. For the Changes is the means by which the sages reveal their subtle and profound teaching. Once the Changes had been made, could anything of their profound meaning remain inaccessible? It is fitting, then, that the Great Commentary should frame its words to reveal it. It is as though it says: “To understand why the sages made the Changes, one should consider how difficult it was for them to express their meaning fully. Now, in teaching the world, the sages used writing to record their words. Yet there may be insights conveyed uniquely in words that writing cannot record; writing is thus inherently insufficient to exhaust what words convey. As for the means by which they expressed their meaning, this was words. Yet there may also be insights grasped uniquely in thought that words cannot express; words, too, are insufficient to exhaust their meaning. If this is so, one certainly cannot seek it in writing, nor can one seek it in words. Must the sages’ meaning, then, remain forever inaccessible? The sages knew how difficult their words were to transmit and were still more concerned that their meaning might not be fully expressed. translation_en:
…transformation has no fixed course. Containing movement within stillness, the images encompass the utmost subtlety of all under Heaven; lodging the imperceptible within the manifest, they encompass its utmost profundity. What is difficult to give form to or describe in the sages’ minds is thus all displayed in the images. Is this not how they fully express their meaning? Yet this is not all. From images come hexagrams: the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—are fully represented, and the six positions take shape according to their times. Times involve waning and waxing, thereby revealing the incipient workings of good and evil; positions may be appropriate or inappropriate, thereby distinguishing the fine boundary between remorse and regret. The principles of things, in their constant alternation of ascendancy, are all encompassed by the hexagrams. Is this not how they fully disclose what is genuine and what is false? Yet even this is not all. From images and hexagrams come statements: the judgments on hexagrams address the whole, while those on individual lines address one aspect. Making the manifest subtle and elucidating the hidden, they can exhaust the principles of what has yet to emerge; expansive and comprehensive, they can encompass inexhaustible applications. The sages’ teachings, which show people everything without concealment, are also all accessible in these statements. Is this not how they give full expression to words?

Thus, by establishing images, they fully express their meaning in images; by setting out hexagrams, they fully express their meaning concerning the genuine and the false; by appending statements, they fully express their meaning in words. At this point, what writing cannot fully express, the hexagrams fully express; what words cannot fully express is fully expressed. Who, then, could say that the sages’ meaning must ultimately remain inaccessible? Yet words are alike in being words: why can some fully express the sages’ meaning while others cannot? The answer is that the sages’ words differ in their purport according to whether they address higher or lower matters; the Book of Changes, however, is a book of human nature and Heaven’s decree, penetrating both the higher and the lower. Human nature and Heaven’s decree are not easily spoken of, but the yin and yang of the Book of Changes contain their principles in full, so these cannot remain hidden. Even so, concerning the principles of human nature and Heaven’s decree, the sages speak only of what can be spoken of.

…As for inspiring trust without speaking, that rests with the person himself.

Book of Documents
The Emperor said: “My ministers serve as my legs and arms, my ears and eyes. I wish to support and guide the people: you must assist me. I wish to exert my strength throughout the four quarters: you must act for me. I wish to see the emblematic designs of the ancients—the sun, moon, stars, mountains, dragons, and pheasants rendered in painting; the ancestral sacrificial vessels, water plants, fire, grains of rice, axe patterns, and paired angular patterns rendered in fine embroidery—with the five colors clearly displayed in their various hues to make ceremonial robes: you must distinguish them clearly. I wish to hear the six pitch standards, the five notes, and the eight classes of musical instruments, discerning whether there is order or neglect, and thereby receiving and issuing words in the five tones: you must listen.”

Fan Shan 梵䄠 [?]

Associate Examiner Xu, Acting Director, commented: “Essays on the Documents of Yu do not lack words; most, however, strain to draw in references and are far from achieving a lucid, concise, substantial, and dignified manner. This composition alone excels.”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Examining Editor, commented: “This composition comes close to exhausting the meaning of ministers as the ruler’s close companions. On consideration, it is selected for inclusion.”

Associate Examiner Xing, Compiler, commented: “The principle that ruler and ministers at the court of Yu formed one body is developed with aptness and immediacy. The conclusion traces the Way of the ruler back to the Way of Heaven, especially displaying learning informed by broad understanding [?]. It should be included as a model for the many candidates.”

Associate Examiner Yong 鄘, Compiler, commented: “Classically disciplined, solemn, and dignified, it also presents affairs methodically. Reading this composition, one can picture the manner in which ruler and ministers dealt with one another at the court of Yu. Might its author be one who cherishes the ambition to set affairs right and bring aid to the realm [?]?”

聖君責大臣以一體之義，而必詳其事焉。盖君臣一體以相成者也，則夫政教禮樂之事，不於大臣是責而何哉？帝舜望禹以弼直，而此則申言臣所以為鄰之義也。意謂君之於臣也，以相臨固有不可易之分，以相成寔有不容已之義。誠以君尊也，尊者體要，猶之元首也；臣卑也，卑者用勞，猶之股肱耳目也。故予以一人之股肱而運用乎天下，力固弗給矣，臣其作予之股肱乎？以一人之耳目而視聽乎天下，用必弗周矣，臣其作予之耳目乎？何則？君有政教，所以興理也。予欲左右有民，而教思之無窮，庶乎從欲以治也，翼而行之，惟汝是資焉。予欲宣力四方，而容保之無疆，庶乎胥匡以生也，代而敷之，惟汝是賴焉。是則所以作予之股肱，而運用乎天下，殆有餘力矣。君有禮樂，所以宣化也。予欲觀象作服，以日月星辰山龍華蟲焉，而繪于衣；以宗彝藻火粉米黼黻焉，而繡于裳，彰施以采色之

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Vice Supervisor of the Household of the Heir Apparent: The wording is concise and the meaning fully expressed.

The sage ruler holds his great ministers responsible according to the principle that they form one body with him, and necessarily specifies their duties in detail. For ruler and ministers form one body and bring one another’s work to completion. To whom, then, should responsibility for government, instruction, rites, and music be entrusted, if not to the great ministers? Emperor Shun expected Yu to assist him and keep him upright; here he further explains the principle by which ministers serve as the ruler’s close companions. The meaning is that, in the ruler’s relationship with his ministers, their respective stations in the hierarchy are indeed unalterable, while their duty to complete one another’s work truly admits of no neglect. The ruler is exalted: the exalted attend to essentials, like the head. Ministers occupy a lower station: those below undertake the labor, like the legs and arms, ears and eyes.

Thus, with only one man’s legs and arms to act throughout the realm, my strength would certainly be insufficient. Will you ministers serve as my legs and arms? With only one man’s ears and eyes to hear and see throughout the realm, my faculties would certainly not reach everywhere. Will you ministers serve as my ears and eyes? Why is this so? The ruler has government and instruction as means to establish good order. I wish to assist the people, with unceasing concern for their instruction, hoping thereby to govern as I desire; it is on you alone that I depend to support and carry this out. I wish to extend my efforts throughout the four quarters, embracing and protecting the people without limit, hoping that they may sustain one another in their lives; it is on you alone that I rely to spread these benefits on my behalf. In this way you serve as my legs and arms, and there will surely be strength to spare for acting throughout the realm.

The ruler has rites and music as means to spread moral transformation. I wish to examine the emblematic designs and make ceremonial garments: the sun, moon, stars, mountain, dragon, and flowery pheasant are to be painted on the upper garment; the ancestral sacrificial vessels, aquatic plants, fire, grains of rice, axe pattern, and paired bow-shaped pattern are to be embroidered on the lower garment, displayed distinctly through the colored patterns of …

From this we also understand that the way of the ruler is precisely the way of Heaven. Heaven does not speak, yet the myriad transformations proceed: the five phases and four seasons simply disseminate its vital force. Yet Heaven never ceases its profound and majestic operation. The ruler does not toil, yet the various accomplishments flourish: the offices and officials simply discharge their duties. Yet the ruler, too, never ceases his reverent and enlightened activity. Surely this is why Shun was praised for governing through nonaction! Hence the saying: “The ruler of men is like Heaven moving above.”

The worthy king praises his great minister’s intention in establishing the capital at Luo and respectfully answers his instruction. For the Duke of Zhou established the capital at Luo so that the dynasty might accord with Heaven’s favor without end; his report of the divination made clear wherein the ruler’s proper way lay. These are the words the king entrusted to a messenger in reply to the Duke, as though saying:

“A minister’s love for his ruler is deep, and thus his plans for the state reach far. Could your construction of Luo, Duke, have been merely a plan for one man’s ease and pleasure? Truly, in enabling us to receive the feudal lords at court and bring peace to the myriad regions, Heaven’s mandate to our Zhou is indeed a blessing. …the blessings of Heaven will likewise arrive in ever greater abundance without end. From this day through countless ages, it will always be here that one is fit to rule as lord and king. If the many regions remain satisfied with our virtue and never weary of it, the selection and bestowal of the great mandate will likewise never cease. Through countless ages, just as today, it will always be here that capable governance and enduring years are secured. Thus, although this foundation was established at a single moment, it enlarges a plan capable of greatness; although devised by one man, it perpetuates an enterprise capable of lasting long. Are not the duke’s expectations of me most exacting?

The excellence of the Duke of Zhou’s intentions was certainly something the king eagerly commended, but it was especially the duke’s words reporting the divination that elicited the king’s reverence. Why? It was Heaven that initiated the undertaking of building Luo; divination conveyed Heaven’s will and revealed it to men; the ruler presided over it; and the duke assisted the ruler in obeying Heaven. When the duke twice indicated that the divination favored Luo, the king understood that he must ponder the Way of occupying the center, planning for greatness, and maintaining strict principles of rule. He also understood that he must fully discharge the responsibility of occupying the commanding center, controlling the outlying regions, and welcoming blessings that would endure forever. He therefore bowed with his hands joined to express his reverence and touched his head to the ground to complete the ritual.

For ritual has its appropriate forms: even King Cheng’s performing such an act entailed no abasement. The Way has its proper place: even the Duke of Zhou’s receiving such an act gave no grounds for objection. Can we not, then, imagine the flourishing relationship between ruler and minister under the Zhou?

Yet building Luo was King Wu’s aspiration. The Duke of Zhou brought it to completion, while the Duke of Shao had in fact first planned and managed it. Why, then, did King Cheng attribute it solely to the Duke of Zhou? Truly, King Wu and the Duke of Zhou were of one mind, and the dukes of Zhou and Shao shared the same virtue. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
民人者顯德之徵也其有以得天而膺眷也宜
哉此公尸所以答鳧鷖也盖曰君者天之所獨
厚者也天厚於君而君之德又有以昭受于天
其眷命寧有窮乎是故我假樂之君子也德懋
於緝熈而昭明有融倬乎並天地之貞觀道原
於丕顯而重明麗正炳乎若日月之照臨王之
德其顯矣故宜於民則綏來動和問之在野而
從欲以治也宜於人則謨明弼諧問之在朝而
咸有一德也夫民者天之心也人者代天之工
===
者也既宜民人則天意得矣寧不受祿于天乎
但見保且右之右且命之俾爾安焉俾爾臧焉
一人建極而百順攸萃矣示之行焉示之事焉
上帝是皇而百神爾主矣然天之眷不但已也
德咸宜而祿亦無不宜無疆維休寵綏乎我后
者盖方至而未艾也德惟常而命亦惟常有秩
斯祜敷錫於萬年者雖歷久而維新也吁天之
純佑吾君者如此是皆顯德之所致也非假樂
之君子而有是哉抑考禮曰周坐尸詔侑武方

translation_en:
…the common people and officials is evidence of manifest virtue. How fitting that this should win Heaven’s favor and receive its care! This is why the august impersonator of the ancestor responds to “Wild Ducks and Gulls” (Fu yi). The meaning is this: the ruler is the one whom Heaven favors above all others. Heaven favors the ruler, and the ruler’s virtue enables him gloriously to receive Heaven’s gifts. How could Heaven’s favor and mandate ever be exhausted?

Thus, our noble lord in “Admirable Happiness” (Jia le) makes his virtue flourish through continuing illumination: his radiant brightness spreads, grandly matching the constant order displayed by Heaven and Earth. His Way has its source in great manifest virtue; with redoubled brightness, he cleaves to what is correct, shining like the sun and moon illuminating all below. How manifest is the king’s virtue! Thus, in being well suited to the common people, he brings them peace and draws them to him, moving them to harmony; he consults those outside the court and governs in accordance with their wishes. In being well suited to his officials, he obtains enlightened counsel and harmonious assistance; he consults those at court, and all share a single virtue. The common people are Heaven’s heart; officials perform Heaven’s work on its behalf. Once he is well suited to both the people and the officials, he has won Heaven’s approval. How could he fail to receive blessings from Heaven?

We see Heaven protect and assist him, assist him and bestow its mandate upon him, granting you peace and granting you goodness. The One Man establishes the supreme standard, and every favorable condition gathers around him. Heaven shows him how to act and how to conduct affairs. He reveres the Lord on High, and the hundred spirits acknowledge you as their master. Yet Heaven’s care does not stop there. His virtue is fitting in every respect, and the blessings he receives are likewise fitting in every respect. Boundless is this goodness: the favor that brings peace to our sovereign is still arriving and has not ceased. His virtue is constant, and Heaven’s mandate is likewise constant. Ordered and enduring are these blessings, bestowed abundantly for ten thousand years: though long continued, they remain ever new.

Ah! Such is Heaven’s unstinting protection of our ruler. All this is brought about by his manifest virtue. Could anyone other than the noble lord of “Admirable Happiness” enjoy this? Moreover, examining the Record of Rites, we read: “Under the Zhou, the impersonator of the ancestor was seated, and prompted and urged [to eat]; wu fang [?]…”

…presumably this was to treat him as a divine being. Yet why does the hymn Wild Ducks (Fu yi) also praise the generosity of the rites for guests? It is simply that the king, in honoring his ancestors and revering his lineage, left nothing wanting in the sincerity of his devotion. The poet of Admirable Happiness (Jia le) therefore borrowed Heaven’s voice to respond to him; and how consummate was his loyalty and love, in his earnest concern for the succeeding king’s worthiness! To approach the illustrious ancestors with manifest reverence and to receive the favor of the Lord on High with manifest virtue follow one and the same Way. Readers who consider this together with the poem Heaven Protects You (Tian bao) will find this still more convincing.
“From those kings Cheng and Kang, who possessed all the four quarters—how discerning was their wisdom!”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Chief Supervising Secretary: The exposition is lucid and elegant, neither hurried nor slow. It achieves a gentle, generous manner and is fully worthy of serving as a model for those who expound the Poetry.
Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Examining Editor: What the topic calls “discernment” reveals substance through its operation; the discussion is grounded in the manifestations of good government. Few writers expound the meaning of a hymn in this way.
Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Compiler: Cheng and Kang manifested their luminous virtue in the achievements of their government: this is the essential meaning of the topic. This essay develops it with fullness and ample detail. It should be selected and placed first among the candidates’ compositions.

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler: It portrays abundant virtue, and its reasoning and expression are lucid and fluent. This is precisely how the meaning of a hymn should be expounded.
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor: Amid its elaborate articulation there is an effortless spirit.

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
周人頌二王之君天下而克明其德也夫君德
莫大乎至明也成康以之其君天下也宜哉此
周人祀先之詩蓋謂天祚周業代有令王故執
競以開後武王之功莫尚矣成康繼世而有天
下其德不有可言者乎自今觀之席燕翼之休
而得統於武成固基天之命而奄有九有矣承
貽謀之慶而繼體於成康亦荷天之寵而君臨
萬邦矣夫履帝位而不疚者徵諸德臨天下而
不眩者存乎明二王之為君何如哉蓋日月照
===
臨先王以明而出治也彼則有以善繼之而致
乎緝熈之學聰明作后先王以明而統天也彼
則有以善述之而對乎光訓之詒是以明德所
發天地昭焉於謨訓則賁如也於法象則粲如
也所謂天子之光將無微不達矣夫孰得而掩
之德輝所動上下察焉以群工則辨治也以庶
物則咸熈也所謂大君之智蓋無遠弗届矣其
明不亦著乎是則成康紹天之明而纘先業於
不怠則克享天心而垂裕後昆遠矣周人之升

莫大乎至明也成康以之君天下也宜哉此
周人祀先之詩蓋謂天祚周業代有令王故執
競以開後武王之功莫尚矣成康繼世而有天
下其德不有可言者乎自今觀之席燕翼之休
而得統於武成固基天之命而奄有九有矣承
貽謀之慶而繼體於成康亦荷天之寵而君臨
萬邦矣夫嚴帝位而不疚者徵諸德臨天下而
不眩者存乎明二王之為君何如哉蓋日月照
臨先王以明而出治也彼則有以善繼之而致
乎緝熙之學聰明作后先王以明而統天也彼
則有以善述之而對乎光訓之詒是以明德所
發天地昭焉於謨訓則貫如也於法象則粲如
也所謂天子之光將無微不達矣夫孰得而掩
之德輝所動上下察焉以群工則辯治也以庶
物則咸熙也所謂大君之智蓋無遠弗屆矣其
明不亦著乎是則成康紹天之明而纘先業於
不忘則克享天心而垂裕後昆遠矣周人之升
===
□於廟也有以成□□□□
punctuated: 周人頌二王之君天下而克明其德也。夫君德莫大乎至明也，成康以之，其君天下也宜哉！此周人祀先之詩，蓋謂天祚周業，代有令王，故執競以開後，武王之功莫尚矣。成康繼世而有天下，其德不有可言者乎？自今觀之，席燕翼之休而得統於武，成固基天之命而奄有九有矣；承貽謀之慶而繼體於成，康亦荷天之寵而君臨萬邦矣。夫履帝位而不疚者徵諸德，臨天下而不眩者存乎明。二王之為君何如哉？蓋日月照臨，先王以明而出治也，彼則有以善繼之而致乎緝熈之學；聰明作后，先王以明而統天也，彼則有以善述之而對乎光訓之詒。是以明德所發，天地昭焉：於謨訓則賁如也，於法象則粲如也。所謂天子之光，將無微不達矣，夫孰得而掩之？德輝所動，上下察焉：以群工則辨治也，以庶物則咸熈也。所謂大君之智，蓋無遠弗届矣，其明不亦著乎？是則成康紹天之明而纘先業於不怠，則克享天心而垂裕後昆遠矣。周人之升
translation_en:
The people of Zhou praised the two kings for ruling All under Heaven and making their virtue shine forth. No virtue of a ruler is greater than perfect discernment. Kings Cheng and Kang possessed it: how fitting that they should rule All under Heaven! This is a poem sung by the people of Zhou in sacrificing to their ancestors. Its meaning is that Heaven blessed the Zhou enterprise, so that worthy kings appeared in every generation. Thus, in holding fast to strength and opening the way for his successors, King Wu’s achievement was unsurpassed. When Cheng and Kang succeeded to the throne and possessed All under Heaven, did their virtue not also deserve to be spoken of?

Viewed from the present, Cheng enjoyed the blessings of provision made for posterity and inherited the succession from Wu; he firmly established Heaven’s mandate and possessed all the Nine Regions. Kang received the blessings of the plans bequeathed to posterity and succeeded Cheng; he too bore Heaven’s favor and ruled over the myriad states. To occupy the imperial throne without fault is something verified through virtue; to preside over All under Heaven without confusion depends upon discernment. What, then, were these two kings like as rulers?

As the sun and moon shine down, the former king brought forth good government through his illumination. They ably carried on his work and attained learning that continually increased their brightness. Through keen hearing and clear sight one becomes a sovereign: the former king, through his illumination, exercised rule in accordance with Heaven. They ably perpetuated his work and answered the luminous instructions he had bequeathed. Thus, wherever their luminous virtue issued forth, Heaven and Earth shone brightly: splendid were their counsels and instructions, brilliant their standards and exemplars. What is called the radiance of the Son of Heaven reached even the smallest things. Who could conceal it? Wherever the radiance of their virtue exerted its influence, those above and below perceived it clearly: the assembled officials attended properly to government, and all things flourished. What is called the wisdom of the great ruler reached even the most distant places. Was its illumination not manifest?

Thus Cheng and Kang continued Heaven’s illumination and tirelessly carried forward their predecessors’ enterprise. They were therefore able to enjoy Heaven’s favor and bequeath abundance to their descendants far into the future. That the people of Zhou raised their voices …

text:
歌於廟也有以哉甞觀有周之君世載明德其
所以綿過歷之祚者固宜也然上之而夏商則
文命懋昭焉唐虞則欽明濬哲焉是知古昔帝
王之治要皆不越乎明德而其高明博厚之徵
聖神功化之極抑豈偶然而致哉噫是可以觀
帝王授守之道矣

translation_en:
…there was indeed reason for singing their praises in the ancestral temple! I have observed that the rulers of Zhou carried forward luminous virtue from generation to generation. It was surely fitting that their dynasty’s blessed tenure should extend beyond its allotted span. Yet, looking further back to Xia and Shang, we find civil teaching splendidly manifest; in the ages of Tang and Yu, reverent illumination and profound wisdom. Thus we know that the essential principles of government under the emperors and kings of antiquity never went beyond luminous virtue. Could the manifestations of their loftiness, brilliance, breadth, and depth, and the supreme achievements of their sagely and spiritual transforming influence, possibly have come about by chance? Ah! Here we may discern the Way by which emperors and kings handed down and preserved their charge.
Spring and Autumn Annals
“In autumn, the duke went to meet the Marquis of Wei at Taoqiu, but did not meet him. In winter, in the twelfth month, on the bingwu day, the Marquis of Qi, the Marquis of Wei, and the Earl of Zheng came to do battle at Lang.” 〔Tenth year of Duke Huan〕
“In spring, in the first month, men of Qi, Wei, and Zheng concluded a covenant at Ecao.” 〔Eleventh year of Duke Huan〕
Bi Qiang

The Spring and Autumn Annals condemns breaches of faith by allied states and invariably reveals them through the events themselves. Here, Duke Xuan of Wei broke faith with Lu; the battle and covenant that followed were both wrong. The Spring and Autumn Annals…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
得不即其事以貶之哉且桃丘何爲而弗遇也
衞侯棄魯而爲齊鄭之從也于是乎有郎之戰
惡曹之盟焉君子曰衞之失信一至此哉吾聞
桃丘之會約在衞也久要之言固非漫然之諾
桃丘之地近在衞也邦域之中初何遠涉之虞
衞苟知此肯中變以從齊鄭邪奈何執德不恒
甘食言而罔恤因人起釁乃委志以相從以故
魯也行李徒勤莫遂儀文之接衞也兵戎是逞
遽翦兄弟之歡是誰之過與人徒知于郎之戰
===
率賦以仇人者列國之罪同也而不知衞之背
信其罪實有浮焉者不然其何事于戰那人徒
知惡曹之盟要言以同歃者列國之惡均也而
不知衞之失信其惡實有甚焉者不然又胡爲
乎盟邪故經於桃丘書曰弗遇者蓋惡之也其
戰于郎直書曰來盟于惡曹俱奪其爵者蓋甚
之也而衞失信之罪於是乎不可掩矣抑魯桓
之罪王法所當治者衞雖棄之可也乃深貶之
者何蓋春秋惇信明義之書也齊鄭業已助桓

punctuated:
得不即其事以貶之哉？且桃丘何爲而弗遇也？衞侯棄魯而爲齊鄭之從也，於是乎有郎之戰、惡曹之盟焉。君子曰：「衞之失信，一至此哉！」吾聞桃丘之會，約在衞也，久要之言，固非漫然之諾；桃丘之地，近在衞也，邦域之中，初何遠涉之虞？衞苟知此，肯中變以從齊鄭邪？奈何執德不恒，甘食言而罔恤，因人起釁，乃委志以相從！以故魯也，行李徒勤，莫遂儀文之接；衞也，兵戎是逞，遽翦兄弟之歡。是誰之過與？人徒知于郎之戰，率賦以仇人者，列國之罪同也，而不知衞之背信，其罪實有浮焉者。不然，其何事于戰那？人徒知惡曹之盟，要言以同歃者，列國之惡均也，而不知衞之失信，其惡實有甚焉者。不然，又胡爲乎盟邪？故經於桃丘書曰「弗遇」者，蓋惡之也；其戰于郎，直書曰「來」，盟于惡曹，俱奪其爵者，蓋甚之也。而衞失信之罪，於是乎不可掩矣。
抑魯桓之罪，王法所當治者，衞雖棄之可也，乃深貶之者何？蓋春秋惇信明義之書也。齊鄭業已助桓
translation_en:
…could it fail to censure them through its account of these events? Moreover, why was there no meeting at Taoqiu? The lord of Wei abandoned Lu to follow Qi and Zheng. Thus followed the battle at Lang and the covenant at E’cao. The gentleman says: “Has Wei’s breach of faith come to this!” I have heard that responsibility for arranging the meeting at Taoqiu lay with Wei: the words of a longstanding agreement were surely no casual promise. Taoqiu itself lay close at hand in Wei’s territory: within its own borders, what concern could there have been about a distant journey? Had Wei understood this, would it willingly have changed course midway to follow Qi and Zheng? Why was it inconstant in holding to virtue, willingly breaking its word without concern, allowing others to provoke hostilities and subordinating its own will to theirs? Consequently, Lu’s envoys labored in vain, unable to carry out the ceremonial exchange, while Wei indulged in warfare, abruptly severing the affection between brother states. Whose fault was this? People know only that, in the battle at Lang, the participating states shared equally in the guilt of leading their levies into hostilities against another state. They do not know that Wei’s betrayal of trust made its guilt greater still. Otherwise, what business had it going to war? People know only that, in the covenant at E’cao, the participating states shared equally in the wrong of binding themselves by oath and jointly tasting the sacrificial blood. They do not know that Wei’s breach of faith made its wrongdoing more grievous still. Otherwise, why enter into a covenant? Thus, when the Classic records “did not meet” at Taoqiu, it expresses condemnation. When it directly records “came” for the battle at Lang, and withholds all their noble ranks in recording the covenant at E’cao, it expresses still stronger condemnation. Wei’s guilt in breaking faith thereby becomes impossible to conceal.
Yet Duke Huan of Lu’s crimes were punishable under the king’s law, so Wei could rightly have abandoned him. Why, then, does it receive such severe censure? Because the Spring and Autumn Annals is a book that upholds good faith and makes righteousness clear. Qi and Zheng had already assisted Huan…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
為惡矣今不能明大義以興師而乃於私忿是
徵牲歃是務尚為知類也哉春秋貶之聖人之
情見矣
冬楚人伐黃僖公十有一年
宋賢

同考試官檢討林批明暢可錄
考試官左庶子江批氣鬯詞蔚
觀春秋紀與國被患而伯主怠義之罪見矣盖
===
國非同盟則於恤患之義猶可諉也楚之伐黃
也而桓其可諉乎假義之烈於是乎隳矣吾聞
春秋紀約而志詳故外諸侯相滅不書伐者為
其非同盟之國耳黃非齊桓之同盟乎當桓之
圖伯也楚方荐食于上國桓將合諸侯而懲之
則恐其與之并力于我也由是偕黃盟貫以斷
右臂之勢會於陽穀以定掎角之謀而黃也慕
義之心專雖觸強夷而不顧從華之志篤乃棄
世好而不辭得非以桓之信義方隆而已之緩
