為惡矣。今不能明大義以興師，而乃於私忿是徵，牲歃是務，尚為知類也哉？春秋貶之，聖人之情見矣。
冬，楚人伐黃。僖公十有一年。
宋賢
同考試官署郎中趙批：善發聖人責齊桓肯綮。
同考試官檢討林批：明暢可錄。
考試官左庶子江批：氣鬯詞蔚。
觀春秋紀與國被患，而伯主怠義之罪見矣。盖國非同盟，則於恤患之義猶可諉也。楚之伐黃也，而桓其可諉乎？假義之烈，於是乎隳矣。吾聞春秋紀約而志詳，故外諸侯相滅不書伐者，為其非同盟之國耳。黃非齊桓之同盟乎？當桓之圖伯也，楚方荐食于上國。桓將合諸侯而懲之，則恐其與之并力于我也。由是偕黃盟貫，以斷右臂之勢；會於陽穀，以定掎角之謀。而黃也慕義之心專，雖觸強夷而不顧；從華之志篤，乃棄世好而不辭。得非以桓之信義方隆，而已之緩
translation_en:
…in doing evil. Now, unable to uphold the great principles of righteousness by raising an army, they instead campaign out of private resentment and concern themselves with sacrificial victims and blood-smeared covenant oaths. Can they still be said to understand how like cases should be judged? The Spring and Autumn Annals censures them, and the sage’s sentiments are thereby revealed.
“In winter, the men of Chu attacked Huang.” Eleventh year of Duke Xi.
Song Xian.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Acting Bureau Director: “Skillfully brings out the crux of the sage’s reproach of Duke Huan of Qi.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Lin, Examining Editor: “Clear and fluent; worthy of inclusion.”
Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Associate Supervisor of Instruction: “Its spirit flows freely; its language is richly expressive.”
When we examine how the Spring and Autumn Annals records an allied state suffering calamity, the hegemon’s culpable neglect of righteousness becomes apparent. If a state were not a fellow member of the covenant, one might still evade the duty to relieve its distress. But when Chu attacked Huang, could Duke Huan evade that duty? The achievements he had won under the mantle of righteousness were thereby undone. I have heard that the Spring and Autumn Annals is concise in its record yet detailed in its purport. Thus, when lords outside Lu destroy one another’s states, it does not record the preceding attacks simply because those states were not fellow members of a covenant. Was Huang not a covenant ally of Duke Huan of Qi?
When Duke Huan was seeking hegemony, Chu was repeatedly devouring the states of the central realm. Huan intended to unite the lords and punish Chu, but feared that Huang would join forces with it against him. He therefore entered into a covenant with Huang at Guan, to cut off Chu’s right arm, and held a meeting at Yanggu to settle a plan for a coordinated attack from two sides. Huang, single-minded in its admiration for righteousness, disregarded the danger of offending powerful barbarians; firm in its resolve to follow the civilized states, it did not shrink from abandoning its hereditary friendship with Chu. Was this not because Huan’s trustworthiness and righteousness were then at their height, and Huang had someone to rely upon in times of ease …

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
急有恃邪今兹楚也興伐黄之師為嘗齊之計
強弱不支民倒懸矣而引手之急能無望於宗
盟衆寡莫禦勢阽危矣而褰裳之援切有傒於
霸主使桓公而追惟管仲之言再申召陵之義
率彼同盟悉心以從事爰整其旅戮力以周旋

translation_en:
…in times of urgency, they would have someone to rely upon? Now Chu raised an army to attack Huang as a means of testing Qi. The weak could not withstand the strong, and the people suffered as though hanging upside down: in their urgent need for an outstretched hand, could they fail to look to the leader of their covenant? The few could not resist the many, and their situation was perilous: they earnestly hoped that the hegemon would lift his robes and hasten to their aid. Had Duke Huan recalled Guan Zhong’s words and reaffirmed the righteous purpose of the covenant at Shaoling, led his fellow allies in wholehearted action, marshalled his troops, and exerted all his strength to meet the crisis, Huang’s distress could have been relieved and Chu’s threatening presence dispelled. Why, then, when the written appeal had already arrived, did no relieving army set out? In the end, Chu’s ferocity grew still fiercer, and Huang’s altars of state were reduced to ruins. While Huang faced danger morning and night, Duke Huan remained inclined to ease and comfort; while Huang entrusted itself to him in complete sincerity, he regarded it with the indifference of Qin toward Yue. He had relied upon Huang, yet ultimately abandoned it; he had allied with it, yet how did he protect it? What benefit did Huang gain from relying upon us, only to bring such disaster upon itself? From this the gentleman knows that Duke Huan could no longer command the allegiance of the feudal lords.

In recording Huang’s destruction, the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically writes “attacked” to show that Huang appealed for help as a fellow member of the covenant, yet Qi ultimately failed to rescue it. Thus Duke Huan’s rise began with his diligent efforts to rescue Xing, while his eventual decline came with the campaign that destroyed Huang. He rescued Xing because he followed Guan Zhong’s advice; he failed to rescue Huang because he disregarded Guan Zhong’s views. Duke Huan’s hegemony thus depended, in the end, upon Guan Zhong alone. The consequences of a ruler’s employing the worthy, from beginning to end, surely offer a lesson!

Associate Examiner Gao, Acting Bureau Vice Director, comments: “The two characters ‘rectifying oneself’ point unmistakably to the root. Your ability to elucidate them suggests that you have devoted yourself to inward inquiry.”

Associate Examiner Chen, Supervising Secretary, comments: “This writing is harmonious, balanced, pure, and correct. Surely its author must be someone capable of expressing his own virtue!”

Examiner Jiang, Left Junior Supervisor of Instruction, comments: “The diction and tone are dignified and unhurried.”

The Music Master discusses how singing is rooted in virtue and thus can bring its transforming efficacy to its fullest greatness. When song is perfected through virtue, its foundation is established. Is not the utmost reach of its transforming efficacy precisely the spontaneous response produced by sympathetic resonance? Such was Music Master Yi’s reply to Zigong. Moreover, although different kinds of singing each have their appropriate uses, why seek their origin far afield? One need only find it within oneself.

The self is established through virtue: when the self is upright, virtue is perfected. Virtue finds expression through song: when virtue becomes manifest, song gives it sustained utterance. Thus, whether maintaining a still and settled resolve or observing standards of reverence and frugality, one leaves nothing unprovided for in cultivating oneself. Whether nurturing a generous and forbearing nature or mastering one’s capacities for firmness and resolution, one leaves nothing incomplete in perfecting oneself. Once the way of uprightness and rectitude is embodied without uncertainty, the stirring radiance of virtue naturally cannot remain concealed in song.

Through this, harmony and accord suffice to bring one’s finest qualities into full expression, and one’s Heaven-endowed nature can unfold the joy of its flowing activity. How, then, could its transforming efficacy stop there? I see…

惟因射而盡其義，斯效大矣。甚矣，德業之備於射也！明其節之義而效獲焉，射之道其重矣哉！且天子、諸侯、卿、大夫、士之射也，曰《騶虞》、《貍首》，曰《采蘋》、《采蘩》，射行而詩以應，是之謂節也。曰備官、時會，曰循法、修職，詩歌而義以存，是之謂志也。誠使射者之於節也，因辭以會其意，而不徒為聞見之知；由聲以析其旨，而必究夫精微之蘊，則志之所趨者定矣。於是以志而見諸用也，隨分以迪夫常，體至理於修為之間；因責以盡其實，服妙道於彌綸之際，則事之所行者力矣。夫如是，殆見其發之為勛業也，加諸天下國家者雖不同，而各懋乎勳庸之盛，文明以普，可大之業斯著焉；蘊之為德行也，具於君臣上下者雖不一，而各臻夫履道之旋，純粹以精，日新之德斯備焉。蓋功者事之積也，德行者功之本也，顧有事舉而功弗成、功成而德行弗立者哉？有志

…one who aspires to achievement and virtue, is he not?
Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor, comments: “The wording has rhythm and cadence and lends itself to recitation.”
Only by fully realizing the meaning of archery through its practice can one achieve these great effects. How fully virtue and accomplishment are embodied in archery! When one understands the meaning of its musical measures and obtains their effects, how weighty the Way of archery proves to be! In the archery of the Son of Heaven, the feudal lords, ministers, grand masters, and servicemen, there are the songs Zouyu, Lishou, Gathering Duckweed, and Gathering White Southernwood. The shooting proceeds in correspondence with the poems: this is what is called musical measure. Staffing the offices fully, assembling at the proper times, following the laws, and fulfilling official duties—the poems are sung and these meanings are preserved within them: this is what is called purpose. If archers truly approached the musical measures by grasping their meaning through their words, rather than merely acquiring knowledge through hearing and seeing, and by discerning their purport through their sounds, thoroughly investigating their subtle depths, then the direction of their aspirations would be settled.
They would then put those aspirations into practice: following enduring norms according to their stations and embodying the highest principles in their conduct and self-cultivation; fulfilling the substance of their responsibilities and practicing the wondrous Way in comprehensively ordering affairs. Thus they would act with vigor in carrying out their duties. In this way, we would surely see their aspirations issue forth as meritorious achievements. Though what they contributed to the world, the state, and the family would differ, each would strive for abundant accomplishment. Cultural refinement would spread widely, and achievements capable of greatness would thereby become manifest. As these aspirations were stored within as virtuous conduct, their expression in rulers and ministers, superiors and inferiors, would vary; yet each would attain success in treading the Way [?]. Pure and refined, their daily renewed virtue would thereby become complete. For achievement is the accumulation of deeds, while virtuous conduct is the foundation of achievement. Could there, then, be duties carried out without achievement being accomplished, or achievement accomplished without virtuous conduct being established? Those who aspire…

…those intent upon achievement and virtue: why should they not seek them in archery? Archery is but one art, yet great moral principles reside within it. The ancients used it to rectify themselves and to select worthy men; through it they attained security and renown throughout the realm, because they valued its moral principles. Thus it is said: “Among activities that fully embody ritual and music and can be practiced repeatedly to establish virtuous conduct, none equals archery. Comment by Associate Examiner Peng, Compiler: Candidates can generally discuss the workings of Heaven, Earth, and the sage. But it is truly difficult to express how being undivided and unceasing constitutes the pivotal principle of the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity. This composition is profoundly antique in style, refined and deep; it probes to the roots and reaches the essentials. Has its author perhaps attained insight into the undertakings of Heaven and humanity?

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler: In discussing the efficacy of utmost sincerity, candidates generally become diffuse and unbounded. Here one sees the meaning of the saying that substance and function have a single source, and that there is no separation between the manifest and the subtle. Yet candidates in the examination hall mostly gather up stale sayings and stitch together rambling phrases to fill their essays, which is exceedingly tiresome. Amid the exhaustion of reading, I suddenly came upon this script. It was an exhilarating release, like roaming through a bright, open expanse and bathing in a pure breeze. I recommend it highly and also record it to demonstrate the learning that investigates principle to the utmost.

The means by which the sage stands alongside Heaven and Earth and brings their transforming work to completion is simply to carry it forward with an unceasing mind. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
不存則自無不應矣無不存且應則常存常應
而其化自無不悠且久矣夫惟其化之悠且久
也則物之囿于其化者又惡得而有弗成者哉
是故自其誠之有常也之謂不息自其化之有
成也之謂悠久而其所以為誠之體則一也天
下之物皆誠之實體而至誠者亦自其實體而
成之耳是道也天得之以覆萬物地得之以載
萬物聖人得之以成萬物而萬物得之以覆載
於天地而成於聖人也其道一也故曰悠久所
===
以成物今夫天下皆知聖人成物之化矣而不
知其所以成之者誠之運悠且久也皆知聖人
誠之運之悠且久矣而不知其所以悠且久者
誠之體自不息也曷不觀諸天地乎今夫天靜
專動直而大生焉今夫地靜翕動闢而廣生焉
此其成物之功何如也然而不能以速成也彼
其氣序之流行也其屈伸則相感往來則相通
所以播而成物者蓋冲然其悠且久也至其貞
觀之理確然而示人以易也隤然而示人以簡

punctuated: 不存，則自無不應矣。無不存且應，則常存常應，而其化自無不悠且久矣。夫惟其化之悠且久也，則物之囿于其化者，又惡得而有弗成者哉？是故，自其誠之有常也之謂不息，自其化之有成也之謂悠久，而其所以為誠之體則一也。天下之物皆誠之實體，而至誠者亦自其實體而成之耳。是道也，天得之以覆萬物，地得之以載萬物，聖人得之以成萬物，而萬物得之以覆載於天地而成於聖人也。其道一也。故曰：「悠久所以成物。」今夫天下皆知聖人成物之化矣，而不知其所以成之者，誠之運悠且久也；皆知聖人誠之運之悠且久矣，而不知其所以悠且久者，誠之體自不息也。曷不觀諸天地乎？今夫天，靜專動直，而大生焉；今夫地，靜翕動闢，而廣生焉。此其成物之功何如也！然而不能以速成也。彼其氣序之流行也，其屈伸則相感，往來則相通，所以播而成物者，蓋冲然其悠且久也。至其貞觀之理，確然而示人以易也，隤然而示人以簡
translation_en: …when there is nowhere it is not present, there is naturally nothing to which it does not respond. Being everywhere present and responsive, it is constantly present and constantly responsive, and its transforming activity is naturally enduring and lasting in every respect. Precisely because its transforming activity endures and lasts, how could anything within its compass fail to reach fulfillment? Thus, the constancy of sincerity is called ceaselessness, and the fulfillment achieved by its transforming activity is called enduring duration; yet the underlying substance of sincerity in both is one. All things under Heaven are concrete embodiments of sincerity, and one possessed of utmost sincerity merely brings them to fulfillment on the basis of their own concrete substance. This Way is what Heaven possesses to cover the myriad things, what Earth possesses to support them, and what the sage possesses to bring them to fulfillment. The myriad things likewise possess it, thereby receiving Heaven’s covering and Earth’s support and attaining fulfillment through the sage. The Way is one. Hence it is said: “Enduring duration is the means by which things are brought to fulfillment.” Now, everyone under Heaven knows of the sage’s transforming activity that brings things to fulfillment, but they do not know that what enables him to fulfill them is the enduring and lasting operation of sincerity. Everyone knows that the operation of the sage’s sincerity endures and lasts, but they do not know that it does so because sincerity’s underlying substance is inherently ceaseless. Why not observe this in Heaven and Earth? Heaven, when still, is concentrated; when moving, it is direct: thus it generates on a grand scale. Earth, when still, gathers inward; when moving, it opens outward: thus it generates far and wide. How great is their achievement in bringing things to fulfillment! Yet they cannot accomplish this hastily. As their vital forces flow through the seasonal succession, contraction and expansion stimulate one another, and departure and return communicate with one another. The means by which they spread their influence and bring things to fulfillment is their expansive, enduring, and lasting operation. As for the principle displayed in their constancy, Heaven stands firm and shows people ease, while Earth is yielding and shows people simplicity…

息之心也所謂誠也物得之以自成而受成於
天地焉者也向使天地而匪誠則其運且息矣
天地而自息其運則乾坤亦幾乎毀矣而尚何

punctuated: 也，則又恒久而不變，致一而有常，是則天地不息之心也，所謂誠也。物得之以自成，而受成於天地焉者也。向使天地而匪誠，則其運且息矣。天地而自息其運，則乾坤亦幾乎毀矣，而尚何以成物哉？觀天地則知聖人矣。今夫天地之間，群然而仰成於聖人者，為物亦衆矣。而聖人者欲參天地而丕成之，則其為化亦豈可以旦夕而幾也乎？是故聖人於此，亦惟運其不息之心而已矣。是心也，即誠之體也，即天地之所以成物而物得之以自成者也。夫惟物得之而不能以卒成，雖天地有不得而自尸其功者，於是乎不能不仰成於聖人。聖人之心通極於性，聖人之性通極於命，聖人之命通極於天，則其成物之心亦自有不得而息者矣。然則聖人之所以參天地而成其化者，又惡得而不自其不息之心以運之哉？且聖人之心之不息，果何如也？彼戒懼者，誠之本也，而聖人則無弗戒懼也；慎獨者，誠之幾也，而聖人則無弗慎獨也；篤恭而不
translation_en:
…it is moreover enduring and unchanging, wholly unified and constant. This is the unceasing heart of Heaven and Earth: what is called sincerity. Things obtain it in order to fulfill themselves, receiving their fulfillment from Heaven and Earth. If Heaven and Earth were without sincerity, their operation would cease. If Heaven and Earth themselves ceased their operation, Qian and Kun—the creative and receptive powers—would come close to destruction; how could they still bring things to fulfillment? By observing Heaven and Earth, one can understand the sage. Among all that exists between Heaven and Earth, numerous indeed are the things that look to the sage for fulfillment. If the sage wishes to stand alongside Heaven and Earth and bring them to great fulfillment, how could he hope to accomplish this transformation in a single day or night? Thus, in this, the sage simply puts his unceasing heart into operation. This heart is the very substance of sincerity: that by which Heaven and Earth bring things to fulfillment, and which things obtain in order to fulfill themselves.

Yet things, though they obtain it, cannot thereby complete their fulfillment; even Heaven and Earth cannot claim sole credit for this achievement. Thus things cannot but look to the sage for fulfillment. The sage’s heart reaches fully into his nature; his nature reaches fully into his Heaven-conferred mandate; and his mandate reaches fully into Heaven. His heart that brings things to fulfillment therefore necessarily cannot cease its activity. How, then, could the sage stand alongside Heaven and Earth and complete their transforming work without setting it in motion through his unceasing heart? And what, indeed, is this unceasing activity of the sage’s heart like? Vigilance and apprehension are the foundation of sincerity, and the sage is invariably vigilant and apprehensive. 已者誠之至也而聖人則無不恭而無所已也
此皆其誠之必至而非有所勉焉者是故其行
之而為達德也推之而為達道也布之而為九
經也立之而為三重也散之而為三千三百也
錯之而為容為執為敬為别也形之而為著為
明為動為變也蓋自其居室之近而達之乎華
夏蠻貊之遠自其言行之庸而察之乎天地之
大皆其成物之事也則亦皆其不息之心而運
之也而安得不悠且久邪故今自其外而觀之
===
則其推也有序不競而不絿也其需也有漸勿
正而勿助也其居也有容不隘而不溢也是何
如其悠也所以行乎其久也自其内而觀之則
其虛也至一而其應自直也其體也至信而其
達自順也其靜也至常而其動自定也是又何
如其久也所以幹乎其悠也又自其合内外而
觀之則盛德大業體用一原時出而無窮也天
德王道顯微無間敦裕而不已也是悠也久也
聖人特自其不息之心而運之雖聖人亦不自

translation_en:
…unceasing [reverence] is sincerity at its utmost; the sage is reverent in everything and never ceases. In all this, his sincerity necessarily reaches its fullest extent, without any forced exertion. Thus, put into practice, it becomes the universally applicable virtues; extended, it becomes the universally applicable relationships; set forth, it becomes the nine guiding principles of government; established, it becomes the three weighty institutions; distributed in detail, it becomes the three thousand and three hundred rules of ritual. Arranged in their proper places, these become ceremonial comportment, the holding of ritual objects, reverence, and distinctions; manifested, sincerity becomes conspicuousness, clarity, the power to move others, and transformation. From the proximity of his own dwelling, its reach extends to the distant lands of Huaxia and the Man and Mo peoples; from his ordinary words and deeds, it is manifest throughout the vastness of Heaven and Earth. All these are his work of bringing things to fulfillment, and all are set in motion by his unceasing heart. How, then, could this fail to be far-reaching and enduring?

Viewed now from without, his extension of it proceeds in order, neither forcefully nor hastily; his waiting proceeds by stages, neither anticipating results nor forcing growth; and his abiding in it has ample capacity, neither cramped nor overflowing. How far-reaching it is! This is how its endurance is put into operation. Viewed from within, his inner emptiness is utterly undivided, and his responses are naturally straight; his essential substance is utterly trustworthy, and its expression naturally accords with things; his stillness is utterly constant, and his activity is naturally settled. How enduring it is! This is what sustains its far-reaching extent. Viewed, further, in the unity of inner and outer, his abundant virtue and great achievements have substance and function springing from one source, emerging as the occasion requires without exhaustion. Heavenly virtue and the kingly Way admit no separation between the manifest and the subtle, remaining generous and ample without cease. This far-reaching extent and endurance the sage sets in motion solely through his unceasing heart; even the sage himself does not…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
知其為悠且久也是故其積之也博厚而不可
極其發之也高明而不可窮始也聖人不過盡
吾之誠以成已之性而其既也則萬物亦各正
其性而受成于聖人之誠矣是何也久於其道
而天下化成言而民莫不信也行而民莫不悅
也見而民莫不敬也達德刑而民作孚也達道
立而民興行也九經正而民報効也三重建而
民寡過也三千三百之禮範圍而曲成民自不
賞而勸不怒而威也然此其感應之間猶有所
===
待耳及夫無待而成則亦殺之弗怨利之弗庸
民日遷善而不知為之者矣夫是以尊親通乎
蠻貊位育極乎天地雖百世以俟聖人而不惑
矣然而聖人不息之心固猶夫初也故曰聖人
所以參天地而成其化亦惟運其不息之心而
已矣雖然聖人誠者也其不息也不思而不勉
也未至於聖人而思有以誠之當如何曰擇善
其端也固執其實也為已而知幾其立心之始
也而程子又曰其要只在謹獨夫能謹獨則心

translation_en:
…know that it is far-reaching and enduring. Thus, what the sage accumulates is broad and substantial beyond all limit; what he manifests is lofty and luminous beyond all exhaustion. At first, the sage does no more than fully realize his own sincerity and thereby fulfill his own nature. In the end, however, the myriad things each attain their proper nature and receive their fulfillment through the sage’s sincerity. Why is this? By enduring in his Way, he transforms and perfects all under Heaven. When he speaks, none among the people fail to trust him; when he acts, none fail to rejoice; when he appears, none fail to show reverence. When the universally applicable virtues are exemplified, the people become trustworthy; when the universally applicable relationships are established, the people rise to put them into practice; when the nine guiding principles of government are set right, the people respond with service; when the three weighty institutions are established, the people commit few errors. The three hundred and three thousand rites encompass them and bring them to fulfillment in every particular: the people are encouraged without rewards and stand in awe without any display of anger. Yet this interaction of influence and response still depends upon something. Once fulfillment comes without such dependence, even those put to death feel no resentment, and those benefited give no credit for it. Day by day the people turn toward goodness without knowing who brings this about. Thus, reverence and affection extend even among the Man and Mo peoples, and the proper ordering and nurturing of things extend to Heaven and Earth. Even were one to await a sage a hundred generations hence, there would be no doubt. Yet the sage’s unceasing heart remains just as it was at the beginning. Hence it is said: the means by which the sage forms a triad with Heaven and Earth and completes their transforming work consists simply in putting his unceasing heart into operation.
Nevertheless, the sage is inherently sincere; his unceasing activity requires neither deliberation nor effort. What, then, should someone who has not attained sagehood do if he seeks to become sincere? The answer is: choosing the good is the starting point; holding firmly to it is the substance of the endeavor; learning for one’s own moral cultivation and discerning the first stirrings of things are the beginning of establishing one’s resolve. 同考試官署郎中許批：恭惟我皇祖《寶訓》一書，中間綱紀兼總，直與典謨並傳。子能撰擬史臣類輯進呈之意，而詞復爾雅，故録。

同考試官檢討張批：恭惟聖祖耿光大烈，實頼此《寶訓》一書昭示無極。此作乃能揄揚盛美，而詞復渾雅，録之不獨以其駢儷之工也。

同考試官編修邢批：我聖祖嘉言善行，載在《寶訓》，所以垂憲萬世者。子能具述先臣忠愛之意，揄揚極盡，且典則而綺麗，莊敬而大，表之佳者也，録之。
translation_en:
…unites human nature and Heaven’s mandate, reaching through to the utmost sincerity, beginning with perfecting oneself and ending with perfecting other things. Upon reaching its fullest realization, one will likewise stand alongside Heaven and Earth.

Memorial

A memorial composed in the voice of Expositor-in-Waiting Song Lian and others, presenting the Precious Instructions of the Imperial Ming.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Acting Bureau Director: Reverently considering the Precious Instructions of our imperial ancestor, this book comprehensively embraces the guiding principles and governing order, and deserves to be transmitted alongside the Canons and Counsels of the Book of Documents. You have successfully recreated the intentions of the court historians in compiling these instructions by category and presenting them to the throne. Your language is also refined and correct; therefore, I select this piece.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhang, Examining Editor: Reverently considering the luminous glory and great achievements of our sagely ancestor, it is indeed through this book, the Precious Instructions, that they are made manifest for all time. This composition succeeds in extolling their abundant excellence, and its language is also harmonious and elegant. Its selection is not solely on account of its skillful parallel prose.

Comment by Associate Examiner Xing, Compiler: The excellent words and virtuous deeds of our sagely ancestor are recorded in the Precious Instructions, thereby bequeathing a model for countless generations. You have fully expressed the loyal devotion of the ministers of former times and have extolled these virtues to the utmost. Moreover, the writing observes classical standards while being richly beautiful, and is reverent and grand. It is an excellent memorial; I select it.

皇明大統，茂膺曆數之傳，豈彼唐室小康，僅有貞觀之治？然《政要》流傳於海内，以吳兢載筆於當時。惟兹《日曆》之成，效古編年之法，諸臣纂錄以上進，臣濂僭敘于篇端，淺薄自慚，揄揚未盡。顧金匱石室，方有詔以秘藏，乃僻壤下方，未獲觀夫盛美。宜從類輯，用徧寰區。誤被眷知，特賜俞允，遵聖訓而析錄，待後紀之續增。
欽惟皇帝陛下，德配乾坤，才兼文武，荷天命而龍飛淮甸，拯民生而電掃胡元。正中國之衣冠，彝倫攸敘；復先王之禮樂，治教維新。聰明睿知以有臨
translation_en:
…the great imperial succession of our august Ming has abundantly received the transmission of Heaven’s allotted rule. How could it be compared with the modest tranquillity of the Tang house, which had only the good government of the Zhenguan era? Yet the Essentials of Government (Zhengyao) circulated throughout the realm because Wu Jing recorded events at that time. The present Daily Calendar (Rili) was compiled in accordance with the ancient annalistic method. The assembled ministers compiled the records and submitted them to the throne; your servant Lian ventured to write a preface at the beginning. Ashamed of my shallow learning, I could not fully express the praise due. An edict had just ordered that the work be kept in a metal coffer in a stone chamber, securely stored away; consequently, those below in remote regions had no opportunity to behold these splendid achievements. It was fitting to compile selections by category and circulate them throughout the realm. Undeservedly receiving your gracious recognition, I was specially granted approval. Following your sage instructions, I have arranged and transcribed the selections, awaiting further additions from subsequent records.
Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor: your virtue matches Heaven and Earth, and your talents embrace both civil and military accomplishments. Receiving Heaven’s mandate, you rose like a dragon in the Huai region; rescuing the people, you swept away the non-Han Yuan like lightning. You restored the proper caps and robes of the Central Kingdom, bringing the enduring human relationships into order; you revived the rites and music of the former kings, renewing government and moral instruction. With keen perception, sagacity, and wisdom, you preside over…

兩階前後逾二十年

御極
絲綸藹仁義之言自敬
天以及制夷綱紀總帝王之範臣濂等謬叨

寵私學本愧于三長愚莫效乎一得給
尚方之筆札青簡難窮飽大官之殽羞素餐
===

溟敢云酌飲而自足惟上廑
重瞳之
睿覽抑先導義例之津涯倬乎雲漢之光言幾
五萬煥乎文章之美傳並六經伏願

translation_en:
…vast and profound as a deep spring, manifesting itself in due season. You have brought carriage gauges and writing into a single unified order, and caused the dance with shields and feathers to be performed between the two stairways. Over a span of more than twenty years, your edicts and instructions fall into forty categories. From your crossing of the Yangzi to your accession to the throne, your imperial pronouncements abound in words of benevolence and righteousness; from revering Heaven to controlling the barbarians, your guiding principles encompass the exemplary standards of emperors and kings.

Your servants, Lian and the others, have undeservedly received selection and promotion, and all have enjoyed your gracious favor. Our learning falls short of the historian’s three strengths, and in our ignorance we cannot offer even a single useful insight. Supplied with brushes and writing materials from the imperial workshops, we could scarcely exhaust the record on bamboo slips; feasting on the delicacies of the imperial kitchen, we fear receiving sustenance without earning it. Gazing at the vast heavens through a tube, how could we presume to depict them? Measuring the boundless sea with a gourd, dare we claim that a draught would suffice us? Since this work will engage Your Majesty’s sagacious gaze, we first offer an introduction to its organizing principles and editorial conventions. Resplendent as the radiance of the Milky Way, its words number nearly fifty thousand; brilliant in literary beauty, it will be transmitted alongside the Six Classics.

We humbly wish that Your Majesty’s sacred life may know no bounds, and that your achievements may endure as long as Heaven and Earth; that your imperial dominion may last forever, and that the main line and branches of your house may behold…

…the renewed radiance of the sun and moon. Your servants Lian and others have respectfully compiled, by subject, the Precious Instructions of the August Ming (Huang Ming baoxun) in five juan and submit it together with this memorial for Your Majesty’s attention.
Third Session
Policy Essays
First Question
Comment by Associate Examiner Lu, Chief Supervising Secretary: Reverence is the foundation of imperial governance. From the time our imperial progenitor established the supreme standard, successive sage sovereigns have carried it forward, and today it flourishes to an exceptional degree. This essay ably expounds it. Its author has clearly steeped himself deeply in the transforming influence of the sage sovereign; his accomplishment is more than mere literary skill.
Comment by Associate Examiner Dong, Compiler: From antiquity, emperors have upheld a single Way in succession: this reverence alone. Our sagely progenitor inaugurated it, and His Majesty has subsequently inherited and continued it. The transmission of this teaching of the mind flourishes to a degree unmatched in past or present. This candidate can bring it forward and expound it [?], and thus may be said to understand something of the intentions underlying the great sage’s establishment of institutions. Include this essay in the record.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wu, a Hanlin Academy Compiler: On the policy question concerning the imperial compositions, candidates generally cited unrelated matters to fill out their responses. This essay alone answers every point without omission and presents its responses in a fitting manner. Its author must be well versed in historical precedents.

Comment by Associate Examiner Mao, a Hanlin Academy Senior Compiler: Reverent attentiveness is essential to sagely learning from beginning to end. Our successive sage emperors, transmitting and receiving this inheritance, have all followed this Way. There is thus good reason why their achievements in government have surpassed those of earlier dynasties. You have been able to expound it fully and give it vigorous expression. Might you be one of those said to have absorbed the transforming influence of sagely rule and gained understanding from it? You certainly deserve a high recommendation.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Secretariat Supervisor: All five policy essays answer their questions well, but this essay, in expounding the essentials of sagely learning and the method of cultivating the mind, captures their essence especially well. It is therefore placed first in this selection.

The Way transmitted among emperors and kings since antiquity, and the source of their method of cultivating the mind, have a long history indeed. In its simplicity and essential import, does it not consist in attending reverently to virtue? Reverent attentiveness is where virtue gathers, the substance of the mind, and the source from which good government proceeds. The government of emperors and kings is rooted in the mind, and the means by which they govern their minds is rooted in reverent attentiveness. Since antiquity this has been unalterable. Yet never has it flourished more greatly than under our dynasty, reaching its culmination today. It carries forward the succession of a thousand years and inaugurates prosperity for ten thousand generations to come. title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
祖訓精誠錄近質以
皇上敬一箴其真有見於
制作之妙傳心之微而思有以對揚其盛矣
乎請敬陳之昔在唐虞授受典謨孔彰始
以精一之言繼以執中之訓精者敬以擇
也一者敬以守也而中則敬之極功也當
時雖不言敬而敬之源始矣故放勳則欽
明允恭重華則温恭允塞斯則能敬之實
而其作歌則敕天時幾昌言則慎憲屢省
===
斯則持敬之功至其儆戒無虞敬修可願
上下協恭則又保敬之道此二帝所以允
蹈敬德而開心學之宗者也禹受舜而王
則兢業懋德慎修思永以敬而入聖湯纘
夏而興則顧諟明命欽崇天道以敬而反
身文武繼商而作則無斁之保敬勝之吉
又皆以敬而永命此三王所以休迪前聖
而傳心學之法者也是故肇人文之盛以
啓後王莫過於二帝垂典則之訓以貽後

punctuated:
《祖訓》《精誠錄》，近質以皇上《敬一箴》，其真有見於制作之妙、傳心之微，而思有以對揚其盛矣乎？請敬陳之。
昔在唐虞，授受典謨，孔彰。始以精一之言，繼以執中之訓。精者，敬以擇也；一者，敬以守也；而中則敬之極功也。當時雖不言敬，而敬之源始矣。故放勳則欽明允恭，重華則温恭允塞，斯則能敬之實；而其作歌則敕天時幾，昌言則慎憲屢省，斯則持敬之功。至其儆戒無虞，敬修可願，上下協恭，則又保敬之道。此二帝所以允蹈敬德，而開心學之宗者也。
禹受舜而王，則兢業懋德，慎修思永，以敬而入聖；湯纘夏而興，則顧諟明命，欽崇天道，以敬而反身；文武繼商而作，則無斁之保，敬勝之吉，又皆以敬而永命。此三王所以休迪前聖，而傳心學之法者也。是故肇人文之盛以啓後王，莫過於二帝；垂典則之訓以貽後
translation_en:
…the Ancestral Instructions (Zuxun) and the Record of Utmost Sincerity (Jingcheng lu), and, drawing on more recent times, examining His Majesty’s Admonition on Reverence and Single-mindedness (Jingyi zhen). Surely you have truly perceived the subtle excellence of these compositions and the profound subtleties of transmitting the mind, and seek thereby to respond to and extol their greatness! Allow me respectfully to set this forth.
In the days of Tang and Yu, the canons and counsels concerning the transmission and reception of rulership were abundantly clear. First came the words concerning refinement and single-mindedness, followed by the injunction to hold fast to the Mean. Refinement means using reverence to discriminate; single-mindedness means using reverence to hold fast; and the Mean is the consummate achievement of reverence. Although reverence was not explicitly named at that time, its source had already appeared. Thus Fangxun [Yao] was reverent, discerning, sincere, and respectful; Chonghua [Shun] was gentle, respectful, sincere, and trustworthy. These were the concrete manifestations of their capacity for reverence. In composing songs, they spoke of attending reverently to Heaven, to the proper moment, and to the first stirrings of events; in their noble counsels, they spoke of being cautious about established rules and repeatedly examining oneself. These were their efforts to maintain reverence. As for remaining vigilant when there was no cause for alarm, reverently cultivating what was worthy of desire, and joining superiors and inferiors in mutual respect, these were also ways of preserving reverence. Through these means the Two Emperors faithfully practiced reverent virtue and established the founding tradition of the learning of the mind.
When Yu received rulership from Shun and became king, he was vigilant and diligent, exerted himself in virtue, cultivated himself cautiously, and thought of the enduring future; through reverence he attained sagehood. When Tang rose to succeed the Xia, he constantly attended to Heaven’s luminous mandate and reverently honored Heaven’s Way; through reverence he examined himself. When Wen and Wu arose to succeed the Shang, there were their tireless efforts to preserve the mandate and the good fortune that comes when reverence prevails; they too prolonged their mandate through reverence. Through these means the Three Kings nobly followed the former sages and transmitted the method of learning of the mind. Thus, in inaugurating the flourishing of human culture to enlighten later kings, none surpassed the Two Emperors; in handing down teachings that served as enduring standards for those who came after…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
裔莫備于三王自是以還漢唐宋之君學
不知要既於聖人之道有所未聞而敬不
知本其於聖人之心又安有所得也哉逮我
皇明
高皇帝有克明濬哲之德有日躋緝熈之心固
已邁王而並帝矣
文皇繼承時則有
聖學心法之書有統言者義難分述君臣二
篇是也有專言者事各有指學問以下是
===
也人倫有五而但言君臣父子者誠以
帝王之書貽範有在自一世以至萬世則父子
之道重以
一人而撫萬方則君臣之道急此書之所以專
於二也然而言內治則有
后妃之道而不廢夫婦也言睦親則有九族
之道而不廢長幼也言臣道則百僚各相
為友而亦不廢也此書之所以統於五也
是書也上繼

文皇繼承，時則有《聖學心法》之書。有統言者，義難分述，君臣二篇是也；有專言者，事各有指，學問以下是也。人倫有五，而但言君臣父子者，誠以帝王之書，貽範有在：自一世以至萬世，則父子之道重；以一人而撫萬方，則君臣之道急。此書之所以專於二也。然而言內治，則有后妃之道，而不廢夫婦也；言睦親，則有九族之道，而不廢長幼也；言臣道，則百僚各相為友，而亦不廢也。此書之所以統於五也。是書也，上繼

…descendants, none were more comprehensive than the Three Kings. From that time onward, the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song did not understand what was essential in learning, and thus remained uninstructed in aspects of the Way of the sages. Nor did they understand the foundation of reverence: how, then, could they have attained any understanding of the sages’ minds? When our august Ming arose, Emperor Gao possessed the virtue of luminous discernment and profound wisdom, and a mind that advanced daily and continually cultivated its brilliance. He had indeed surpassed the Three Kings and equaled the Two Emperors.
Emperor Wen succeeded him, and in his time there appeared the book Essential Methods of the Mind in Sagely Learning (Shengxue xinfa). Some sections speak comprehensively, their meanings being difficult to expound separately: these are the two chapters on rulers and ministers. Others speak specifically, each addressing a particular matter: these are the chapters from “Learning and Inquiry” onward. There are five human relationships, yet the book speaks expressly only of ruler and minister, and father and son. This is because a book by an emperor has a particular purpose in bequeathing exemplary guidance. For succession from one generation through ten thousand generations, the Way of father and son is of great importance; for one man to govern all regions, the Way of ruler and minister is urgent. This is why the book concentrates on these two relationships. Yet when it discusses governance within the palace, it includes the Way of empresses and consorts, and so does not neglect the relationship of husband and wife. When it discusses harmony among relatives, it includes the Way of the nine degrees of kinship, and so does not neglect the relationship of elder and younger. When it discusses the Way of ministers, the officials are all friends to one another, and so friendship, too, is not neglected. This is why the book encompasses all five relationships. text:

世世修德無敢或懈其始終一於敬有如是
者大哉敬乎帝王傳之至
皇祖而益明
文皇述之至
皇上而大著自此與
天地無疆皆是道也是以
東宮育德仰瞻
帝躬至教固有所承矣然而
===
祖
宗之製固為
聖子
神孫發也他日以備
出閤講讀正所以衍此道於無疆者又何疑
邪若夫唐之帝範此特

可倫乎謹對
第二問

宗之製固爲
聖子

第二問
punctuated:
君經歷艱難，終言世世修德，無敢或懈。其始終一於敬，有如是者。大哉，敬乎！帝王傳之，至皇祖而益明；文皇述之，至皇上而大著。自此與天地無疆，皆是道也。是以東宮育德，仰瞻帝躬，至教固有所承矣。然而祖宗之製，固為聖子神孫發也。他日以備出閤講讀，正所以衍此道於無疆者，又何疑邪？若夫唐之《帝範》，此特聖人盛德之至，取其篇名之義耳。何啻天壤，而可倫乎？謹對。

第二問
translation_en:
…the ruler who endured hardships, and ends by saying that generation after generation must cultivate virtue, never daring to slacken. Such is its unwavering commitment to reverence from beginning to end. Great indeed is reverence! Emperors and kings transmitted it, and with Your Majesty’s imperial ancestor it became still clearer; Emperor Wen expounded it, and with Your Majesty it has become fully manifest. Henceforth, for as long as Heaven and Earth endure, this same Way will prevail. Thus, as the Crown Prince cultivates his virtue and looks up to Your Majesty’s person, he assuredly has a source from which to receive the highest teaching. Yet the writings of the imperial ancestors were expressly produced for their sage sons and divine grandsons. To provide them hereafter for lectures and readings when the Crown Prince leaves the inner palace to begin his formal education is precisely the means of extending this Way without end. What doubt can there be?

As for the Tang work Models for Emperors (Difan), it is merely that the sage, in the utmost fullness of his virtue, has adopted the meaning of its title. The distance between them is greater than that between Heaven and Earth: how could they be compared? Respectfully submitted in reply.

同考試官署郎中許批：「心法並用，內外咸舉，此成周所以有道之長。子能援古條答，宛然在目。至我朝立國延休，配周遠邁，與我皇上覲揚光大、高出隆古之意，且敷揚有體，忠懇無窮。錄之，不直取其文也。」

同考試官檢討張批：「本之誠意憂勤，以成經綸大業，蓋自古帝王致治之道。而我聖祖、皇上之所以軼三代而上躋唐虞者，亦以此。是作獨能敷揚闡悉，不遺餘旨。其嘗究心於治化之源而有得者歟？」

同考試官編修邢批：「修內攘外，諸士子類能言之，而其誠意憂勤之實，此策發明詳盡，蓋非以其徒法焉耳。經綸之學，舍子其誰？」

Zhou Shizuo

Associate Examiner Xu, Acting Director, comments: “Employing both the mind and institutional methods, attending fully to both internal and external affairs: this is what enabled the Zhou to sustain good government for so long. You draw on antiquity and answer point by point, making everything vividly present before the reader. As for our dynasty’s establishment and enduring blessings, matching and far surpassing Zhou, and our emperor’s purpose of carrying forward and magnifying its glory [?], rising far above high antiquity, you expound these fittingly, with boundless loyalty and earnestness. In selecting this essay, we value more than its literary qualities.”

Associate Examiner Zhang, Examining Editor, comments: “To take sincerity of intention and anxious diligence as the foundation for accomplishing the great work of ordering the realm has been the way emperors and kings have brought about good government since antiquity. This, too, is how our sagely founder and our emperor have surpassed the Three Dynasties and risen to the level of Tang Yao and Yu Shun. This essay alone expounds and elucidates these matters fully, leaving none of their significance unexplained. Have you perhaps devoted yourself to investigating the source of good government and moral transformation, and gained insight into it?”

Associate Examiner Xing, Compiler, comments: “Cultivating internal affairs and repelling external threats are matters most candidates can discuss. Yet this policy essay explains fully and in detail the substance of sincerity of intention and anxious diligence underlying them; it plainly does not treat them merely as institutional methods. In the learning required to order the realm, whom could we turn to but you?”

text:

皇上之神功大業同符先王尤為有見子其潜心王道者乎

經綸之道合內外而一之者故儒先每每稱之子能剖
析此義至於我
皇上聖德神功同符
聖祖而上躋古之帝王之盛者尤能揄揚以風来世亦可以占子經綸之蘊

聖祖、皇上之神功大業，同符先王，尤為有見。子其潜心王道者乎？
考試官左庶子江批：天保、采薇諸詩，乃古帝王經綸之道合內外而一之者，故儒先每每稱之。子能剖析此義，至於我皇上聖德神功同符聖祖，而上躋古之帝王之盛者，尤能揄揚，以風来世，亦可以占子經綸之蘊矣，是用錄之。
帝王經綸之迹，布在方冊，廣大精密，賾然而莫可究者，其文也。而其憂勤惻怛，本諸心，以達諸政，以致諸其民人，盎然而有不可解之情，其實也。得其實，則其文舉矣；不得其實，而惟其文之慕，則亦徒法而已也，其何以幾帝王之盛乎哉？執事策士而及此，是將以俊傑望士也。顧愚何足以知此？雖然，亦嘗觀之詩而得其槩矣，請述以對。
昔者有周盛時，文武成康，聖賢繼作；周召畢榮，篤棐夾輔。內而宅俊登庸，民物煕皥，
translation_en:
…the divine achievements and great undertakings of our Sacred Ancestor and His Majesty accord with those of the ancient kings: this is especially insightful. Are you one who devotes himself deeply to the Kingly Way?
Examiner Jiang, Left Mentor, comments: The poems “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao), “Gathering Ferns” (Caiwei), and others embody the ancient emperors’ and kings’ art of ordering the realm, uniting domestic and external affairs as one. Thus earlier Confucian scholars repeatedly praised them. You have analyzed this meaning clearly. In particular, you have eloquently extolled how His Majesty’s sagely virtue and divine achievements accord with those of our Sacred Ancestor and rise to the heights attained by the ancient emperors and kings, thereby offering an example to future ages. This also allows us to discern your store of learning in the art of government. For this reason, I have selected this essay for inclusion.
The traces of how emperors and kings ordered the realm are set out in written records. Vast and precise, intricate beyond exhaustive investigation—these are its outward forms. But their anxious diligence and compassionate concern originated in their hearts, reached into their administration, and extended to their people, overflowing with an affection that could not be dissolved: this is its substance. Grasp that substance, and the outward forms can all be put into effect. Fail to grasp it and merely admire the outward forms, and these remain nothing more than bare methods. How could one thereby approach the flourishing rule of the emperors and kings? By addressing this matter in your policy question to the candidates, you gentlemen show that you expect outstanding talent from them. Yet how could someone as foolish as I be qualified to understand it? Nevertheless, I have studied it in the Book of Odes and gained some understanding of its general principles. Allow me to set these out in reply.
In the flourishing age of Zhou, Kings Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang—sages and worthies—arose in succession. The dukes of Zhou, Shao, Bi, and Rong faithfully supported and assisted them. Within the realm, outstanding men were placed in office and advanced to service, and the people and all living things flourished in harmony…

外而九夷八蠻罔不通道其治蓋極其盛
矣自今觀之其治內也於鹿鳴吾得其燕

棣吾得其親親焉於伐木吾得其故舊不
遺焉此其恩意之聯屬悃愊之浹孚所謂
如元首股肱一體之相須如家人父子一
堂之相與今讀其詩尚可想見也是以實
勝者也其諸敦本辨族選材敘位之制如
封建學校之類之見於周禮者其文非不
===

遣役焉於出車吾得其勞帥焉於杕杜吾
得其勞戍焉此其憂傷勞苦之情體䘏軫
愛之至所謂說以使民而民忘其勞說以
犯難而民忘其死今讀其詩亦可想見也
是亦以實勝者也其諸井邑車甸責伐擅
削之制如井田軍旅之類之見於周禮者
其文非不犁然設也今試取而行之其又

勝者也其諸敦本辨族序材敘位之制如
封建學校之類之見於周禮者其文非不
===
較然著也今試取而行之其能感人動物
如彼其盛矣乎其治外也於采薇吾得其
遣役焉於出車吾得其勞帥焉於杕杜吾
得其勞戍焉此其憂傷勞苦之情體卹彰
愛之至所謂說以使民而民忘其勞說以
犯難而民忘其死今讀其詩亦可想見也
是亦以實勝者也其諸井邑車甸書役糧
削之制如井田軍旅之類之見於周禮者
其文非不犂然該也今試取而行之其又
punctuated: 外而九夷八蠻罔不通道，其治蓋極其盛矣。自今觀之，其治內也，於《鹿鳴》吾得其燕惠焉；於《四牡》，於《皇華》，吾得其使臣焉；於《常棣》，吾得其親親焉；於《伐木》，吾得其故舊不遺焉。此其恩意之聯屬，悃愊之浹孚，所謂如元首股肱一體之相須，如家人父子一堂之相與，今讀其詩尚可想見也。是以實勝者也。其諸敦本辨族、選材敘位之制，如封建、學校之類之見於《周禮》者，其文非不較然著也。今試取而行之，其能感人動物如彼其盛矣乎？其治外也，於《采薇》吾得其遣役焉；於《出車》吾得其勞帥焉；於《杕杜》吾得其勞戍焉。此其憂傷勞苦之情，體䘏軫愛之至，所謂說以使民而民忘其勞，說以犯難而民忘其死，今讀其詩亦可想見也。是亦以實勝者也。其諸井邑車甸、責伐擅削之制，如井田、軍旅之類之見於《周禮》者，其文非不犁然設也。今試取而行之，其又
translation_en:
…Abroad, none of the Nine Yi and Eight Man peoples failed to establish communication with them. Their government had indeed reached the height of flourishing.

Viewed from the present, their domestic government is revealed to me in “The Deer Call” (Lu ming), through their gracious hospitality at feasts; in “The Four Stallions” (Si mu) and “The Splendid Flowers” (Huang hua), through their employment of envoys; in “The Cherry Tree” (Chang di), through their affection for kinsmen; and in “Felling Trees” (Fa mu), through their refusal to neglect old friends. These show the bonds of their benevolence and the pervasive mutual trust born of sincerity. This is what is meant by head and limbs depending upon one another as parts of a single body, or fathers and sons living together as members of one household. Even today, reading their poems, we can picture it. Here, substance prevailed.

As for their institutions for strengthening fundamental bonds, distinguishing kin groups, selecting talent, and ordering ranks—such as enfeoffment and schools, recorded in the Rites of Zhou—their outward forms were certainly clearly set forth. Yet if we were now to adopt and implement them, could they move people and other beings as profoundly as they did in that flourishing age?

As for their government abroad, in “Gathering Bracken” (Cai wei) I perceive how they dispatched men on military service; in “Sending Out the Chariots” (Chu che), how they honored returning commanders; and in “The Solitary Pear Tree” (Di du), how they welcomed and comforted returning garrison troops. These reveal their feelings of sorrow over toil and hardship, and the utmost sympathetic concern and loving care. This is what is meant by employing the people through gladness so that they forget their toil, and leading them into danger through gladness so that they forget the prospect of death. Even today, reading their poems, we can picture it. Here too, substance prevailed.

As for their institutions of well-field settlements and chariot levies, and of reprimand, punitive expedition, and reduction of territory [?]—such as the well-field system and military organization recorded in the Rites of Zhou—their outward forms were certainly distinctly established. Yet if we were now to adopt and implement them, could they again…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
能感人動物如彼其盛也夫乎是何也情見
乎詩而制存於禮得於其禮而不得於其
詩者徒法也苟得於其詩則其實舉矣何
有於内何有於外何有於修且攘之莫舉
邪夫固周之所以盛也嗣是而漢而唐而
宋吾惑焉彼其幾於攘也而内日以虚幾
於修也而外日以不振甚則雜夷為治并
其内外而失之極矣尚惡足言哉洪惟我
朝
===
太祖高皇帝再開天宇汛掃腥穢
成祖文皇帝三犁虜庭廓靖氛孽
神聖繼作謨烈重光以關雎麟趾之心而行立
政周官之法其在外也節鎮外連督府内
制屯戍萬里守在四夷濯靈赫聲如風霆
之流行保大定功如嶽鎭之底奠盖自有
周以還未之能過矣其在内也藩郡將尉
以聯其族部寺院司以辨其職司府州縣
以比其屬鄉學國雍以明其教則壤辨方

punctuated: 能感人動物如彼其盛也夫乎？是何也？情見乎詩，而制存於禮。得於其禮而不得於其詩者，徒法也。苟得於其詩，則其實舉矣。何有於内？何有於外？何有於修且攘之莫舉邪？夫固周之所以盛也。嗣是而漢，而唐，而宋，吾惑焉。彼其幾於攘也，而内日以虚；幾於修也，而外日以不振。甚則雜夷為治，并其内外而失之極矣，尚惡足言哉！洪惟我朝太祖高皇帝再開天宇，汛掃腥穢；成祖文皇帝三犁虜庭，廓靖氛孽。神聖繼作，謨烈重光，以《關雎》《麟趾》之心，而行《立政》《周官》之法。其在外也，節鎮外連，督府内制，屯戍萬里，守在四夷。濯靈赫聲，如風霆之流行；保大定功，如嶽鎭之底奠。盖自有周以還，未之能過矣。其在内也，藩郡將尉，以聯其族；部寺院司，以辨其職；司府州縣，以比其屬；鄉學國雍，以明其教；則壤辨方
translation_en:
…could they move people and stir all beings with such magnificent effect? Why is this? Feelings are manifest in the Odes, while institutions are preserved in the Rites. To grasp what is in the Rites without grasping what is in the Odes is to possess mere regulations. If one grasps what is in the Odes, their substance is fully realized. What difficulty would there be in domestic affairs? What difficulty in external affairs? How could either internal cultivation or the repulsion of foreign enemies remain unaccomplished? This, indeed, was why the Zhou flourished. Thereafter came the Han, the Tang, and the Song, and I am perplexed by them. When they approached success in repelling foreign enemies, they grew daily weaker within; when they approached success in internal cultivation, their position abroad grew daily less vigorous. At worst, they mingled with barbarians in governing and utterly lost control both within and without. What more is there worth saying?

Reverently considering our dynasty: Emperor Taizu Gao reopened the realm beneath Heaven and swept away its foul pollution; Emperor Chengzu Wen thrice ploughed through the enemy’s court and cleared away pernicious disorder. Divine and sagely rulers arose in succession, renewing the radiance of their plans and achievements. With the spirit of “The Ospreys” (Guanju) and “The Qilin’s Hoofs” (Linzhi), they implemented the principles of “Establishing Government” (Lizheng) and “The Officers of Zhou” (Zhouguan).

In external affairs, regional military commands formed a network beyond the capital, while the Chief Military Commissions exercised control from within. Military colonies and garrisons stretched ten thousand li, and defense extended to the lands of the barbarians on all four sides. Their resplendent might and illustrious renown spread like wind and thunder; their preservation of greatness and establishment of lasting achievements were as firmly grounded as the great guardian mountains. Since the Zhou, nothing has surpassed this.

In internal affairs, princes, commandery princes, generals, and commandants bind together the imperial clan; ministries, courts, bureaus, and offices distinguish official duties; commissions, prefectures, subprefectures, and counties organize subordinate jurisdictions; local schools and the Imperial University make moral instruction manifest; soils are assessed and regions distinguished…

text:

綿絡如江海之流轉蓋□有周以還亦未
之能及矣

皇上神功聖德益有以覲揚而光大之以修則
盡倫而盡制以攘則克懐而克威是以重
熈累洽迅邁渙敷積之而益博厚發之而
益髙明蓋將上下與天地同流矣猗歟休
哉而執事者尤欲責之以萬一之獻愚固
===
游於大化順
帝則而弗知者也尚何能言愚甞聞之吳季札請
觀周禮而魯太史為之工歌二南國風雅頌
宋龜山考亭論述天保以上采薇以下諸
詩一則曰先王作處本之誠意一則曰文
武之治始於憂勤終於逸樂此實帝王經
綸之大本而我
祖宗
列聖暨我

列聖紹休，茂隆無替。迨我皇上，神功聖德，益有以覲揚而光大之。以修則盡倫而盡制，以攘則克懐而克威。是以重熈累洽，迅邁渙敷，積之而益博厚，發之而益髙明，蓋將上下與天地同流矣。猗歟休哉！而執事者尤欲責之以萬一之獻，愚固游於大化，順帝則而弗知者也，尚何能言？愚甞聞之，吳季札請觀周禮，而魯太史為之工歌二南、國風、雅、頌。宋龜山、考亭論述《天保》以上、《采薇》以下諸詩，一則曰：「先王作處，本之誠意。」一則曰：「文武之治，始於憂勤，終於逸樂。」此實帝王經綸之大本，而我祖宗列聖暨我
translation_en:
…to regulate their tribute. The hierarchical order is dignified and august, like the illumination of “工八日” [?]; its power and influence extend in unbroken continuity, like the circulating waters of rivers and seas. Indeed, from [illegible] the Zhou onward, nothing has equaled it.
The successive sage emperors carried forward this excellence, flourishing in greatness without decline. With our present Emperor, divine achievements and sagely virtue have further displayed and magnified it. In internal cultivation, he fulfills every human relationship and perfects every institution; in repelling external threats, he both wins allegiance and inspires awe. Thus brilliance and harmony accumulate through successive reigns, advancing swiftly and spreading far. The more these virtues accumulate, the broader and deeper they become; the more they manifest themselves, the loftier and brighter they grow. Indeed, above and below, they will flow together with Heaven and Earth. Ah, how splendid!
Yet you, gentlemen in charge, still wish to demand from me a contribution of even one ten-thousandth. I, in my ignorance, dwell within this great transforming influence, following the Emperor’s standards without being conscious of them. What more can I say? I have heard that when Ji Zha of Wu requested to observe the rites of Zhou, the Grand Scribe of Lu had musicians sing for him the Two Southern Sections, the Airs of the States, the Elegantiae, and the Hymns. The Song scholars Guishan and Kaoting discussed the poems up to and including “Heaven Protects” (Tianbao), and those from “Gathering Bracken” (Caiwei) onward. One said, “The actions of the former kings were rooted in sincerity of intention.” The other said, “The government of Kings Wen and Wu began in anxious diligence and ended in ease and enjoyment.” This is truly the great foundation of emperors’ and kings’ ordering of the realm, and our founding ancestors, the successive sage emperors, and our…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
皇上巳試之明効也愚尚何能言哉不然則季
札亦何取於詩而安內攘外之道要亦不
外於鹿鳴諸什而得之是必有說矣請以
是終幸執事進而教之
第三問
瞿景淳
同考試官都給事中周批據事論事不必皆同得
尚友法而體裁即逾出
同考試官檢討王批吾子品擬宛然以當世
===
知所行不惑矣
同考試官編修袁批古人心事不同惟類情者
能一之子能劑量不爽可謂有真見矣
同考試官編修彭批論世者非素有權度鮮
不眩于異同子能就事論事真千古斷案矣
同考試官修撰沈批古人事未易折衷此作
根據詳明議論渾厚是可與論其世也
考試官左庶子江批人物一策正欲觀諸士處心制
事之微而因以占諸它日子能隨事折衷不隨不亢

皇上巳試之明効也。愚尚何能言哉？不然，則季札亦何取於詩？而安內攘外之道，要亦不外於鹿鳴諸什而得之，是必有說矣。請以是終，幸執事進而教之。

第三問
瞿景淳

同考試官都給事中周批：據事論事，不必皆同，得尚友法，而體裁即逾出。

同考試官檢討王批：吾子品擬宛然，以當世，知所行不惑矣。

同考試官編修袁批：古人心事不同，惟類情者能一之。子能劑量不爽，可謂有真見矣。

同考試官編修彭批：論世者非素有權度，鮮不眩于異同。子能就事論事，真千古斷案矣。

同考試官修撰沈批：古人事未易折衷，此作根據詳明，議論渾厚，是可與論其世也。

考試官左庶子江批：人物一策，正欲觀諸士處心制事之微，而因以占諸它日。子能隨事折衷，不隨不亢
translation_en:
…His Majesty the Emperor has already put these principles to the test with manifest results. What more could I, in my ignorance, say? Otherwise, what would Jizha have valued in the Odes? The way to secure peace within and repel threats from without is, in essentials, likewise to be found within the poems beginning with “The Deer Call” (Lu ming). There must surely be an explanation for this. Let me conclude here, hoping that you, sir, will offer me further instruction.

Third Policy Question
Qu Jingchun

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Chief Supervising Secretary: You discuss matters on the basis of the facts, without insisting that all must agree. You have grasped the method of befriending the ancients, and your composition also stands out in its form and organization.

Comment by Associate Examiner Wang, Examining Editor: Your assessments and comparisons are vividly apt. Applied to the present age, they enable you to know how to act without perplexity.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yuan, Compiler: The intentions and affairs of the ancients differed; only someone who can discern similarities in their underlying feelings can bring them into unity. Your weighing and measuring are unerring: this may be called true insight.

Comment by Associate Examiner Peng, Compiler: Those who discuss past ages, unless they have long possessed sound standards of judgment, seldom escape being bewildered by similarities and differences. You can discuss each matter on its own terms: this is truly a definitive judgment for the ages.

Comment by Associate Examiner Shen, Senior Compiler: It is not easy to reach balanced judgments on the affairs of the ancients. This composition offers detailed and clear supporting evidence, and its arguments are substantial and measured. Its author is someone with whom one may discuss the age in which those men lived.

Comment by Examiner Jiang, Left Vice Supervisor of Instruction: This policy question on historical figures was intended precisely to reveal the subtleties of the candidates’ intentions and their handling of affairs, and thereby to gauge their future conduct. You can reach a balanced judgment appropriate to each matter, neither following others submissively nor standing aloof in obstinacy…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
權度蓋精切矣中行君子亦在于平是用高薦
君子之於天下也本之貞固以立其幹通
之權變以達其施而天下之能事畢矣何
也所貴乎君子者貴其同而能異也夫惟
匪貞既無以自異而匪變又無以大同於
是乎矯以為亢則亂常而拂倫詭以為隨
又習非而徇俗是二者皆非也君子弗由
也君子之所由者惟同而能異是故圓神
不倚而舉世不敢以為隨獨立不懼而舉
===
世不敢以為亢以是而通天下之志而成
天下之務蓋沛乎其順矣又何疑於其跡
之同弗同請因執事之問而陳之今夫周
公之吐握延賢以相成王而當天下之任
也彼孫抃之薦唐介為侍御史或謂抃未
之識則曰抃豈求識臺官者正以避市恩
之嫌耳若德宗時謁禁方嚴執政至闔門
謝客而裴度之拜相也則建請還第延訪
士夫以濟時艱此其心雖未必周公之誠

君子之於天下也，本之貞固以立其幹，通之權變以達其施，而天下之能事畢矣。何也？所貴乎君子者，貴其同而能異也。夫惟匪貞，既無以自異；而匪變，又無以大同。於是乎矯以為亢，則亂常而拂倫；詭以為隨，又習非而徇俗。是二者皆非也，君子弗由也。君子之所由者，惟同而能異。是故圓神不倚，而舉世不敢以為隨；獨立不懼，而舉世不敢以為亢。以是而通天下之志，而成天下之務，蓋沛乎其順矣，又何疑於其跡之同弗同？請因執事之問而陳之。今夫周公之吐握，延賢以相成王，而當天下之任也。彼孫抃之薦唐介為侍御史，或謂抃未之識，則曰：「抃豈求識臺官者？」正以避市恩之嫌耳。若德宗時，謁禁方嚴，執政至闔門謝客；而裴度之拜相也，則建請還第，延訪士夫，以濟時艱。此其心雖未必周公之誠
translation_en:
…Your standards of judgment are indeed precise and incisive. The gentleman who follows the mean likewise rests on balance; on this account I recommend you highly.

In his dealings with the world, the gentleman takes steadfast rectitude as his foundation, establishing his mainstay, and employs adaptability to circumstances to put his principles into practice. Thus he accomplishes all that can be accomplished in the world. Why is this? What we value in the gentleman is his ability to accord with others while also differing from them. Without rectitude, he has no means of distinguishing himself; without adaptability, he has no means of achieving broad concord. If, then, he adopts a strained posture of aloofness, he disrupts enduring norms and violates human relationships; if he resorts to dissimulation in order to conform, he becomes habituated to wrongdoing and panders to prevailing customs. Both courses are wrong, and the gentleman follows neither. The course he follows is simply to accord with others while remaining capable of differing from them. Thus, being versatile and perceptive without partiality, he cannot be charged by anyone with mere conformity; standing alone without fear, he cannot be charged by anyone with aloofness. In this way he brings the aspirations of the world into communication and accomplishes its affairs, proceeding with ample ease. Why, then, should we be troubled over whether his outward conduct accords with that of others or differs from it? Allow me to explain in response to your question.

Consider the Duke of Zhou: he spat out his food and held his unbound hair in his hand to receive worthy men, assisting King Cheng and shouldering responsibility for the realm. When Sun Bian recommended Tang Jie as Attendant Censor, someone remarked that Bian did not know him. He replied, “Would I, Bian, seek acquaintance with officials of the Censorate?” His purpose was precisely to avoid suspicion of buying their gratitude. Under Emperor Dezong, restrictions on visits were so strict that chief ministers went so far as to close their doors and turn away visitors. Yet when Pei Du was appointed chief minister, he proposed that he be allowed to return to his residence and receive and consult scholar-officials, in order to overcome the difficulties of the time. Although their intentions may not have possessed the sincerity of the Duke of Zhou…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
而其恪共則可尚矣祁奚之舉親舉賢以
答晉侯而嗣中軍之任也若王旦之薦寇
準為樞密使上謂準嘗短卿則曰臣位久
多闕正益見其無隱之忠耳至神宗時呂
正獻每因公議數列安石而正獻之執政
也則多所汲引獨於其子不用此其心雖
不及祁奚之公而其直諒亦可嘉矣察吏
治者所以奠民膚也故范文正為叅政每
見監司之不才者輒一筆勾之蓋有得于
===
周官弊治之義矣而韓公億見諸路攟摭
官吏小過者輒不懌曰柰何錮人於聖世
是又虞廷宥過之仁焉顧一則亟於元惡
一則原於小眚跡雖異也而其心何嘗有
不同集衆思者所以廣忠益也故司馬光
之榜客位請以奏牘聞朝廷書狀規過失
蓋有契于孔明之心矣而李文靖常言在
位無補惟中外所陳利害一切報罷則又
曹參寧一之風焉顧一則用之飭蠱一則

translation_en:
…yet his reverent diligence deserves esteem. Qi Xi recommended both his kinsman and a worthy man in response to the lord of Jin’s inquiry, to provide successors to posts in the Central Army. Similarly, when Wang Dan recommended Kou Zhun as Military Affairs Commissioner, the emperor said, “Zhun has spoken ill of you.” Wang replied, “Your servant has long held office and has many shortcomings. This only further demonstrates his loyalty in concealing nothing.” In Emperor Shenzong’s time, Lü Zhengxian repeatedly invoked public opinion to enumerate Wang Anshi’s faults [?]. Yet when Zhengxian held executive office, he advanced many men, declining only to employ his son. Although his intentions did not equal Qi Xi’s impartiality, his uprightness and sincerity also deserve praise.

Scrutinizing officials’ administration serves to secure the people’s well-being [?]. Thus, when Fan Wenzheng was Participant in the Determination of Governmental Matters, whenever he encountered an incompetent surveillance official, he struck out his name with a single stroke of the brush. He had evidently grasped the principle of assessing administration in the Offices of Zhou. Yet whenever Han Yi saw people in the various circuits ferreting out officials’ minor faults, he was displeased and said, “Why bar men from office in an age of sage rule?” This, in turn, embodied the benevolence of Shun’s court in pardoning inadvertent errors. The one acted urgently against great wrongdoing; the other pardoned minor faults. Although their actions differed, how were their intentions ever at odds?

Drawing together the thoughts of many serves to broaden the benefits of loyal counsel. Thus Sima Guang posted a notice in his reception room, asking visitors to bring matters before the court through memorials and to correct his faults through letters. His intentions evidently accorded with those of Zhuge Kongming. Yet Li Wenjing often said that he had made no contribution while in office, except to reject all proposals concerning advantages and disadvantages submitted from within and outside the capital. This, in turn, followed Cao Can’s example of maintaining peace and stability. The one employed his approach to remedy disorder; the other…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
用之保泰時則殊矣而其忠何嘗有不一
以任官言之萊公之却例簿誠識體之言
也故曰宰相用人安用例若必例則一執
簿吏足矣若仲淹之圖上百官則以矯夷
簡之專耳不然豈以公之賢而踵光庭之
敝邪以事君言之文潞公復中書每侍對
而禮甚恭盖老臣之體也故曰某以耆舊
禮不得不恭若伊川為說書每侍講而色
甚莊則以任賓師之道耳不然豈以頤之
===
賢而昧孟軻氏之訓邪是則身之所履既
殊而道之所錯遂異亦惟其時義之當焉
耳且本之貞固既不至於狥人達之變通
又不至於失己是以公是公非與天下共
義好義惡惟皇極游卓然而立於君子之
塗也由此其選與故曰君子亦仁而已矣
何必同
第四問
畢鏘

禮不得不恭若伊川爲説書每侍講而色
甚莊則以任賓師之道耳不然豈以傾之
===
賢而昧孟軻氏之訓邪是則身之所履既
殊而道之所錯遂異亦惟其時義之當焉
耳且本之貞固既不至於徇人達之變通
又不至於失已是以公是公非與天下共
義好義惡惟皇極游卓然而立於君子之
塗也由此其選與故曰君子亦仁而已矣
何必同
第四問
畢鏘
punctuated:
用之保泰，時則殊矣，而其忠何嘗有不一？以任官言之，萊公之却例簿，誠識體之言也。故曰：「宰相用人，安用例？若必例，則一執簿吏足矣。」若仲淹之圖上百官，則以矯夷簡之專耳。不然，豈以公之賢而踵光庭之敝邪？以事君言之，文潞公復中書，每侍對而禮甚恭，盖老臣之體也。故曰：「某以耆舊，禮不得不恭。」若伊川為說書，每侍講而色甚莊，則以任賓師之道耳。不然，豈以頤之賢而昧孟軻氏之訓邪？是則身之所履既殊，而道之所錯遂異，亦惟其時義之當焉耳。且本之貞固，既不至於狥人；達之變通，又不至於失己。是以公是公非，與天下共；義好義惡，惟皇極游。卓然而立於君子之塗也，由此其選與？故曰：「君子亦仁而已矣，何必同？」

第四問
畢鏘
translation_en:
…the other employed it to preserve peace and prosperity. Their circumstances differed, but how could their loyalty ever have been other than one? Speaking of appointments to office, Duke Lai’s rejection of the register of precedents was indeed an expression of his understanding of the essential principles. Thus he said: “When a chief councilor appoints men, what use has he for precedents? If precedents must govern everything, a single clerk holding a register will suffice.” As for Zhongyan’s submitting a chart of the officials, this was simply to correct Yijian’s monopolization of authority. Otherwise, how could a man of his worth have perpetuated Guangting’s abuses?

Speaking of service to the ruler, when Duke Wen of Lu returned to the Secretariat, he observed the utmost reverence in his conduct whenever he attended an imperial audience. This befitted a veteran minister. Thus he said: “As an old and longstanding servant, I cannot but be reverent in my observance of ritual.” As for Yichuan, when he served as an Expositor, his expression was invariably solemn whenever he attended to lecture. This was simply because he undertook the proper role of an honored guest and teacher. Otherwise, how could Yi, with his worthiness, have failed to understand the teaching of Meng Ke?

Thus, when the circumstances in which one acts differ, the application of the Way accordingly differs: what matters is simply that it accord with what is right at that time. Moreover, by grounding oneself in steadfast rectitude, one avoids merely accommodating others; by extending this through adaptation to changing circumstances, one also avoids losing oneself. Hence one shares with all under Heaven an impartial judgment of right and wrong; in approving and disapproving according to righteousness, one moves solely within the Supreme Standard. To stand resolutely upon the gentleman’s path—is this the means by which one becomes outstanding [?]? Thus it is said: “The gentleman need only be benevolent. Why must gentlemen be alike?”

Fourth Question
Bi Qiang

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
相推而禮行焉盖至周而大備故曰周禮
其禮儀威儀三千三百所以品節民用而
錯綜官常者則曰儀禮二者聖人之經也
至于禮記則或錄舊禮之文或述變禮之
由而其中又多儀禮之疏義故特謂之傳
是三禮者果何自而傳哉自夫河洛效靈
圖書象出鳳鳥秘瑞刪述功成聖人經世
之具已萃於六經之文矣然韓起聘魯見
易象春秋始嘆周禮之在魯孟子論王制
===
謂諸侯去籍泊至於秦商鞅棄禮法典籍大
壞則禮經之缺在春秋戰國已然而不特
灰於秦政之烈矣天右斯文漢除挾律於
是遺書間出而魯高堂生傳儀禮十七篇
與古文經出淹中者篇目相合然皆止於
士大夫禮其朝覲會同郊祀大饗遂逸而
莫攷河間獻王購集所得諸禮凡百三十
篇獨周禮晚出李氏獻之秘府然五官僅
存而冬官遂逸厥後戴德刪八十五為大

punctuated: 相推而禮行焉，盖至周而大備，故曰《周禮》。其禮儀威儀三千三百，所以品節民用而錯綜官常者，則曰《儀禮》。二者，聖人之經也。至于《禮記》，則或錄舊禮之文，或述變禮之由，而其中又多《儀禮》之疏義，故特謂之傳。是三禮者，果何自而傳哉？自夫河洛效靈，圖書象出，鳳鳥秘瑞，刪述功成，聖人經世之具已萃於六經之文矣。然韓起聘魯，見《易》象、《春秋》，始嘆周禮之在魯。孟子論王制，謂諸侯去籍。泊至於秦，商鞅棄禮法，典籍大壞，則禮經之缺在春秋戰國已然，而不特灰於秦政之烈矣。天右斯文，漢除挾律，於是遺書間出，而魯高堂生傳《儀禮》十七篇，與古文經出淹中者篇目相合。然皆止於士大夫禮，其朝覲、會同、郊祀、大饗，遂逸而莫攷。河間獻王購集所得諸禮凡百三十篇，獨《周禮》晚出，李氏獻之秘府。然五官僅存，而冬官遂逸。厥後戴德刪八十五為大
translation_en:
…Through mutual deference, ritual was put into practice. It reached its full development under the Zhou; hence the title Rites of Zhou (Zhou li). The three thousand and three hundred rules of ritual observance and dignified deportment, which regulate the people’s activities and coordinate the established duties of officials, are called the Ceremonies and Rites (Yi li). These two are classics of the sages. As for the Record of Rites (Li ji), some passages record the texts of ancient rites, while others explain the reasons for changes in ritual. Much of it also elucidates the meaning of the Ceremonies and Rites; hence it is specifically designated a commentary. How, then, were these Three Ritual Texts transmitted?

From the time when the Yellow River and the Luo River manifested their numinous power, the Chart and the Writing emerged in figured forms, and the phoenix displayed mysterious auspicious signs [?], the work of editing and exposition was brought to completion, and the sages’ instruments for ordering the world were gathered into the texts of the Six Classics. Yet only when Han Qi visited Lu on a diplomatic mission and saw the images of the Changes and the Spring and Autumn Annals did he exclaim that the rites of Zhou were preserved in Lu. When Mencius discussed royal institutions, he said that the feudal lords had removed the records. By the time of Qin [?], Shang Yang had discarded ritual regulations, and the canonical records had suffered great destruction. Thus the ritual classics were already incomplete in the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods; they were not reduced to ashes solely by the ferocity of Qin rule.

Heaven protected this cultural tradition. The Han abolished the law prohibiting possession of books, and surviving writings then appeared from time to time. Master Gaotang of Lu transmitted seventeen chapters of the Ceremonies and Rites, whose chapter titles matched those of the ancient-script classic recovered at Yanzhong. Yet these dealt only with the rites of gentlemen and great officers. The rites for court audiences, interstate meetings and assemblies, suburban sacrifices, and great ceremonial feasts were consequently lost and could no longer be investigated. The various ritual texts acquired and collected by Prince Xian of Hejian amounted to 130 chapters. The Rites of Zhou alone appeared late, when a member of the Li family presented it to the imperial repository. However, only the sections on five offices survived; the Office of Winter had been lost. Subsequently, Dai De abridged the material to eighty-five chapters to form the Greater …

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
戴禮戴聖刪四十六為小戴記而馬融傳
小戴之學足以明堂月令等篇共為四十
九是為禮記鄭玄受馬融之學為三禮疎
先王典章煩縟之數各有訓攷而離經殆
合矣此漢儒傳經之畧也且周官之考工
記不類經文儀禮之王朝禮又多遺缺聖
人經世之大典鬱而弗明是以漢武以為
黷亂不經何休以為六國陰謀世莫有傳之
者獨劉歆知其為周公致太平之迹乃用
===
之以輔莽唐太宗知其為聖人之作乃不
能用之以致治他尚何說哉至于韓愈大
賢亦苦儀禮之難讀而謂今誠無所用則
禮經之不行盖自劉歆輩誣之而不獨壞
於王安石棄經之失矣逮于有宋諸儒輩
出篤信遺經講明理學淳熙有俞廷椿復
古之編嘉熙有王次點補遺之作丘葵訂
二家以為成書吳澂集三禮以為考註其
羽翼之功固皆有可言者而大儒朱熹則

二家以為成書吳澂集禮以為考註其
羽翼之功固皆有可言者而大儒朱熹則
punctuated:
戴禮，戴聖刪四十六為小戴記，而馬融傳小戴之學，足以明堂月令等篇，共為四十九，是為禮記。鄭玄受馬融之學，為三禮疎，先王典章煩縟之數，各有訓攷，而離經殆合矣。此漢儒傳經之畧也。且周官之考工記不類經文，儀禮之王朝禮又多遺缺，聖人經世之大典鬱而弗明，是以漢武以為黷亂不經，何休以為六國陰謀，世莫有傳之者。獨劉歆知其為周公致太平之迹，乃用之以輔莽；唐太宗知其為聖人之作，乃不能用之以致治，他尚何說哉？至于韓愈大賢，亦苦儀禮之難讀，而謂今誠無所用，則禮經之不行，盖自劉歆輩誣之，而不獨壞於王安石棄經之失矣。

逮于有宋，諸儒輩出，篤信遺經，講明理學。淳熙有俞廷椿復古之編，嘉熙有王次點補遺之作，丘葵訂二家以為成書，吳澂集三禮以為考註，其羽翼之功，固皆有可言者。而大儒朱熹則
translation_en:
…Dai’s Rites. Dai Sheng abridged the material to forty-six chapters, forming the Younger Dai’s Record. Ma Rong transmitted the Younger Dai’s learning and supplemented it with chapters on the Hall of Enlightenment, the Monthly Ordinances, and others, bringing the total to forty-nine. This became the Record of Rites. Zheng Xuan received Ma Rong’s learning and wrote subcommentaries on the Three Ritual Classics. The intricate particulars of the former kings’ institutions and regulations each received explanations and investigation, and the scattered classics were nearly reunited. Such, in outline, was the Han scholars’ transmission of the classics.

Moreover, the Record of Artificers in the Offices of Zhou does not resemble the text of the classic, while the Ceremonies and Rites has many omissions in its rites for the royal court. The sages’ great canon for ordering the world thus remained obscured and unclear. Consequently, Emperor Wu of Han considered it confused and contrary to canonical norms, and He Xiu regarded it as a conspiracy of the Six States; no one in the world transmitted it. Liu Xin alone recognized it as a record of how the Duke of Zhou brought about supreme peace, yet used it to assist Wang Mang. Emperor Taizong of Tang knew it to be the work of a sage, yet could not use it to achieve good government. What more can be said of others? Even so worthy a man as Han Yu found the Ceremonies and Rites difficult to read and said that it truly had no use in his own day. Thus, the failure to put the ritual classics into practice originated in their misrepresentation by Liu Xin and his like; their undoing was not solely due to Wang Anshi’s error in discarding the classic.

With the advent of the Song, Confucian scholars emerged in succession, firmly believing in the surviving classics and elucidating the learning of principle. During the Chunxi era, Yu Tingchun compiled his Restoration of Antiquity; during the Jiaxi era, Wang Cidian [?] wrote his Supplement to Omissions. Qiu Kui revised the works of these two scholars into a finished book, and Wu Cheng brought together the Three Ritual Classics to produce his critical annotations. Their contributions in supporting the classics certainly all merit discussion. As for the great Confucian scholar Zhu Xi, he…

脩復王朝等禮，以喪祭二禮付門人黄幹紹成之，其書曰《通解》。汪克寛又因其成法為補逸，於是千載不完之書賴以彙稡，而群疑亦定矣。此宋儒衛經之畧也。雖然，傳經者傳其文也。昔之言漢儒者曰：「註疏出而經義晦。」則傳經者既不免有病經之虞。衛經者衛其道也。昔之言宋儒者曰：「議論多而成功少。」則衛經者亦未必致用經之效。是以真儒不見，而帝王之治寥乎未之聞也。
天啓聖明，大昌景運。祖宗建極，表章六經，一道德以同風，定章程以作士。百七十餘年以來，鴻儒碩學作楨王國，而經生學士亦皆褒然抱藝以求實用。猗歟盛哉！顧愚竊有見焉。朱子曰：「六經之道同歸，而禮樂之用為急。」故其在當時有修復三禮劄疏，惓惓懇懇，篤具陳於上，而不
translation_en:
…restored the rites of the royal court and other rites, entrusting the two sections on mourning and sacrifice to his disciple Huang Gan to continue and complete. The resulting book was called Comprehensive Explanations (Tongjie). Wang Kekuan then followed its established method to supplement its omissions. Thus a work that had remained incomplete for a thousand years was brought together and compiled, and the many uncertainties were also resolved. Such, in outline, were the Song Confucians’ efforts to defend the classics. Nevertheless, those who transmit the classics transmit their wording. Someone once said of the Han Confucians: “When commentaries and subcommentaries appeared, the meaning of the classics became obscure.” Thus those who transmit the classics cannot escape the risk of impairing them. Those who defend the classics defend their Way. Someone once said of the Song Confucians: “They offered much discussion but achieved little.” Thus those who defend the classics may not necessarily succeed in putting them into practice. For this reason, true Confucians have not appeared, and scarcely anything has been heard of government like that of the ancient sage emperors and kings.
Heaven has brought forth our sagely and enlightened rulers, greatly advancing this glorious age. The imperial ancestors established the supreme standard, honored and elucidated the Six Classics, unified moral teaching to bring customs into accord, and established regulations to cultivate scholars. For more than 170 years, eminent Confucians and profound scholars have served as pillars of the realm, while students of the classics and men of learning have all confidently brought forth their accomplishments in pursuit of practical application. Ah, how flourishing it is! Yet I, in my ignorance, venture to offer an observation. Master Zhu said: “The Ways of the Six Classics converge upon the same end, but putting rites and music into practice is most urgent.” Accordingly, in his own day he submitted memoranda and memorials on restoring the Three Ritual Classics, earnestly and sincerely laying the matter fully before the throne [?], but did not…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
獲行盖真儒衞道之功固有待於
今日禮樂盛明之世
皇上以天縱之資邁日新之德履中樂和會道
器於一身明天察地貫性命而成則是於
王朝享覲大禮固已兼統而會萃之矣若夫
民風士俗古鄉三物之禮所以養其德性
而秩之倫彝者似猶未淪浹於海宇豈三
禮之訓未盡昭布邪執事倘不以愚言為
狂即以朱子之意上徹
===

生皆獲誦習聖經之全以觀
盛世之化將見敷錫之下因聖人之遺經而
務求聖人之至意因聖人之至意而務得
性命之全體下以率訓於
皇極上以弼治於太和俾諸儒衞翼之功獲收
實用而我
列聖表章之制一惟
皇上統總而大成之不其偉與若夫會通彙粹

punctuated: 獲行。盖真儒衞道之功，固有待於今日禮樂盛明之世。皇上以天縱之資，邁日新之德，履中樂和，會道器於一身，明天察地，貫性命而成則，是於王朝享覲大禮，固已兼統而會萃之矣。若夫民風士俗，古鄉三物之禮，所以養其德性而秩之倫彝者，似猶未淪浹於海宇，豈三禮之訓未盡昭布邪？執事倘不以愚言為狂，即以朱子之意上徹聖明，折衷全禮，彙為一經，分列科試，俾海隅鯫生皆獲誦習聖經之全，以觀盛世之化。將見敷錫之下，因聖人之遺經而務求聖人之至意，因聖人之至意而務得性命之全體，下以率訓於皇極，上以弼治於太和，俾諸儒衞翼之功獲收實用，而我列聖表章之制，一惟皇上統總而大成之，不其偉與？若夫會通彙粹
translation_en:
…put into effect. Indeed, the work of true Confucian scholars in defending the Way has awaited this present age, resplendent in rites and music. His Majesty, endowed by Heaven, advances in virtue renewed each day, practices the Mean and delights in harmony, and unites the Way and its concrete manifestations in his own person. Understanding Heaven and discerning Earth, he comprehends human nature and destiny and establishes standards. Thus, the great court rites of offerings and audiences have already been comprehensively integrated and brought together. As for popular customs and the habits of scholars, however, the ancient district rites of the three categories of instruction, which nurtured people's moral nature and ordered their enduring human relationships, seem not yet to have permeated the realm. Could this be because the teachings of the Three Ritual Classics have not been fully made known?
If you, sir, do not regard my humble words as wild presumption, convey Zhu Xi's intention to His Majesty's sagely understanding: critically reconcile the complete body of ritual writings, compile them into a single classic, and arrange them as distinct subjects for examination. Then even humble students in the remotest coastal regions may recite and study the sacred classics in their entirety and witness the transforming influence of this flourishing age. We shall then see those receiving this widely bestowed instruction strive, through the classics bequeathed by the sages, to grasp the sages' deepest meaning, and through that deepest meaning strive to apprehend human nature and destiny in their entirety. Below, they will follow the instruction of the August Ultimate; above, they will assist government in achieving Supreme Harmony. Thus the protective and sustaining efforts of the Confucian scholars will yield practical results, while the institutions through which our successive sage emperors honored and elucidated the classics will be comprehensively united and brought to full fruition by His Majesty alone. Would this not be magnificent? As for comprehensively integrating these teachings and gathering their finest elements…

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
謹之於事定之後者也盖先事而不定則
失之疎臨事而不决則失之懾後事而不
慮則失之玩以是而處常且猶不免於撥
患而况於制狄哉故曰毋恃其不來恃吾
有以待之是智勇而嚴之說也請因明問
而敢陳之夫夷狄之患自古有之雖以殷
周之盛亦所未免顧其撻伐之威以翼商
邑而服諸侯者為之地而其順治威嚴之
治乃所以成薄伐之績也自漢以還叛服
===
不常則有可疑矣盖高文盛時皆屡厪於
應虜而宣元之間漢幾頓矣而虜乃稱臣
焉是其狡啓於治朝非吾力之不足也彼
之勢趨於強也獻忱於季世非吾力之有
餘也彼之勢趨於弱也迄唐而宋勢且寝
長盖至胡元而極矣
天啓我
明
太祖高皇帝一起而殲之殆盡

===
不常則有可疑矣蓋高文盛時皆屢壓於
應虜而宣元之間漢幾頓矣而虜乃稱臣
焉是其狡啓於治朝非吾力之不足也彼
之勢趨於強也獻忱於季世非吾力之有
餘也彼之勢趨於弱也迄唐而宋勢且寖
長蓋至胡元而極矣

明
太祖高皇帝一起而殲之殆盡
punctuated:
謹之於事定之後者也。盖先事而不定，則失之疎；臨事而不决，則失之懾；後事而不慮，則失之玩。以是而處常，且猶不免於撥患，而况於制狄哉？故曰：「毋恃其不來，恃吾有以待之。」是智勇而嚴之說也。請因明問而敢陳之。
夫夷狄之患，自古有之。雖以殷周之盛，亦所未免。顧其撻伐之威，以翼商邑而服諸侯者，為之地；而其順治威嚴之治，乃所以成薄伐之績也。自漢以還，叛服不常，則有可疑矣。盖高文盛時，皆屡厪於應虜；而宣元之間，漢幾頓矣，而虜乃稱臣焉。是其狡啓於治朝，非吾力之不足也，彼之勢趨於強也；獻忱於季世，非吾力之有餘也，彼之勢趨於弱也。迄唐而宋，勢且寝長，盖至胡元而極矣。
天啓我明，太祖高皇帝一起而殲之殆盡。
translation_en:
…and exercising caution after affairs have been settled. For failure to settle matters beforehand is an error of negligence; failure to decide when confronting events is an error of timidity; and failure to give thought afterward is an error of carelessness. Even in ordinary circumstances, proceeding thus would leave one unable to avoid troubles [?]; how much more so when restraining the Di! Thus it is said: “Do not rely on their not coming; rely on our having the means to await them.” This expresses what is meant by wisdom, courage, and strict vigilance. In response to your discerning question, I venture to set forth my views.
The troubles caused by the Yi and Di have existed since antiquity. Even Yin and Zhou at the height of their prosperity could not escape them. Yet the might of their punitive campaigns, which protected the Shang capital and brought the feudal lords into submission, provided the foundation; and their orderly government and stern authority enabled them to achieve success in those campaigns. From the Han onward, however, the alternation between rebellion and submission presents grounds for doubt. In the flourishing reigns of Gaozu and Wendi, both rulers were repeatedly burdened with responding to the enemy. Yet in the time of Xuandi and Yuandi, when the Han had nearly fallen into decline, the enemy instead professed allegiance as subjects. Their treachery arose under well-governed courts not because our strength was insufficient, but because their power was growing. They offered professions of loyalty in a dynasty’s declining age not because our strength was more than sufficient, but because their power was weakening. Through the Tang and into the Song, their power gradually increased, reaching its height under the alien Yuan.
Heaven inaugurated our Ming. Taizu, the Gao Emperor, rose and all but annihilated them.

title: 嘉靖二十三年會試錄
text:
成祖文皇帝又從而三犁其庭斯時也非不可
翦此而後朝食也然而
皇仁天覆假之喙息乃今孽遺滋蔓擾我邊陲
賴我
皇上聰明神武上繼
二聖祖之烈赫然而
命將出師設總督之憲臣以一其權擇專閫之
虎帥以董其旅司農之錢穀支發不貲司
空之軍器申飭必再其所以惓惓於制虜
===
者盖已計之定而裁之決矣是以
聖武布昭邊鄙不聳者已再易年第戎心叵測
出沒靡常則撤備而不虞與備之而勞費
誠有如執事之所慮者也顧今日之勢以
守為戰即勞且費亦有不得而惜者何也
愚所謂嚴之之說是也且昔蘇洵亦嘗曰
凡戰之道未戰養其力將戰養其氣既戰
養其財夫既戰矣可以無事矣而猶欲養
其財豈非嚴為之備以守而為戰也乎夫
